albums.albumStory: By the late 1980s Bob Dylan was widely seen as creatively adrift, and on Bono's recommendation he turned to producer Daniel Lanois, decamping to a converted New Orleans house in spring 1989 to record with a loose Louisiana crew of session players. Lanois built a swampy, reverberant sonic world of tremolo guitars and distant percussion around Dylan's songs, and the sessions were famously tense, the two clashing over arrangements even as they drew strong performances from one another. The material ranks among Dylan's strongest of the era, from the apocalyptic 'Political World' and noir-tinged 'Man In The Long Black Coat' to the world-weary 'Most Of The Time' and hymn-like 'Ring Them Bells' and 'What Good Am I?', with 'Everything Is Broken' supplying blues grit. Dylan later devoted a lengthy chapter of his memoir Chronicles: Volume One to the sessions, including regret that outtakes like 'Series of Dreams' and 'Dignity' didn't make the final cut. Critics greeted the album as an unambiguous comeback, the first Dylan record in a decade discussed alongside his classic 1960s-70s work, restoring his standing as a songwriter at a pivotal moment. Its atmospheric, weathered production directly foreshadowed the Lanois-produced Time Out of Mind (1997) and the acclaimed late-career run that followed, making it a foundational record of Dylan's third act.
albums.lpNotes: 2020 MoFi 45 RPM numbered reissue (edition of 4,000) - MFSL 2-488 with 'Kw@MoFi' (Krieg Wunderlich) etched in all four runouts, RTI pressing, Gain 2 Ultra Analog cut; not an original Columbia pressing.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show MoFi's standard matte-black design with the orange/red 'Mobile Fidelity Sound Lab' rim band, script MoFi logo, GAIN 2 Ultra Analog badge, STEREO arrow, and a single small licensed Columbia 'walking eye' box - one logo, not a Columbia-branded label. The dual copyright line '© 1989, 2018 Columbia Records...Manufactured for Mobile Fidelity Sound Lab, Inc. by Sony Music Entertainment' documents the Sony license governing MoFi's Dylan reissue series from this era. This is MoFi's Sebastopol Gain 2 Ultra Analog period, when Sony-catalog titles were plated and pressed at RTI as numbered 4,000-copy 45 RPM sets. Only one MoFi vinyl variant of this title exists, so the label design and runout etchings fully settle provenance; it sits as a licensed audiophile reissue rather than any Columbia-label pressing in the title's broader hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Krieg Wunderlich (assisted by Shawn R. Britton) at MoFi's Sebastopol facility on the Gain 2 Ultra Analog system and pressed at RTI, among the quietest 180g US pressings available. Spreading the ten tracks over four 45 RPM sides gives Lanois's swamp-reverb production noticeably more air, low-end weight and longer ambient decay than the 1989 Columbia LP or early CD issues. Steve Hoffman forum consensus is strongly favorable toward the drums, bass and atmosphere on this cut, with only scattered reports of non-fill defects on some RTI copies. As with other 2015-2022 MoFi titles, a DSD256 digital step reportedly sat between tape and lacquer, so this is a high-resolution-sourced rather than pure-analog cut. It sits at the top of the album's fidelity hierarchy alongside MoFi's companion SACD, well ahead of the original Columbia LP and later Sony represses, with no Analogue Productions, One-Step, or comparable audiophile rival for this title.
albums.generalNotes: 2020 Mobile Fidelity Sound Lab MFSL 2-488 - numbered limited-edition 45 RPM double LP, licensed from Sony/Columbia rather than an original Columbia pressing. Runouts MFSL 2-488 Ar3/Br2/Cr2/Dr2 carry 'Kw@MoFi' (Krieg Wunderlich; the collector's 'KEVIN@MOFI' transcription is a misread) and lacquer numbers 33249/32943, matching the single known Discogs variant for this title. Silver MoFi banner jacket, the rear 'Limited Edition of 4,000' line, and the hand-numbered box confirm the standard numbered retail edition rather than a promo or test pressing. The original US Columbia LP dates to September 1989; only one MoFi vinyl variant exists, leaving no ambiguity about pressing identity.

albums.albumStory: Charles Earland, the Philadelphia-born Hammond B-3 organist known as "The Mighty Burner," built his reputation fusing hard-bop technique with blues, gospel, and funk grooves aimed squarely at the dancing club audience. Living Black! captures him leading a hot, tightly-drilled band before a packed house at Newark's Key Club on September 17, 1970, arriving on the heels of the successful Black Talk! and Black Drops, which had already established him as one of Prestige's most commercially exciting soul-jazz artists. Remarkably, the band was barely rehearsed as a unit: trumpeter Gary Chandler had joined only three days before the date, and Grover Washington Jr. stepped in on tenor as a last-minute replacement, yet the performance is completely unified and confident throughout. The original Key Club Cookout and the contemporary radio hit Westbound #9 set a driving, celebratory tone, while extended readings of Benny Golson's Killer Joe and Miles Davis's Milestones tie the record's dance-floor energy back to modern jazz repertoire. The nearly fifteen-minute Killer Joe stands out as an important early recorded spotlight for Washington shortly before his emergence as a major solo star in his own right. The album was warmly received by critics and fans alike and reached the lower rungs of the Billboard LP chart, and it remains one of the defining live documents of early-1970s soul-jazz and a high point of Earland's prolific Prestige run.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (stereo, 1971) - US purple top-logo Bergenfield label; stamped VAN GELDER both sides.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries Prestige's purple/violet stereo label: a circled trident logo with PRESTIGE STEREO at 12 o'clock and the full PRESTIGE RECORDS INC., 203 S. WASHINGTON AVE., BERGENFIELD, N.J. rim text. The Bergenfield address dates to 1958, but this purple top-logo design belongs to the label's final design phase just before Fantasy's 1971 acquisition of Prestige. For a new 10000-series title issued in 1971, this Bergenfield-address, purple-label configuration matches the initial US issue rather than the later 1976-era P-10009 reissue series. The typed runouts show stamped VAN GELDER on both sides, confirming original Rudy Van Gelder lacquer lineage consistent with Discogs' documented PRST 10009 A/B matrix family; a green top-logo variant also circulated in this era, so the exact sequencing of purple vs. green survivors is not fully settled, but this is the canonical original RVG configuration.
albums.fidelity: Rudy Van Gelder recorded the Key Club performance and cut the lacquers, with stamped VAN GELDER present in both typed runouts, confirming original mastering lineage. The purple-label US original is the fidelity benchmark for this title: full-bodied and dynamic, with convincing club ambience and a wide, engaging soundstage, though it remains a live remote recording rather than a polished studio production, so surface noise and room bleed are inherent to the source. Discogs owner comments single out this pressing's rich, room-filling sound, though no substantial Steve Hoffman forum shootout thread was found comparing pressings. No pressing-plant identifier was transcribed here beyond the era-typical US Prestige manufacture. Later US P-10009 and overseas reissues (France, South Africa) have thinner documented mastering provenance, and no Tone Poet, Analogue Productions, Music Matters, Mobile Fidelity, or comparable audiophile vinyl reissue of this title is known to exist, leaving this original as the top of the fidelity hierarchy.
albums.generalNotes: 1971 Prestige PRST 10009 stereo - original US first-pressing configuration. The purple top-logo labels carry the 203 S. Washington Ave., Bergenfield rim text, matching the back jacket's Prestige Records Inc. credit line. The typed deadwax transcriptions show stamped VAN GELDER on both sides, the decisive original-lacquer marker for this release. This copy shows standard retail labels and jacket with no promo markings. Released in 1971.

albums.title: The Night of the Cookers - Live at Club La Marchal, Volume 1
albums.musicians: Freddie Hubbard (trumpet), Lee Morgan (trumpet), James Spaulding (alto sax, flute), Harold Mabern Jr. (piano), Larry Ridley (bass), Pete La Roca (drums), Big Black (congas)
sides: 1. Pensativa (Clare Fischer)
1. Walkin' (R. Carpenter)
albums.albumStory: Recorded live on April 9-10, 1965 at Club La Marchal in Brooklyn, The Night of the Cookers documents one of hard bop's great trumpet summits: Freddie Hubbard, then 27 and fresh off his early Blue Note breakthroughs, matched against Lee Morgan, his closest rival among the era's young trumpet stars. The date arose from 'Just Us,' a Brooklyn jazz-appreciation circle of young women (including wives of Hubbard, Cedar Walton and Billy Higgins) devoted to promoting the music and giving it a home at the club. Hubbard brought his working quintet of Spaulding, Mabern, Ridley and La Roca, augmenting it with Morgan and conguero Big Black for the occasion. Volume 1 rests on two extended performances: Clare Fischer's Latin-tinged 'Pensativa,' which became a Hubbard signature, and Richard Carpenter's blues-drenched 'Walkin',' a hard-driving vehicle for trumpet trading. Issued across two volumes in 1965-66, the set captures the tail end of Blue Note's golden club-recording era and stands as a career highlight for both trumpeters. It remains widely regarded by critics as one of the finest live hard bop documents of its time, prized above all for the ferocious Hubbard-Morgan interplay.
albums.lpNotes: 2nd press (stereo, c. 1966-70) - Blue Note 'A Division of Liberty Records' blue/white label; Van Gelder stamp in dead wax = East Coast pressing from original Van Gelder metal.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the blue-and-white 'BLUE NOTE RECORDS - A DIVISION OF LIBERTY RECORDS, INC.' label visible in the photos, the design Blue Note adopted after Liberty's mid-1966 acquisition and used through 1970 (per LondonJazzCollector's Liberty-era labelography). The upper-and-lower-case 'Side 1'/'Side 2' typesetting matches Keystone Printed Specialties label stock, Blue Note's original East Coast printer, versus Bert-Co's all-caps West Coast 'SIDE' printing seen on other Liberty pressings. That points to East Coast manufacture using original Van Gelder metal shipped by Liberty, consistent with the VAN GELDER stamp reported in the runouts. This places the copy squarely in the second-tier Liberty reissue window (c.1966-70), after the 1965 NY USA first pressing but sonically descended from the same lacquer.
albums.fidelity: This East Coast Liberty pressing was stamped from Rudy Van Gelder's original metal, so the cut itself is the genuine RVG master, and collectors on Steve Hoffman forums and LondonJazzCollector rate these Keystone-labeled Liberty copies well above the West Coast Research Craft re-masters (Bert-Co labels, no Van Gelder stamp) and later Capitol/United Artists-era reissues. The source material is Orville O'Brien's remote club recording, with Van Gelder handling only re-recording and mastering, so the sound is energetic and lively but somewhat raw compared to a proper Van Gelder studio date. In the title's fidelity hierarchy this pressing sits just below the 1965 NY USA stereo original (same metal lineage but earlier stampers) and above non-Van Gelder reissues, with Japanese King/Toshiba cuts as the main vintage alternative.
albums.generalNotes: Blue Note BST 84207 stereo, Liberty-era US reissue (c. 1966-70), not the 1965 NY USA first pressing. Decisive evidence: blue/white 'A Division of Liberty Records, Inc.' labels (post-1966 acquisition design), Keystone-style 'Side 1/2' typesetting indicating East Coast label stock, and the VAN GELDER stamp in the runouts confirming pressing from original Van Gelder metal. The Liberty 'First Family of Recorded Entertainment' company inner sleeve is consistent with this era. The typed runout numbers ('84208'/'84028') appear to be transcription slips, as the labels clearly print BNST 84207-A / 84207-B.

albums.albumStory: All That Was East Is West Of Me Now is Glen Hansard's fifth solo album and his first in four years, born from an unusually public writing process: over five Tuesdays in November 2022 he road-tested new songs before an unassuming crowd in the back room of a small west Dublin pub, believing a song is only completed once it has been witnessed. The record was then tracked quickly and intuitively at longtime collaborator David Odlum's home studio outside Dublin, with a band drawn largely from the circle around Hansard's long-running band The Frames. Hansard first found fame fronting The Frames, then reached a global audience via The Swell Season with Markéta Irglová and the film Once, whose song 'Falling Slowly' won the Academy Award for Best Original Song. The title reflects a fifty-something artist's sense that there is more behind him than ahead, yet the eight songs favor endurance and grace over regret, running from the sprawling opener 'The Feast Of St John' through a theremin-tinged mid-album stretch to the closing pairing of the defiant 'Bearing Witness' and the mortality-facing 'Short Life.' Musically it is his most rock-oriented, band-driven statement since The Frames' Burn the Maps era, weaving Irish folk roots and orchestral color into the loose communal energy of his live shows. Critics responded warmly, praising its emotional candor and the lived-in, unpolished feel of its songs.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (2023) - US Anti- standard black vinyl retail edition; custom dark/light lunar-photograph art labels (no logos or rim text), '87976-1' printed on both labels, deadwax etched 'EPITAPH 87976-1 A/B'.
albums.labelNotes: Both sides use a fully custom, full-bleed greyscale 'lunar surface' art-photo label with no manufacturer logo, address, rim text, or arc band anywhere on the printed surface - Side A is a dark/shadowed version with white tracklist and a red 'A', Side B a bleached/overexposed version with red tracklist and a black 'B'; '87976-1' is printed in small type at the bottom of both. Since Anti- has issued only this one vinyl configuration (black standard plus a clear indie-exclusive using identical label art) since the 20 October 2023 release, there is no evolving label-era timeline to place this against - the design itself is definitive proof of authenticity for this catalog number rather than a marker of pressing order. The absence of any 'TCL' sticker or clear vinyl confirms this is the standard black retail pressing, first in the hierarchy alongside its European twin.
albums.fidelity: Produced and mixed by David Odlum, almost certainly cut from high-resolution digital masters with no separately credited vinyl mastering engineer. As the only vinyl mastering that exists for this album (shared by the black standard and clear indie-exclusive editions), it stands as the reference pressing by default, with no vintage original or audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, etc.) to rank it against. Epitaph/Anti- pressings of this era are generally quiet and competently cut, and the dense rock-with-strings production translates reasonably well to vinyl, though some buyer reports note surface noise/manufacturing issues on certain copies. No meaningful Steve Hoffman forum consensus has emerged yet given the album's recency.
albums.generalNotes: 2023 Anti- 87976-1 - original (and to date only) black vinyl pressing, released 20 October 2023. The labels carry no manufacturer text or logo, only the lunar-photograph art and '87976-1' at the bottom of each side, identical in layout to the limited clear edition, so labels alone do not distinguish color variants. The US UPC 045778797615 on the jacket confirms the US retail edition versus the European Proper Music pressing (UPC 8714092797619), and the deadwax etching (collector transcribed 'EPITAH', properly 'EPITAPH' 87976-1 A/B, Epitaph/Anti-'s standard etched prefix) matches the verified matrix for this catalog number. This is the common black-vinyl configuration, not the limited indie-exclusive clear edition (87976-1TCL sticker).

albums.albumStory: Didn't He Ramble, released in September 2015, is Glen Hansard's second solo studio album, arriving three years after his solo debut Rhythm and Repose. Hansard had already built a long career fronting the Dublin band The Frames before an unexpected second act: starring in the 2007 film Once, whose song "Falling Slowly" won the Academy Award for Best Original Song, and touring internationally as half of the duo The Swell Season. For this record he worked with co-producers Thomas Bartlett (Doveman) and David Odlum, framing his weathered, generous voice in folk arrangements colored by horns and strings, recorded across sessions in New York, France, Chicago, and Dublin, with guest vocals from Iron & Wine's Sam Beam and Sam Amidon. The songs function as a loose set of traveler's meditations on endurance, gratitude, and staying the course, with titles like "Winning Streak," "Her Mercy," "Lowly Deserter," and "McCormack's Wall" (a nod to Irish tenor John McCormack) blending contemporary Dublin songwriting with old-time Appalachian textures. Critics responded warmly to its warmth and craft, and the album earned a Grammy nomination for Best Folk Album, cementing Hansard's standing as a distinct solo voice apart from both The Frames' rock intensity and the hushed duets of the Once era.
albums.lpNotes: 2015 Anti- 87419-1 original-release-era pressing in apparent promo configuration (generic cream sleeve, hand-written titling) - RJ (Ryan Smith)/Sterling Sound lacquer signatures in the runout, identical metalwork to the retail editions.
albums.labelNotes: Both sides carry Anti-'s 2010s-era picture labels: side A shows a scratchy, high-contrast portrait graphic with a large printed 'A' and the catalog number 87419-1 at the rim; side B repeats the same portrait art but has the full A-side/B-side track listing printed directly on the label instead of a logo, a layout shared across this pressing's variants. Anti- Records, the Los Angeles sister label of Epitaph founded in 1999, has released Hansard's solo work since 2012's Rhythm and Repose, and its mid-2010s catalog runs in the five-digit 87xxx series with no address or rim-text era markers to date it further. There is no printed promo text on the labels themselves, so the promo designation for this copy rests on the plain, hand-annotated cream jacket, a configuration documented on Discogs as the 2015 US promo LP (only a handful logged). The runout signatures 'RJ' (Ryan Smith) and 'STERLING' match the retail pressings exactly, confirming this uses the original 2015 campaign metalwork rather than a later repress.
albums.fidelity: Lacquers were cut by Ryan Smith ('RJ') at Sterling Sound, who handled much of the Anti-/Epitaph vinyl catalog in this era, producing a clean, quiet, dynamic cut from the album's digital masters (tracked and mixed digitally across several studios). The retail 180g US black and European clear pressings share this identical RJ/Sterling metalwork, so this promo-configuration copy sits at the top of a shallow fidelity hierarchy, as there are no audiophile reissues, alternate cuts, or all-analog editions of this title. Collector commentary on Discogs describes the pressing as clean and dynamic with good clarity and separation, with no reported pressing-quality complaints.

albums.albumStory: Jay McShann was one of the last great links to Kansas City's swing-era heyday, a blues-drenched pianist and vocalist whose late-1930s orchestra gave the young Charlie Parker his first important bandstand and recording debut. Recorded at Atlantic's New York studios in August 1978, The Big Apple Bash was conceived as an all-star celebration of McShann's music, pairing veterans of his own era - Basie alumni Earle Warren, Doc Cheatham and Dicky Wells, plus bassist Milt Hinton - with younger admirers like Gerry Mulligan, Herbie Mann (here on tenor rather than his usual flute), Joe Morello, Connie Kay and a then up-and-coming John Scofield, all framed by Ernie Wilkins' big-band arrangements. The program revisits McShann touchstones, including 'Dickie's Dream,' the Basie flag-waver he co-wrote with Lester Young, and 'Jumpin' The Blues,' recreating the tune he first recorded with Parker. Manhattan Transfer's Janis Siegel drops in for a playful vocal duet on 'Ain't Misbehavin',' and McShann's weathered, rock-solid voice and two-fisted piano carry the session throughout. Liner notes by New York Times critic Robert Palmer frame the record as proof of the timelessness of McShann's music at a moment when Kansas City jazz was enjoying renewed attention. Critics received it warmly, and it stands as one of the strongest major-label showcases of McShann's late career, bridging classic Kansas City swing and the modern jazz mainstream.

BY ATLANTIC RECORDING CORP., 75 ROCKEFELLER PLAZA, N.Y., N.Y. / A WARNER COMMUNICATIONS COMPANY' rim text plus a (c) 1979 line - the standard Atlantic original-issue design used from roughly 1977-79, ahead of the revised label used on the 1982 reissue. This Rockefeller Plaza label plus RI plant code places the copy in the first 1979 pressing generation, on par with the other 1979 plant variants and ahead of the 1982 reissue.
albums.fidelity: Recorded and mixed by Bobby Warner and mastered by George Piros at Atlantic Recording Studios, New York, a clean, well-engineered late-1970s Atlantic analog production. The RI plant (Philips/PRC, Richmond, Indiana) pressed to Atlantic's usual solid late-70s standard, generally considered a notch below the Monarch and Presswell pressings some collectors prefer, though still a full-bodied, reasonably quiet cut. No audiophile reissue of this title exists (no Analogue Productions, Music Matters, or Speakers Corner edition), so a clean 1979 US original sits at the top of the album's fidelity hierarchy, with the 1982 reissue a step behind.

albums.albumStory: Country Soul (1962) came early in King Curtis's tenure at Capitol Records, a stop between his celebrated 1950s session work (Coasters, Chuck Willis, Clyde McPhatter) and the R&B chart breakthroughs he'd achieve later at Atco with 'Soul Serenade' and 'Memphis Soul Stew'. The concept - a saxophonist steeped in R&B and rock and roll tackling honky-tonk and Western standards like 'Your Cheatin' Heart,' 'Tennessee Waltz,' and 'Tumbling Tumbleweeds' alongside instrumental staples 'Raunchy' and 'High Noon' - reflected a period fascination among R&B artists with crossing genre lines for a broader pop audience. King Curtis, born Curtis Ousley in Fort Worth, Texas, had already built a reputation as one of the most influential saxophonists in rock and roll and R&B, having supplied the famous solo on the Coasters' 'Yakety Yak' and countless other hits as a first-call New York session man. His Capitol albums of this era, including Country Soul, were commercially modest compared to his 1960s Atco work but showcase his facility for melodic, blues-drenched improvisation applied to unlikely repertoire. The liner notes, contributed by NBA star Wilt Chamberlain (a Small's Paradise regular who knew Curtis from the Harlem club scene), speak to Curtis's reputation as a versatile, soulful bandstand performer capable of moving effortlessly between jazz, R&B, and pop idioms. While Country Soul itself remains a minor, largely overlooked entry in Curtis's discography, it illustrates the breadth of his musical curiosity in the years just before he became one of the most in-demand saxophonists in soul and rock, later backing Aretha Franklin, Sam Cooke, and the Rolling Stones' touring/session circles. Critically, the album is chiefly of interest to Curtis completists and country-soul crossover collectors rather than being considered a landmark in his catalog.

albums.albumStory: Everybody's Talkin' is a posthumous compilation assembled by Atco/Atlantic following King Curtis's murder in August 1971, gathering studio odds and ends, cover versions, and instrumental sides recorded during his final years as house bandleader and A&R man for Aretha Franklin and the Atlantic soul roster. Curtis, born Curtis Ousley, was one of soul music's defining tenor saxophonists, whose honking, vocal-toned solos powered hits from The Coasters to Aretha Franklin and whose own instrumental hits like "Soul Serenade" and "Memphis Soul Stew" made him a star in his own right. The tracks here find him reworking contemporary pop and soul staples - King Floyd's "Groove Me," Sly Stone's "You're The One," Stephen Stills's "Love The One You're With," Tim Hardin's "If I Were A Carpenter," and the Nilsson-popularized title cut - alongside originals like "Central Park" and "Wet Funk," backed by his working band the Kingpins and the Memphis Horns. The album captures the tail end of a career that helped define the Muscle Shoals/Atlantic soul-instrumental sound, bridging 1950s R&B saxophone tradition with early-1970s funk. Critically it was received as a minor, somewhat scattershot posthumous cash-in compared to his tighter late-60s/early-70s studio LPs, but it remains valued by collectors and soul-jazz enthusiasts for its stellar session personnel and Curtis's typically muscular, soulful playing. Its lasting legacy is less as a landmark statement than as a coda to one of the era's most influential session and bandleader careers, cut short at just 37.

albums.albumStory: King Curtis was already the era's most in-demand R&B saxophonist, a session ace behind the Coasters, the Shirelles and countless Atlantic dates, when Atco captured him fronting his own road band for a live date at Small's Paradise, the storied Harlem club, in the mid-1960s. The set is a tour of the mid-'60s soul-instrumental landscape - Curtis's own gritty originals like "Preach" and "Soul Theme" sit alongside covers of the day's dance and pop hits, Rufus Thomas's "Philly Dog," the Holland-Dozier-Holland-penned "Road Runner," Henry Mancini's "Peter Gunn," and a bristling reading of Bob Dylan's "Blowin' In The Wind." His touring band - Cornell Dupree on guitar, Melvin Lastie on cornet, Willie Bridges on baritone, Charles Rainey on bass and Ray Lucas on drums - was a tight, funky unit that would go on to seed the first-call New York soul-session scene of the following decade. The album stands as one of the era's definitive documents of black nightclub showmanship, capturing the call-and-response energy, honking solos and dance-floor immediacy that made Curtis's live shows legendary among musicians and audiences alike. It further cemented Curtis's reputation as a bridge figure between jazz, R&B and soul, and its loose, horn-driven grooves have been cited by generations of soul and funk revivalists as a touchstone of instrumental soul. Critically it has endured as a high point in Curtis's discography, valued as much for atmosphere and band chemistry as for individual solos.

Collectors on forums such as Steve Hoffman generally regard mid-60s Atlantic/ATCO in-house New York pressings as solid, warm, dynamic cuts, if occasionally limited by the boominess inherent to a nightclub live recording of the period. This stereo copy, being the first and only significant vinyl issue, sits at the top of the title's available fidelity hierarchy; the only alternative format is the contemporaneous mono LP, which club-soul purists sometimes prefer for a punchier, more unified horn sound, and later CD reissues, which are digitally remastered and generally rated as secondary to the original vinyl cut.

albums.albumStory: King Curtis, the Fort Worth-born tenor saxophonist who had already made his mark as a session player on hits like 'Yakety Yak,' built 'Soul Serenade' around his gift for turning familiar instrumental staples into greasy, danceable big-beat workouts. Rather than an album of new compositions, the set is a covers showcase - taking chart-proven instrumentals like 'Tequila,' 'Night Train,' 'Honky Tonk,' 'Java,' and 'Watermelon Man' and running them through Curtis's driving, vocalized tenor sound backed by a tight studio rhythm section. The title track, 'Soul Serenade,' co-written by Curtis with Luther Dixon, became one of his signature compositions and a much-covered soul standard in its own right. The album arrived at a pivotal moment in Curtis's career, as he was transitioning from jazz and R&B session work toward the funkier, dance-oriented instrumental sound that would define his mid-1960s Capitol output before his later, more celebrated Atlantic years fronting the Kingpins. Within the saxophone-instrumental genre that flourished on jukeboxes and in dance halls through the early-to-mid 1960s, Curtis was among its most reliable hitmakers, and this collection captures him at the height of that commercial run. It remains valued less as an artistic statement than as a solid, swinging document of the era's instrumental dance-music trend and of Curtis's own irresistible tone.

Collector discussion of 'Soul Serenade' centers more on scarcity and cover art than on sonics, and the mono mix is generally considered punchier and more focused than the rechanneled or true-stereo counterpart for this vintage of Capitol saxophone-instrumental LPs. Within this title's own fidelity hierarchy, this original 1964 mono Scranton pressing sits at the top, ahead of any later reissue pressings and well ahead of digital transfers.

albums.albumStory: King Curtis, born Curtis Ousley in Fort Worth, Texas, was one of the defining tenor saxophonists of R&B and early soul, celebrated for his "yakety" honking style heard on hits by the Coasters and countless New York session dates of the late 1950s. The tracks gathered here - "Soul Twist," "Big Dipper," "Camp Meetin'," "What'd I Say," and companions - stem from his early-1960s instrumental sax-combo recordings for Bobby Robinson's Harlem-based Enjoy/Tru-Sound labels, cut in the wake of his Prestige jazz dates and just before his mid-1960s Capitol and Atco/Atlantic years. "Soul Twist" itself was a genuine national hit, riding the twist-dance craze to the top of the R&B charts in 1962 and becoming one of Curtis's signature instrumentals. These sides capture Curtis at a pivotal, transitional moment - moving from raw honking rock and roll saxophone toward the funkier, groove-driven instrumental soul he would perfect later in the decade - and they helped cement the tenor sax as a lead voice in soul music rather than a mere backing texture. The music's blend of gospel-tinged organ grooves, twist-era backbeats, and Curtis's blistering solos made it a favorite on jukeboxes and in dance clubs, and it remains prized by soul and R&B collectors as some of Curtis's most purely danceable, unpretentious work. Critically, Curtis's catalog from this era is regarded as foundational to instrumental soul-jazz, bridging 1950s rock and roll sax and the Memphis/Muscle Shoals soul sound he would later champion as a bandleader and session ace for Aretha Franklin and others.

No deep groove is visible. Up Front was a subsidiary of Springboard International, a New Jersey/Los Angeles budget-reissue operation that recycled licensed masters (here, King Curtis's early-1960s Tru-Sound/Enjoy sax instrumentals) onto cheap repackaged LPs through the 1970s under a rotating cast of titles and covers. The Rahway, NJ address and this specific catalogue design place the pressing squarely in Springboard's mid-1970s budget-line output, not an original or first-issue pressing of any of the individual tracks.
albums.fidelity: The source masters are early-1960s mono studio recordings for Bobby Robinson's Enjoy/Tru-Sound operation; the "STEREO" billing on this Up Front pressing is very likely an electronic rechanneling job typical of Springboard International's budget reissue line rather than a true stereo master. Mastering and pressing quality on Springboard/Up Front product is generally utilitarian - thinner vinyl, minimal EQ care, and audible surface noise are common collector complaints (see general Springboard/Trip discussion on forums.stevehoffman.tv). Within the fidelity hierarchy for these King Curtis performances, the original Tru-Sound/Enjoy mono 45s and LP represent the closest, most faithful cut to the master tape; this Up Front stereo repackage sits well below that, and any later CD compilations sourced from cleaner tape transfers likely surpass it sonically as well.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in New York on April 25, 1961 for Prestige's short-lived Tru-Sound subsidiary, this LP is the only album on which King Curtis, otherwise renowned as the era's premier R&B/soul tenor and soprano saxophonist, stepped forward as a lead vocalist. Curtis had grown up steeped in Texas church singing and the sound of blues shouters, and here he applies that grounding to a program of blues and lightly gospel-tinged standards, backed by a compact combo (guitar, piano, bass, drums) and a female vocal trio for gospel-styled call-and-response. He also plays alto sax and, unusually for him, guitar on several tracks rather than his customary tenor. The album arrived amid Curtis's peak years as New York's most in-demand session saxophonist, and stands as a curious, personal side-project rather than a genre-defining statement, valued by collectors chiefly for its rarity and for the glimpse it offers of Curtis outside his usual studio-cat role. Contemporary reviews, including a favorable notice in Down Beat, treated it as a surprisingly assured blues-singing debut. It remains a minor but historically interesting entry in Curtis's catalog, illuminating the breadth of a musician far better known for his instrumental hits and his later work with Aretha Franklin and the Coasters.

albums.albumStory: Black Acid Soul is the 2021 debut album by Lady Blackbird, the reborn persona of Los Angeles singer Marley Munroe, who had spent years as a journeyman vocalist under other names before producer Chris Seefried helped her recast herself in the image of the great jazz-soul divas. Recorded largely live in Sunset Sound's Studio B in Hollywood - a room steeped in Prince and Doors history - the album strips soul, jazz and blues to voice, piano, double bass and brushed percussion, putting Munroe's huge, scarred, Nina Simone-evoking voice front and center. The set is built on daring reinterpretations: Simone's civil-rights anthem "Blackbird" opens the record as a statement of identity, Irma Thomas's "Ruler Of My Heart" (itself a reworking of "Time Is On My Side") becomes a slow-burn showcase, and Tim Hardin's "It'll Never Happen Again" closes the cycle with devastating restraint, alongside originals like the title track co-written with Seefried. Trombone Shorty drops in a trumpet cameo on the gospel-inflected "Nobody's Sweetheart," underscoring the album's New Orleans soul undercurrents. Critics on both sides of the Atlantic hailed it as one of the standout vocal debuts of the year, with particular praise for Munroe's ability to sound simultaneously ancient and new, and it established Lady Blackbird as a major festival and jazz-club draw. The record taps directly into the lineage of Simone, Billie Holiday and Esther Phillips while remaining unmistakably contemporary in its stark, minimalist production.

The caveat is pressing consistency: user reports across nearly every variant of this title cite surface noise, pops and occasional warps from the European plant, making individual copy quality the variable rather than the cut. The 2022 2xLP Deluxe adds remixes but uses the same core mastering, and no audiophile-tier reissue (Analogue Productions, MoFi, etc.) exists as of this writing - the Grundman-mastered LP is the top vinyl tier available.

albums.title: Cornbread
albums.musicians: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Jackie McLean (alto sax), Hank Mobley (tenor sax), Herbie Hancock (piano), Larry Ridley (bass), Billy Higgins (drums)
sides:
1. Cornbread
2. Our Man Higgins

1. Ceora
2. Ill Wind
3. Most Like Lee
albums.albumStory: Cornbread was recorded by trumpeter Lee Morgan on September 8, 1965, for Blue Note, reuniting him with fellow Jazz Messengers-connected players Jackie McLean and Hank Mobley alongside a young Herbie Hancock, bassist Larry Ridley, and drummer Billy Higgins. Arriving in the wake of Morgan's crossover hit "The Sidewinder," the album found him balancing the same soulful, boogaloo-tinged accessibility with the harder-edged, more harmonically adventurous hard bop he had built his reputation on since his teenage years with Dizzy Gillespie and later Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. The title track and "Our Man Higgins" showcase the blues-drenched, two-tenor-plus-alto frontline interplay, while "Ceora" became one of Morgan's most enduring compositions, a lyrical Latin-tinged ballad that has since become a jazz standard covered widely by other artists. "Ill Wind," the sole standard, gives space to McLean's astringent alto voice against the rhythm section, and "Most Like Lee" closes the set with a churning minor blues. Morgan, one of the defining post-bop trumpet voices of his era, was at a creative peak in the mid-1960s, and Cornbread is frequently ranked among his strongest and most fully realized Blue Note dates from that period. Despite its quality, the album was held back from release until 1967, arriving after several other Morgan Blue Note titles had already reached the public. Critics and collectors have long regarded Cornbread as an underappreciated gem in Morgan's catalog, prized for its cohesive band chemistry and the compositional strength of "Ceora" in particular.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1967) - Blue Note "New York, USA" label, no Liberty credit; Van Gelder stamp in deadwax; promo "Audition Copy" stamp on jacket.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are the plain white-top/blue-bottom Blue Note design reading only "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC \u2022 NEW YORK USA" with no "47 West 63rd St" street address and, critically, no "A DIVISION OF LIBERTY RECORDS" text. Blue Note dropped its West 63rd Street address in the early-to-mid 1960s in favor of the plain "New York, USA" credit, and this design continued to be used for a period even after Liberty Records acquired the label in 1965, before Liberty's corporate credit was added to the perimeter text later in the pressing run. Cornbread was recorded in September 1965 but not released until 1967, so this "New York, USA"-only label without the Liberty line places this copy at the very front of the BLP 4222 pressing run - the true first-pressing label for this title. The back cover's "AUDITION COPY" rubber stamp further indicates this particular copy was distributed as a promotional pressing rather than a standard retail unit.
albums.fidelity: This is an original Rudy Van Gelder mono cut, mastered directly from the analog session tapes at his Englewood Cliffs studio, and pressed in the mid-to-late-1960s Blue Note/Liberty era plant with the characteristic dense, punchy Van Gelder sound collectors prize. Steve Hoffman forum consensus generally rates these mid-60s Van Gelder-stamped Blue Note mono originals as sonically superior to the later United Artists and Liberty reissue pressings, and to the 1985 Toshiba-EMI Japanese reissue, which is competent but noticeably softer. Modern audiophile reissues (Music Matters 45rpm, Analogue Productions, Blue Note Classic Vinyl/Tone Poet series) offer quieter surfaces and often wider dynamic range from remastered tapes, but many Van Gelder-era purists still prefer the tonal immediacy of this original cut. Within Cornbread's own fidelity hierarchy, this Van Gelder-stamped "New York, USA" mono original sits at or near the top, surpassed sonically only by top-tier modern audiophile remasters where available.
albums.generalNotes: BLP 4222 mono, "New York, USA" labels without any Liberty Records credit, matched with the "VAN GELDER" machine stamp in the deadwax on both sides, identify this as the true first-pressing configuration for Cornbread's belated 1967 release. The back-cover "AUDITION COPY" rubber stamp confirms this specific copy was a label promo sent to radio or press rather than a standard retail copy. No street address or Liberty corporate line appears on the labels, consistent with the brief transitional label window used just before Liberty's credit was added to later Blue Note pressings.

albums.title: Delightfulee
albums.musicians: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Joe Henderson (tenor sax), McCoy Tyner (piano), Bob Cranshaw (bass), Billy Higgins (drums); Ernie Royal (trumpet), Tom McIntosh (trombone), Jim Buffington (french horn), Phil Woods (alto sax, flute), Wayne Shorter (tenor sax, bass clarinet), Danny Bank (baritone sax, flute), Philly Joe Jones (drums)

3. The Delightful Deggie (Morgan)
albums.albumStory: Delightfulee was assembled from two 1966 Van Gelder Studio sessions that found Lee Morgan working in two very different settings: a tight quintet with Joe Henderson, McCoy Tyner, Bob Cranshaw and Billy Higgins, and a larger, more ambitious nonet-plus session featuring Wayne Shorter, Phil Woods, Philly Joe Jones and a horn section arranged with unusual colors like French horn and bass clarinet. The album arrived at a pivotal moment in Morgan's career, coming after the massive crossover success of "The Sidewinder" (1964) had made him Blue Note's most commercially valuable young trumpeter, and it shows him balancing that newfound visibility with genuinely exploratory hard-bop writing rather than repeating a hit formula. Original compositions like "Ca-Lee-So" and "Zambia" sit alongside a soulful reading of the Beatles' "Yesterday" and the Broadway standard "Sunrise, Sunset," reflecting the era's growing jazz appetite for pop and show tunes. Morgan, a Philadelphia prodigy who had already passed through Dizzy Gillespie's band and the Jazz Messengers before his Blue Note stardom, plays with the fluid, blues-drenched brilliance and biting tone that made him one of the defining hard-bop trumpet voices of the 1960s. Liner notes by noted critic Leonard Feather situate the record within Morgan's ongoing evolution as both composer and bandleader. Though somewhat overshadowed commercially by the earlier boogaloo hits, Delightfulee is valued by collectors and critics as a showcase of Morgan's compositional range and his gift for pairing top-tier sidemen in service of adventurous small- and medium-group hard bop.
albums.lpNotes: Original 1967 pressing - Blue Note/Liberty white-and-blue label ("A Division of Liberty Records, Inc."), Van Gelder stamp in the deadwax on both sides.
albums.labelNotes: The labels on this copy are white with a blue rim and read "BLUE NOTE RECORDS · A DIVISION OF LIBERTY RECORDS, INC." arcing above the spindle, with no NY address text - this is the design cvinyl.com/bsnpubs class as the "sixth" Blue Note label, used c.1966-1970 after Liberty's 1965 acquisition of the company. Because Delightfulee was recorded in 1966 and not issued until November 1967, it was released entirely within this Liberty-ownership window, so this white/blue Liberty label IS the original first-pressing design for this title (there is no earlier Lexington Ave. or W. 63rd St. label for this specific album, since those addresses predate the recording date). The BNST 84243-A / BNST 84243-B matrix with VAN GELDER stamp on both sides matches the design and era, confirming this as an original first pressing rather than the later 1970 United Artists-address label or subsequent reissues.
albums.fidelity: Both sides were cut and stamped by Rudy Van Gelder directly from his original 1966 session tapes, as confirmed by the VAN GELDER etch in the runout, giving this pressing the direct, punchy Van Gelder studio sound typical of period Blue Note stereo LPs. Collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv generally regard these Liberty-era Van Gelder-mastered originals as sonically very close to the true first pressings, since Van Gelder continued to cut the lacquers himself through the late 1960s despite the change in label ownership. This pressing outranks the 1970 United Artists-address reissue and the 1985 Manhattan-era reissue, both of which used later stampers, and it is considerably more desirable than the 2007 CD reissue, which some listeners have criticized as sounding harsher than the analog originals; no audiophile (Music Matters/Analogue Productions/Tone Poet) reissue of this specific title currently exists.

The white label with blue rim reading "A Division of Liberty Records, Inc." is the design Blue Note used from 1966-1970 following the Liberty buyout, and since this title wasn't recorded until 1966 and not released until late 1967, this Liberty-era label is the true first-issue design for this catalog number. Matrix BNST 84243-A / B-1 with the VAN GELDER stamp on both sides confirms Van Gelder mastering from the original session tapes and matches the earliest known runout configuration reported for this title, distinguishing it from the later United Artists-address labels and 1970s/1985 reissues.

albums.title: The Rumproller
albums.musicians: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Joe Henderson (tenor saxophone), Ronnie Mathews (piano), Victor Sproles (bass), Billy Higgins (drums)
sides:
1. The Rumproller (Andrew Hill)
2. Desert Moonlight (Lee Morgan)

albums.albumStory: Recorded at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio on April 9 and 21, 1965, The Rumproller found Lee Morgan chasing the funky, boogaloo-inflected momentum of his massive 1964 hit "The Sidewinder," this time leaning on outside writers - including Andrew Hill for the loping title cut - rather than his own pen for the lead single. By this point Morgan was Blue Note's reigning young star, a former Jazz Messengers and Art Blakey alumnus whose trumpet combined dazzling technique with an unmistakably soulful, blues-rooted sensibility. Joining him is tenor saxophonist Joe Henderson, then emerging as one of the label's most vital voices, alongside a fresh rhythm section of pianist Ronnie Mathews, bassist Victor Sproles and drummer Billy Higgins. The record captures the mid-1960s hard-bop mainstream at its most commercially minded, pairing groove-oriented material with the harmonic sophistication that defined the era's Blue Note house style. Critical reception was mixed-to-positive at the time and has remained so since, with some critics viewing it as a somewhat formulaic attempt to replicate "The Sidewinder's" success, while others praise the strength of the individual performances, particularly Henderson's soloing and Higgins' propulsive drumming. Nonetheless, the album holds a solid place in Morgan's prolific mid-1960s Blue Note run and remains a favorite among soul-jazz and boogaloo collectors for its instantly catchy title track.

albums.labelNotes: The label on this copy is the classic Blue Note "New York, USA" design: white top band reading "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC. " over "NEW YORK USA", blue lower band with "BLUE"/"NOTE" in large white letters, no "Division of Liberty Records" text and no deep groove (deep groove had ended by the early 1960s). This design ran continuously on Blue Note catalog numbers roughly BLP 4081 through BLP 4247 (c. 1962-1966), before being replaced by the Liberty-era label following the January 1966 sale of Blue Note to Liberty Records. Since BLP 4199 was recorded in April 1965 and released in January 1966, this NY USA label is the correct and only label design for a true first pressing of this catalog number - there is no earlier
albums.fidelity: This is a Rudy Van Gelder original cut, mastered directly from his session tapes at his own Englewood Cliffs facility and pressed by Plastylite - collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv consistently rate original Van Gelder Blue Note masterings as the gold standard for the label's mid-60s sound, prized for warmth, presence, and Higgins' cymbal detail. This NY USA mono pressing sits at the top of the fidelity hierarchy for this title, ahead of the Liberty-era NY reissues (still Van Gelder-mastered but without the ear/Plastylite pressing), the 1970s United Artists-era blue label reissues, and later 1980s-90s EMI/Manhattan reissues, all of which use lesser-quality vinyl and mastering chains. The modern Blue Note Classic Vinyl Series reissue (Kevin Gray remaster from analog tapes, RTI pressing) is excellent but voiced differently and is generally regarded by purists as a fine alternative rather than a replacement for this original pressing.

albums.title: The Sidewinder
albums.musicians: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Joe Henderson (tenor sax), Barry Harris (piano), Bob Cranshaw (bass), Billy Higgins (drums)
sides:
1. The Sidewinder (Lee Morgan)
2. Totem Pole (Morgan)

1. Gary's Notebook (Lee Morgan)
2. Boy, What A Night (Morgan)
3. Hocus-Pocus (Morgan)
albums.albumStory: Recorded on December 21, 1963 at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio, The Sidewinder was cut as a fairly routine Blue Note date built entirely from five new Lee Morgan originals, with the loping title track added almost as an afterthought to round out the program. Morgan, a prodigy who had joined Dizzy Gillespie's big band as a teenager and later anchored Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, was rebuilding his career after a period of personal decline when this session became his unexpected comeback vehicle. Joining him were tenor saxophonist Joe Henderson, newly signed to Blue Note himself, pianist Barry Harris on loan from Riverside, bassist Bob Cranshaw, and drummer Billy Higgins, who together lock into a loose, blues-drenched boogaloo groove that leaves wide-open space for extended solos over simple harmonic vamps. The title track's easy backbeat and earworm bassline caught on unexpectedly with radio and jukebox audiences, turning what Blue Note had pressed in only a few thousand copies into the label's best-selling record and, according to producer Michael Cuscuna's account, a financial lifeline for the company. Its crossover success also proved influential and controversial in equal measure, spawning a wave of similarly groove-based "boogaloo" jazz-funk sides across the mid-1960s hard bop catalog and drawing some critical grumbling that commercial appeal was overtaking artistic ambition. Decades on, The Sidewinder is regarded as a cornerstone of the hard bop/soul-jazz idiom and a high point in Morgan's celebrated run of Blue Note leader dates, prized by critics and listeners alike for its irresistible groove and the quality of the blowing from Morgan and Henderson.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1964) - Blue Note "New York, USA" label; BNLP-4157 Van Gelder matrix prefix consistent with original stamper.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are the plain blue-and-white two-tone Blue Note design with the arc reading "BLUE...NOTE", "33 1/3 MICROGROOVE LONG PLAYING" in the upper arc, and "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC • NEW YORK USA" printed flat beneath the title - with no street address and no "Division of Liberty Records" text. No deep groove is visible in the label photos on either side. This "New York, USA" address format replaced the earlier street-address labels (767 Lexington Ave / 47 West 63rd St) around 1963 and remained in use until Liberty's 1966 buyout added "A DIVISION OF LIBERTY RECORDS" beneath it, so this label design places the pressing in the 1964-1966 window. Combined with the BNLP-4157 Van Gelder matrix format documented as the original stamper prefix for this title (later pressings often show a plain "BLP 4157" or "BLN" style matrix), this is consistent with an early pressing in the "New York, USA" era, ranking it ahead of the Liberty-era and later United Artists/Manhattan reissues in the label hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: This is a Van Gelder mono cut, mastered directly by Rudy Van Gelder at his Englewood Cliffs studio and (if a true first stamper) pressed at Plastylite, the pressing plant collectors regard as producing the punchiest, most dynamic vintage Blue Note sound. Steve Hoffman forum consensus consistently ranks original Van Gelder-cut New York-label mono pressings of The Sidewinder above the 1966+ Liberty-era repressings and well above the Manhattan/Capitol CD-era reissues in warmth and impact. Among later options, the Music Matters 45rpm mono/stereo audiophile reissues and the Blue Note Classic Vinyl series are well regarded for tape-sourced clarity but are generally described by collectors as smoother/cleaner rather than possessing the raw punch of an original Van Gelder-Plastylite pressing. If this copy carries the Plastylite ear (unconfirmed from the transcription), it sits at or near the top of the fidelity hierarchy for this title; if it lacks the ear (a slightly later New York-label pressing), it would still rank above Liberty-era and reissue pressings but below a documented first stamper.

The runout is transcribed as "BNLP 4157 A/B VAN GELDER," the matrix prefix documented on genuine first pressings of this title; the transcription does not explicitly note the Plastylite "ear" etching that most first-run copies carry, so that detail should be confirmed by direct deadwax inspection before certifying this as a true first stamper. No deep groove is visible on either label, which is normal for Blue Note pressings from this later, deep-groove-phased-out era. Barry Harris is credited as appearing courtesy of Riverside Records, consistent with the original 1964 sleeve credit.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in August 1956 when Lee Morgan was barely eighteen, this session captures the young trumpeter already fluent in the Clifford Brown-influenced hard bop language after his stint with Dizzy Gillespie's big band. Arranger Benny Golson supplied three of the six compositions along with Philadelphia friend Owen Marshall, giving the date a cohesive, big-band-inflected writing sensibility despite the small sextet format. The frontline pairing of Morgan with Hank Mobley and little-known altoist Kenny Rodgers, backed by Horace Silver, Paul Chambers and Charlie Persip, produced a set balancing Golson's melodic, sophisticated charts with blowing room for the young leader. This was Morgan's second Blue Note leader date, arriving as he was quickly establishing himself as one of the label's brightest new voices and would soon join Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. The album stands as an early testament to Morgan's precocious talent and to Golson's emerging skill as a composer-arranger within the hard bop idiom. It was well received in its day, with liner notes from critic Leonard Feather praising Morgan's rapid maturation, and it remains valued by collectors and historians as a formative document in the trumpeter's brief but towering career.

That address places this pressing at the front of the BLP 1541 pressing hierarchy, made not long after the August 1956 recording date. The deep groove plus the Lexington Ave rim text are the two decisive dating markers separating this earliest label from the later West 63rd St and "New York, USA" variants that followed.

albums.albumStory: Mississippi-born and church-trained, Margie Joseph arrived at Stax's Volt imprint in 1970 after early sessions cut with Muscle Shoals players while she was still based in New Orleans, and this debut LP became her definitive introduction to soul audiences. Producers Fred Briggs and Darryl Carter, working as the Colsoul team, built the record around a striking reinterpretation of the Supremes' "Stop! In the Name of Love," stretching it into an extended, dramatically monologue-prefaced centerpiece that showcased Joseph's gospel-trained phrasing and improvisational daring. The remaining material blended fresh Stax-Memphis originals with Muscle Shoals-cut sides, giving the album a hybrid Southern-soul sound that sat between the grit of Memphis funk and the polish of Alabama session musicianship. Joseph's voice - flexible, melodic, and more restrained than the era's belters - distinguished her from contemporaries and helped establish her as an underappreciated but critically respected deep-soul singer. The album arrived at a pivotal moment for Stax, newly independent from Atlantic and reshaping its Volt subsidiary's identity, and it helped signal the label's continued vitality in the early 1970s soul marketplace. Though never a major commercial blockbuster, it has grown in stature among soul collectors and critics as a showcase for both Joseph's artistry and the fertile Stax/Muscle Shoals creative exchange of the period.
albums.lpNotes: Original US press (stereo, c. 1970) - Monarch yellow-bolt-label plant-error variant; VS-0157/VS-0158, Mastercraft marks, Δ15323/Δ15323-X.
albums.labelNotes: Both side labels show a bright yellow field with the black "VOLT RECORDS" wordmark and a single large freestanding black double-zigzag/bolt device beneath it, followed by the artist name, quoted album title, catalog number VOS-6012, STEREO, and side/matrix data (VS-0157/VS-0158) at upper right - no ring text or arc band is present. This bold yellow-and-black bolt design is Volt's earlier/mid-1960s Atlantic-distribution-era house style; by the time this LP was actually issued in the newly-independent post-1970 Stax/Volt era, the era-correct VOS-6000-series design had shifted to the dark-blue label with red bolt seen on most confirmed VOS-6012 copies (including the Terre Haute and standard Monarch pressings documented on Discogs). Collectors have documented that Monarch's pressing plant used leftover stock of this older yellow-bolt label in error on some VOS-6000-series titles, and the printed matrices (VS-0157/VS-0158) with Mastercraft/Monarch stampers on this copy are consistent with that recognized plant-error variant rather than the standard contemporary blue-label pressing.
albums.fidelity: This is the original-era analog US cut, with Mastercraft metalwork and Monarch pressing. The documented yellow-label variant's cutting engineer initials are typically read as HC (Howard Craft) on standard blue-label pressings; the supplied transcription reads HL, so that attribution should be treated as probable rather than fully confirmed. Monarch's work here is competent but not audiophile-grade, yielding a warm, dense midrange and the somewhat compressed presentation typical of early-1970s Stax/Volt product; clean vinyl is especially important through the extended eight-minute "Stop! In the Name of Love." No dedicated Steve Hoffman forum consensus or standalone modern audiophile LP reissue exists for this title, so a clean original US pressing (blue or yellow label) remains the sonic reference point; the 1993 CD twofer reissue is not a fidelity competitor to a well-preserved original vinyl copy.
albums.generalNotes: Original US Volt VOS-6012 stereo, pressed by Monarch, bearing the scarce older-style yellow-and-black double-bolt Volt label rather than the era-correct dark-blue/red-bolt design used on most copies of this title. The decisive evidence is that yellow label design itself, the printed side matrices VS-0157 (Side One) and VS-0158 (Side Two), and the supplied Mastercraft marks with Monarch Δ15323/Δ15323-X. Discogs documents the standard issue with blue labels (both Terre Haute and Monarch pressings), reinforcing that this yellow-label copy is the deviant plant-error pressing. The album was first advertised/released in late 1970, though Discogs, RYM, and many dealers assign 1971 based on its chart run; it is not the 1972 "Phase II" follow-up, VOS-6016.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in October 1976 at London's Palladium during a triumphant European tour, this live document caught Marvin Gaye newly free of the stage fright that had kept him largely off the road for years, performing with renewed confidence and showmanship. Three sides survey his career in revue form: recent material, then two extended medleys spanning his 1960s Motown hits and his early-70s message-music era, and a third medley of his classic duets with guest vocalist Florence Lyles standing in for Tammi Terrell and Diana Ross. The fourth side breaks format entirely with a new studio recording, "Got To Give It Up," a sparse, extended party jam Gaye built after Motown pushed him toward the disco era; it became one of the biggest hits of his career, topping pop, R&B and dance charts. Released in March 1977, the double album arrived at the commercial peak of Gaye's career, bridging the sensuality of Let's Get It On and I Want You with the raw confession of the forthcoming Here, My Dear, and it went on to double-platinum sales. Critics were unusually receptive to a live album of this scale, praising both the concert sides' polish and the audacity of closing out a live record with a full studio side. Decades later its legacy took an unexpected turn when "Got To Give It Up" became the centerpiece of the landmark "Blurred Lines" copyright litigation, reasserting the song's cultural footprint.
albums.lpNotes: Original US press (1977) - Tamla T7-352R2 brown/gold globe label; 'W' deadwax etch identifies a Wakefield Manufacturing (Phoenix) pressing.
albums.labelNotes: This copy shows the mid-to-late-1970s Tamla design: a brown upper panel with the gold Tamla globe logo in a cream box, a yellow lower field, and rim text reading "A Product of Motown Record Corp." This design superseded the earlier black "globe on map" Tamla label around 1975 and remained in use until Motown began folding artists onto the plain Motown label in the early 1980s. The mixed 1976/1977 copyright lines across the four sides track the October 1976 concert taping versus the later-finished studio side, and the T7-352R2 number with job numbers 2697-S through 2700-S matches the March 1977 first-issue run. Discogs documents this title pressed concurrently by several contract plants (Monarch, Wakefield, Columbia/CTH, PRC) distinguished by runout suffixes; the etched 'W' on this copy points to Wakefield Manufacturing (Phoenix), one of the documented original-pressing plants rather than a later reissue.
albums.fidelity: Mastering is uncredited on the jacket and labels, as is typical for late-70s Motown product of this scale; this copy was pressed by Wakefield Manufacturing in Phoenix, a competent but not top-tier Motown contract plant compared with Columbia's or RCA's better facilities. The album is a heavily produced, sweetened live document overall, with the stripped-down studio cut of "Got To Give It Up" standing out as the sonic highlight of the set. No audiophile reissue series (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, Tone Poet or similar) has ever tackled this title, so original US pressings like this one remain the reference cut; the 2013 UMe/Motown reissue, sourced digitally, sits below any well-preserved original vinyl pressing regardless of plant.

albums.albumStory: Marvin Gaye Live! documents Gaye's return to the stage after years of self-imposed exile triggered by Tammi Terrell's 1967 onstage collapse and her subsequent death, an ordeal that left him gripped by stage fright and reluctant to tour. By the time of this concert he had reinvented himself as a studio auteur with What's Going On, Trouble Man and Let's Get It On, the latter becoming his biggest-selling album and making him Motown's top-selling artist during his lifetime, success that helped push him back onto a stage. He performed before more than 14,000 fans at the Oakland Coliseum Arena on January 4, 1974, reportedly sending his brother out first to gauge the crowd's reception. The set leaned into his 1970s persona with Trouble Man, Inner City Blues, Distant Lover, Let's Get It On and What's Going On, while his 1960s Motown hits were compressed into a self-deprecatingly titled, up-tempo "Fossil Medley", and he premiered the new song "Jan", written for his girlfriend Janis Hunter. The slowed, smoldering rendition of "Distant Lover" became the night's breakout moment and a hit single, remaining his onstage signature for years afterward. Backed by a 40-piece orchestra of Los Angeles studio musicians under arranger/conductor Gene Page, the performance translated his intimate, studio-crafted 1970s sound into a large-scale arena seduction, and the resulting album stands as a defining artifact of 1970s live soul and a beloved chapter in Gaye's career.

The typed runouts (T6-333S1-D5RS-7651-1 O3B / -7652-2 O3B) match a documented US original Discogs stamper configuration; Discogs also lists a distinct RCA Indianapolis plant run of this same pressing bearing an explicit "I" stamp. No runout photo was supplied, so the exact plant (Hollywood-area vs. RCA Indianapolis) cannot be confirmed with certainty from the transcription alone. Either way, the die-cut inner gatefold and 1974 Motown copyright text on the jacket firmly place this copy within the original first-issue print run rather than any later Motown reissue.
albums.fidelity: This is a Motown in-house cut of a Wally Heider live remote recording, mixed at Motown's Hitsville U.S.A. studios and lacquer-cut at RCA Studios Hollywood; the sound is typical mid-70s Motown - warm and midrange-forward, with horns and strings somewhat congested and arena ambience compressed, so the ceiling is set by the tape and mix rather than by any particular stamper. The O3B stampers on this copy are mid-run rather than the very first lacquers, but original 1974 US Tamla pressings are generally quiet and well-manufactured, and Steve Hoffman forum consensus favors these originals over the thinner 1980s Motown represses. There is no dedicated audiophile reissue program (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, etc.) for this title comparable to treatments given What's Going On or Let's Get It On, so a clean original US Tamla pressing like this one sits at or near the top of the album's realistic fidelity hierarchy.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in New York in June 1958, Legrand Jazz paired the young French composer-arranger Michel Legrand with an all-star cast of American jazzmen - including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Bill Evans, Ben Webster and Art Farmer - to reinterpret jazz standards spanning Fats Waller, Django Reinhardt, Dizzy Gillespie, Jelly Roll Morton, Duke Ellington and Bix Beiderbecke. Legrand, already an established pop arranger in France, had fallen in love with American jazz and used the sessions to fuse his European harmonic sophistication with the swing and blues vocabulary of his heroes, assembling several different large-ensemble lineups across the dates to suit each arrangement's mood. The album is something of an anomaly in Miles Davis's discography, a sideman appearance on someone else's date during the same period he was shaping Milestones and preparing for Kind of Blue, and it captures Coltrane and Evans together on record months before their more celebrated pairing on Kind of Blue. For Legrand the record stands as a rare mainstream American jazz statement before he turned decisively toward the film-scoring career that would make him internationally famous. Critics have long praised the record's inventive, occasionally dense big-band charts and its unusual blending of European classical color with hot American jazz repertoire, and it remains a valued curiosity for the rare glimpse it offers of Davis, Coltrane and Evans as sidemen in someone else's ambitious arranging vision.
albums.lpNotes: 1958 US Columbia six-eye mono promo pressing - white/red "Demonstration - Not For Sale" label, deep groove, matrix XLP 44188-1F/44189-1D.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the white-field, red-print six-eye Columbia label with "DEMONSTRATION" and "NOT FOR SALE" printed directly into the label design, plus a flat deep-groove ring on both sides - hallmarks of a genuine 1958 Columbia promotional pressing rather than a later stock or reissue copy. Columbia's six-eye label design ran roughly 1955 into the early 1960s before being replaced by the black "Guaranteed High Fidelity" label and later the orange label, so the six-eye placement alone dates this pressing to the 1958-61 window. The deep groove and matrix suffixes (XLP 44188-1F / 44189-1D) are consistent with an early stamper generation cut close to the original lacquers, placing this copy at or very near the front of the CL 1250 mono pressing hierarchy - ahead of the later "CBS"-logo six-eye reissue (1961-62) which reused the same stampers, and well ahead of the black-label and orange-label reissues that followed.
albums.fidelity: Mono mix cut directly from the 1958 Columbia 30th Street Studio session tapes; Columbia's uncredited in-house engineering team of the period is generally well regarded for natural, warm big-band sound on six-eye era pressings. Collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv debate whether some Legrand Jazz mono copies are true mono or fold-downs, but original six-eye mono pressings like this one are considered the most authentic and best-sounding version, ahead of any later stereo remix or reissue. No audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, etc.) of this specific title is documented; modern colored-vinyl European reissues (c. 2017-2022) are widely regarded as sonically inferior to an original six-eye pressing.

Records), John McLaughlin (guitar), Steve Grossman (soprano saxophone), Billy Cobham (drums), Michael Henderson (Fender bass); additional session personnel compiled into the LP include Chick Corea (electric piano), Dave Holland (electric bass), Jack DeJohnette (drums), Sonny Sharrock (guitar) and Bennie Maupin (bass clarinet), with Brock Peters as the voice of Jack Johnson.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in early 1970 as the soundtrack to William Cayton's documentary about heavyweight boxing champion Jack Johnson, this album finds Miles Davis pushing the electric, rock-inflected direction he had opened on Bitches Brew even further toward raw, riff-based jamming. The centerpiece, 'Right Off', reportedly grew out of an impromptu studio warm-up: guitarist John McLaughlin began vamping while waiting for Davis, and was quickly joined by bassist Michael Henderson and drummer Billy Cobham, prompting Davis to walk in and improvise trumpet lines over the groove that producer Teo Macero then edited into a side-long piece. 'Yesternow' was assembled by Macero from multiple sessions and musicians, splicing together a slow-burning, bass-riff-driven mood piece that closes with dialogue from the film. The record arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, following his full turn to electric jazz-rock fusion, and it stands as one of the most focused and rock-influenced statements of that period, prized by many listeners for its visceral, funk-driven energy. Though a modest commercial performer on release, it has since come to be regarded by critics and musicians as a high point of the jazz-fusion era and an essential entry in Davis's 1970s electric catalog, admired for the interplay of McLaughlin's guitar with Henderson and Cobham's rhythm section.
albums.lpNotes: Early US pressing (stereo, c.1971) - Columbia red label, KC 30455 catalog, Pitman NJ plant stamp in the matrix.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the plain red Columbia label with orange 'COLUMBIA' logotype repeating around the rim and the small two-eye logo box, with no white '360 Sound Stereo' overprint - a design Columbia used circa 1970-72 immediately before that wording was added to the same red livery. The catalog number is printed as KC 30455 on both labels and jacket (spine/back), the original Columbia numbering used before the company's mid-1970s renumbering to the PC prefix. Discogs variant data confirms later copies carry a PC sticker over the printed KC number or a '360 Sound Stereo' white-text label, both markers of a later print run. The matrix suffixes (MAL-30455-1A, MBL-30455-1F) with the 'P' code point to Columbia's Pitman, NJ plant, consistent with early-1970s US manufacturing for this catalog block. Taken together (KC prefix, plain red/orange label lacking 360 Sound text, Pitman stamp, low lacquer-cut letter suffixes) this sits at or very near the front of the domestic US pressing run rather than a mid-70s PC-era repress or Canadian pressing.
albums.fidelity: Engineered by Stan Tonkel and produced/edited by Teo Macero from the original 1970 Columbia studio masters; this US Pitman pressing represents Columbia's standard early-1970s cutting rather than an audiophile mastering, with quality generally solid but variable by copy, as was typical of Columbia's high-volume plants of the era. Collectors on forums such as Steve Hoffman's generally regard original Columbia pressings of this title as punchy but not particularly quiet or deep-bass extended compared to modern remasters. The 2016 Mobile Fidelity MFSL 1-440 180g reissue is widely considered the sonic high-water mark for the album, offering greater clarity, quieter surfaces and tighter bass than any vintage Columbia pressing, including this one. Within the vintage-pressing tier, an early KC-prefix red-label copy like this one is regarded as among the more desirable original variants, ranking above later PC-era reissues and Canadian pressings but below the MFSL and other modern audiophile cuts.
albums.generalNotes: This is an early domestic US Columbia pressing rather than a later PC-era repress. The KC 30455 catalog prefix (versus the later PC 30455 renumbering used from roughly 1973 onward, sometimes applied via sticker over the original KC print) and the plain orange-on-red Columbia label without the '360 Sound Stereo' overprint both point to a 1971-72 manufacturing window. albums.albumStory: Bags' Groove compiles two Miles Davis sessions from 1954: a December 24 date with vibraphonist Milt Jackson, pianist Thelonious Monk, Percy Heath and Kenny Clarke, and an earlier June 29 session featuring Sonny Rollins on tenor and Horace Silver on piano. The December date has become one of the most mythologized sessions in jazz history, fueled by later, partly embellished accounts of friction between Davis and Monk over how the pianist should comp behind the trumpeter's solos. Whatever the truth of that tension, the two contrasting takes of Jackson's title tune capture the loose, blues-drenched interplay that defined small-group jazz of the era. The June session, essentially an early Rollins showcase, produced enduring Rollins originals including Oleo, Airegin and Doxy alongside two takes of the Gershwins' But Not for Me. The album arrives at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, just before he assembled his classic quintet with John Coltrane and signed with Columbia, and it stands as a landmark documenting both Davis's maturing conception and Rollins's emergence as a major composer-improviser. It is widely regarded as one of the essential hard bop recordings of the 1950s, prized for its blend of blues feeling, harmonic sophistication, and unresolved creative tension that has fascinated critics and musicians for decades.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1957) - Prestige yellow/black label, 446 W. 50th St. NYC address, deep groove, hand-etched RVG in the runout.
albums.labelNotes: The label photographed is the classic Prestige yellow-and-black design with the swirl and star graphics, reading "PRESTIGE RECORDS INC. \u2022 446 W. 50th ST., N.Y.C." around the rim, and both sides show pronounced deep groove. Per bsnpubs.com's Prestige timeline, this 446 W. 50th St. NYC address was used from the label's founding through the 1958 relocation to Bergenfield, New Jersey, after which the address text and deep groove disappeared from the labels. The hand-etched "RVG" plus "AB" (Abbey Record Manufacturing) suffix in the runouts is consistent with Prestige's earliest custom-pressed runs of this catalog number. This combination of address, deep groove and runout etching places this copy squarely as a first-pressing example, ahead of the Bergenfield-address second pressing and all later reissues in the hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: Mastered from Rudy Van Gelder's original Hackensack tapes and lacquers, with his hand-etched RVG stamp confirming a Van Gelder-cut original rather than a later re-cut. Collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv generally regard these mid-1950s Prestige/Van Gelder mono originals as warm but narrow-band by modern standards, a function of the era's mastering chain rather than pressing quality, with Abbey's pressings considered solid if unspectacular. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy, this RVG/deep-groove 446 W. 50th St. original sits at the top for vintage collectors, ahead of the later Bergenfield-address repress, the 1960s-70s blue-label reissues, and the OJC reissue. The more recent Analogue Productions/Craft audiophile remaster from the original tapes is generally rated the most refined-sounding cut but is prized for surface quiet and extended top end rather than vintage authenticity.
albums.generalNotes: 1957 Prestige PRLP 7109 mono - original first pressing. The 446 W. 50th St. NYC label address (pre-1958 Bergenfield move) combined with deep-groove labels and hand-etched RVG runouts (PRLP-7109-A/B RVG A AB) is the canonical marker of this variant. The "AB" suffix confirms Abbey Record Manufacturing as the pressing plant, consistent with Prestige's own custom pressing arrangement of the period. VG+ vinyl grade with deep groove intact supports the first-pressing attribution.
