albums.albumStory: Birth of the Cool compiles twelve sides Miles Davis recorded with a specially assembled nine-piece band across three 1949-1950 New York sessions, growing out of a brief but pivotal engagement the group had played at the Royal Roost in 1948. Davis conceived the project with close collaborators Gil Evans and Gerry Mulligan, drawing on writing contributions from John Lewis, John Carisi and George Wallington, and on the unusual instrumentation of French horn and tuba to create softer, more arranged ensemble textures than the prevailing bebop idiom. Coming immediately after Davis stepped out from Charlie Parker's quintet, the sessions announced him as a bandleader and conceptual arranger rather than simply a virtuoso soloist, a role he would return to repeatedly across his career. Though the original singles sold modestly on release, the music's restrained tempos, chamber-like counterpoint and unusual voicings anticipated the cool and West Coast jazz movements that flourished in the years before Capitol finally compiled the sides as this LP. The record is now regarded as one of the most influential documents in jazz history, foundational to cool jazz and an early example of "third stream" thinking that blended jazz with classical arranging sensibilities. Its collaborative writing and unusual sonic palette shaped generations of arrangers and small-group composers, and it remains central to Miles Davis's legacy as an artist whose impact often came as much through concept, personnel and arranging as through his trumpet playing.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1957) - Capitol turquoise dome-logo label, plain 'Long Playing' text, no anvil stamper mark, matrix T1-762-B2 #2 / T2-762-D1.
albums.labelNotes: This copy shows the early turquoise Capitol label with the large white "dome" (Capitol building) logo centered at top and the plain "LONG PLAYING" legend at bottom of both side labels, with no "High Fidelity" suffix text and rim text reading "MANUFACTURED BY CAPITOL RECORDS, INC. \u2022 HOLLYWOOD, CALIFORNIA \u2022 U.S.A." Per Discogs variant listings and bsnpubs/cvinyl label-design timelines, this large dome-logo turquoise design with plain "Long Playing" wording (rather than "Long Playing * High Fidelity") and no Scranton anvil symbol in the runout is documented as the first-pressing configuration for T-762, made shortly after the album's original 1957 release; the near-identical label but with "Long Playing * High Fidelity" and a Scranton anvil stamper mark constitutes the second pressing. The plain wording plus absence of the anvil mark and the Hollywood, California manufacturing text together confirm this is a first-issue-window US pressing rather than a Scranton, export, or later colorband/reissue copy.
albums.fidelity: Mono mastering drawn from the original 1949-50 session tapes, cut for Capitol's 1957 LP compilation; the sound is inherently limited by the vintage 10-inch-era source rather than by this cutting itself. Collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv generally rate the early no-anvil turquoise-label Capitol pressings as warmer and more natural than the later black-colorband reissues or the 1971 expanded 'Complete Birth of the Cool' compilation, which some find brighter and thinner sounding. This early turquoise, plain-'Long Playing', no-anvil pressing sits at or near the top of the vintage mono fidelity hierarchy for T-762, ranking above the Scranton-anvil second pressing, the colorband reissue, Pathe Marconi European pressings, and the expanded Capitol Jazz Classics/Complete compilations, while modern audiophile reissues (where they exist) trade some of this vintage warmth for quieter surfaces.
albums.generalNotes: 1957 Capitol T-762 mono - earliest documented label/stamper state of the original LP compilation. Large white dome-logo turquoise label with plain 'LONG PLAYING' (no 'High Fidelity' suffix) and no Scranton anvil symbol in the runout place this ahead of the later 'Long Playing * High Fidelity' anvil-stamped copies, per matching Discogs variant listings. Catalog number T-762 and the Hollywood, California manufacturing rim text confirm a US Capitol domestic pressing rather than an export, Bovema/Holland, or later colorband reissue. The B2/D1 stamper suffixes are consistent with early-run dies for this catalog number.

albums.title: Bitches Brew
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Wayne Shorter (soprano sax), Bennie Maupin (bass clarinet), Joe Zawinul (electric piano), Chick Corea (electric piano), Larry Young (electric piano), John McLaughlin (electric guitar), Dave Holland (bass), Harvey Brooks (electric bass guitar), Jack DeJohnette (drums), Lenny White (drums), Don Alias (drums, congas), Jim Riley aka Jumma Santos (percussion, shaker)
sides: 1. Pharaoh's Dance - J. Zawinul

albums.albumStory: Recorded over three days in August 1969 at Columbia's 30th Street Studio, Bitches Brew marked Miles Davis's decisive commitment to electric, rock- and funk-inflected jazz after the tentative steps of In a Silent Way. Davis assembled a sprawling ensemble of overlapping electric keyboards, electric bass and guitar, multiple drummers and percussionists, and Bennie Maupin's bass clarinet, then worked with producer Teo Macero to splice, loop, and layer the freewheeling studio jams into the album's dense, hypnotic long-form pieces. Arriving as Davis, already a towering figure across bebop, cool, hard bop, and modal jazz, sought to reach a younger rock audience, the record's uncompromising sound alienated segments of the traditional jazz establishment even as it became a commercial breakthrough unprecedented for a Davis jazz release. Anchored by the sprawling, cyclical groove of the title track, it is now regarded as the founding document of jazz-fusion, reshaping the genre's possibilities for the following decade. Critically divisive on release, its influence proved lasting and profound, paving the way for Davis's own subsequent electric period and for a generation of fusion musicians who followed in its wake.
albums.lpNotes: 1970 US Columbia PG26 stereo, red label with repeating orange rim text (post two-eye design), Shorter-only Sanctuary credit, mixed Santa Maria/Terre Haute pressing - a second-wave 1970 pressing, not the original two-eye first press.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show Columbia's continuous repeating rim design - 'COLUMBIA' text alternating with a small diamond-framed eye icon runs all the way around the red field, not the earlier design with only two large CBS eye logos fixed at 9 and 3 o'clock. Per bsnpubs/Discogs timelines, Columbia introduced this repeating-rim-text red label around July 1970, superseding the original two-eye label used on the true first-pressing run from March-June 1970, and it was itself later replaced by a plain solid-orange label around 1972. Side 4 already credits 'Sanctuary' to W. Shorter alone (the initial dual Davis/Shorter mis-credit was corrected mid-way through the two-eye era), confirming this copy postdates both two-eye stamper states. This places the pressing in Columbia's second major 1970 label-design wave - a genuine 1970 US pressing, but not the more collectible earliest two-eye first press.
albums.fidelity: Original 1970 Columbia pressings were assembled under Teo Macero's supervision without a separate mastering-engineer credit on the disc; quality varies by plant, and Santa Maria and Terre Haute pressings of this era are generally rated by collectors (forums.stevehoffman.tv) as solid, warm, dynamic vintage cuts, though somewhat less consistently quiet than the best Pitman copies. This mixed Santa Maria/Terre Haute, rim-text-label example sits below the rarer two-eye first pressings in the collector hierarchy but above later 1970s solid-orange-label represses in punch and perceived dynamics. Modern audiophile reissues (Mobile Fidelity, Music On Vinyl, and other 180g remasters) offer quieter surfaces and extended low end but are valued by some collectors more for consistency than for matching the analog immediacy of a good original pressing.
albums.generalNotes: This is not a two-eye pressing: the label carries the continuous repeating orange 'COLUMBIA' rim text with small eye icons that Columbia adopted from around July 1970 onward, replacing the original two-eye (two large CBS logos at 9/3 o'clock) design used on the true first pressings. Sanctuary is already correctly credited to W. Shorter alone, consistent with this later label state. Runout etchings show Santa Maria (S) plant markings on sides 1-3 and Terre Haute (T) on side 4, a normal mixed-plant setup for Columbia's high-volume 1970 manufacturing of this title. Net verdict: a genuine 1970 US original release, but from the second label-design generation rather than the more collectible two-eye first pressing.

albums.albumStory: Blue Haze compiles three separate Prestige sessions Miles Davis led in 1953-54, a period when heroin addiction had made him, in Ira Gitler's contemporaneous phrase, close to jazz's "forgotten man of 1955." The earliest material, a May 1953 quartet date with John Lewis, Percy Heath and Max Roach, is joined by a March 1954 session featuring Horace Silver and Art Blakey and an April 1954 quintet date with alto saxophonist Davey Schildkraut that produced the album's most celebrated track, "I'll Remember April." Musically the record captures Davis honing the lyrical, harmonically searching trumpet voice that would soon anchor hard bop, moving through standards like "That Ole Devil Moon" and "When Lights Are Low" alongside originals such as "Tune Up," "Miles Ahead," and the brooding title cut "Blue Haze," co-credited to bassist-composer Charles Mingus. The sessions predate Davis's galvanizing comeback appearance at the 1955 Newport Jazz Festival, so the album effectively documents raw talent critics had begun to overlook amid his personal struggles. It is prized less as a unified artistic statement than as an essential window into Davis's early-to-mid-1950s Prestige period, pairing him with musicians - Silver and Blakey, Lewis and Roach - who would become architects of the emerging hard-bop idiom. Decades on, Blue Haze remains a steady fixture in critical surveys of Davis's formative Prestige years, valued for capturing the trumpeter mid-transformation, not long before his move to Columbia Records would redefine modern jazz.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1956) - Prestige yellow/black fireworks label, 446 W. 50th St. NYC address, "HI FI" text, deep groove; hand-etched RVG in the deadwax with AB/1 stamper codes.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the yellow-and-black "fireworks" Prestige label with the "PRESTIGE RECORDS INC. \u2022 446 W. 50th ST., N.Y.C." address and abbreviated "HI FI" legend, with a deep groove stamped into the label field - the earliest 12-inch Prestige label design, used while the company's office was on West 50th Street in Manhattan. Prestige relocated to Bergenfield, New Jersey in 1958, after which the same fireworks artwork was reprinted in a slightly different "egg-yolk" yellow with the Bergenfield address and fuller "HIGH FIDELITY" wording, marking the second-pressing label; that later label also generally lacks the deep groove. The NYC address, "HI FI" abbreviation, and deep groove together place this copy in the first Prestige pressing run following the LP's 1956 release, itself a repackaging of the 1954 10-inch Prestige 161. The hand-etched "RVG" plus machine-stamped "AB"/"1" stamper codes in the deadwax are consistent with Van Gelder-cut lacquers from this earliest pressing era.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Rudy Van Gelder directly from his Hackensack studio tapes, this deep-groove NYC-label pressing represents the earliest and most sought-after cut of Blue Haze, made when Van Gelder's lacquers were pressed close to the source without intervening tape generations. Collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv generally regard these mid-1950s Van Gelder-mastered Prestige originals as warmer and more immediate than later Bergenfield-era repressings, though the mono masters can sound somewhat boxy by modern standards, reflecting 1953-54 tape and small-room recording limitations rather than the cutting itself. There is no audiophile reissue series (Analogue Productions, Music Matters, etc.) specifically for Blue Haze, so within its own reissue lineage this NYC first pressing sits at the top, followed by the 1958 Bergenfield second pressing, and further below by 1960s Prestige/Fantasy reprints and later OJC reissues, which use further-generation tape masters and are generally considered sonically inferior.
albums.generalNotes: This is the original 1956 Prestige PRLP 7054 mono first pressing. The yellow/black fireworks label reads "PRESTIGE RECORDS INC. 446 W. 50th ST., N.Y.C." with "HI FI" (not the later "HIGH FIDELITY"), and the vinyl shows a deep groove - the combination collectors use to distinguish this NYC-era issue from the 1958 Bergenfield, NJ second pressing. The deadwax transcription (RVG hand-etched, with AB and 1 machine-stamped codes) confirms Van Gelder-cut lacquers consistent with this first-pressing run; pressing was by Abbey Record Manufacturing Co. for Prestige. No later label variant elements (Bergenfield address, egg-yolk yellow, non-deep-groove pressing) are present on this copy.

albums.title: Blue Moods
albums.countryOfOrigin: Denmark (licensed pressing of the US Debut master, distributed by Skandinavisk Grammofon A/S)
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Britt Woodman (trombone), Teddy Charles (vibraphone, credited on label as "percussion"), Charles Mingus (bass), Elvin Jones (drums)
sides:
1. Nature Boy (Eden Ahbez)
2. Alone Together (Dietz - Schwartz)

3. There's No You (Adair - Hopper - Durgom)
4. Easy Living (Robin - Rainger)
albums.albumStory: Blue Moods was recorded on July 9, 1955, at Van Gelder Studio in Hackensack, New Jersey, for Charles Mingus and Max Roach's fiercely independent, artist-owned Debut Records, cut as Miles Davis was climbing back from the personal low point of his heroin years toward the triumphant Prestige and Columbia periods that followed within months. Rather than assembling a conventional hard-bop unit, Mingus paired Davis with an unusual chamber-jazz lineup built around Teddy Charles's vibraphone and Britt Woodman's trombone, with Mingus himself on bass and a young Elvin Jones on drums, producing a spare, unhurried session built on standards plus Mingus's own arrangement of "Alone Together" (the remaining tracks were arranged by Charles). The album's brevity - just four tunes across a lean twenty-seven minutes - and its moody, unhurried restraint anticipated the cool, spacious aesthetic Davis would refine within a few years on Kind of Blue, making it a small but telling document of Davis mid-transformation. Davis reportedly resented the unconventional instrumentation Mingus assigned him, and the resulting session captures an uneasy but fruitful tension between a leader eager to move forward and a co-op label pursuing its own experimental agenda. Blue Moods has long been regarded by historians less as a commercial landmark than as a fascinating way-station in Davis's stylistic evolution, and it remains a significant artifact of the short-lived but historically important Mingus-Roach Debut label. Critical assessment has generally been favorable if modest, with the album prized chiefly by collectors of Davis's complete discography and of the Debut catalogue rather than ranked among his major statements.
albums.lpNotes: Danish Debut pressing (c. 1957-early 1960s) - grey "debut" label with "MADE IN DENMARK" rim text, licensed by Skandinavisk Grammofon A/S/Brande Boghandel; stamped DEB-120-A/DEB-120-B matrices, not the 1955 US first pressing.
albums.labelNotes: The label photos show the grey Debut label with the star-topped script "debut" logo and small "33 1/3 rpm LONGPLAY" banner, with "MADE IN DENMARK" arced at the top rim in place of the New York street address printed on the 1955 US original grey label. Danish label history (documented via steppeulvene.com and Danish discography sources) records that in 1957 the Brande Boghandel bookshop, working with Skandinavisk Grammofon A/S, secured rights to press the American Debut catalogue for the Scandinavian market, retaining the original US catalogue number (DEB 120) and cover artwork. That places this copy in the post-1957 Danish licensed pressing run - later than the true 1955 US first pressing but predating Debut's absorption into the Fantasy reissue program (1962) and the later French and OJC reissue generations. The stamped (rather than etched) DEB-120-A/DEB-120-B matrix format is consistent with an early-generation Danish plate rather than a later re-cut, though without a runout photo the exact stamper/plant details cannot be confirmed beyond the label design itself.
albums.fidelity: The back cover documents the original 1955 mastering approach: cut at 160 lines per inch instead of the usual 210-260, deliberately widening and deepening the grooves to allow greater bass extension and level - a hallmark of the Debut/Mingus-supervised Van Gelder cutting rather than a later remaster. This Danish pressing reproduces that mastering philosophy via a European-cut lacquer derived from the US plates/tape rather than the original US metal parts, so fidelity is generally regarded by collectors as respectable but a step below a clean US first pressing pressed directly from Van Gelder's original masters. Steve Hoffman forum consensus favors the original 1955 US Debut pressing or the 1962 Fantasy red-vinyl reissue for the most faithful, full-bodied transfer, with the Danish pressing occupying a middle tier and the later French fake-stereo and OJC reissues ranked lowest in the overall fidelity hierarchy. Surface quality on Danish Debut pressings varies by copy since the exact stamping/plant chain is not independently documented.
albums.generalNotes: This is a Danish licensed Debut pressing of DEB-120, not the 1955 US first pressing, produced under the Brande Boghandel/Skandinavisk Grammofon A/S arrangement that began in 1957. The "MADE IN DENMARK" rim text on an otherwise US-style grey Debut label, paired with stamped (not later fake-stereo etched) DEB-120-A/B matrices, places this within the early Danish run rather than the 1960s French or US reissue lines. Cover and label copy reproduce the original 1955 back-cover text and mastering notes verbatim, indicating the Danish pressing used plates derived from the US artwork and liner notes rather than a redesigned Scandinavian issue. No runout photo was supplied, so stamper/plant-level confirmation beyond the label design itself is not possible.

albums.title: Decoy
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet, synthesizer), John Scofield (guitar), Branford Marsalis (soprano saxophone), Bill Evans (soprano/tenor sax, flute, electric piano), Robert Irving III (synthesizer, electric drum programming), Darryl 'The Munch' Jones (electric bass), Al Foster (drums), Mino Cinelu (percussion), Gil Evans (arranger on 'That's Right')
sides:
1. Decoy
2. Robot 415
3. Code M.D.
4. Freaky Deaky

1. What It Is
2. That's Right
3. That's What Happened
albums.albumStory: Decoy, released in June 1984, captures Miles Davis deep into his 1980s electric comeback following his return from retirement with The Man with the Horn and We Want Miles. The album blends dense, moody electro-funk grooves largely shaped with young keyboardist Robert Irving III alongside more open, guitar-driven material co-written with John Scofield, who was becoming an increasingly important foil in Davis's working band. Two tracks were captured live at the 1983 Montreal jazz festival, giving the record a mix of tightly produced studio funk and looser stage improvisation, while 'That's Right' features an arrangement by longtime collaborator Gil Evans, tying the record back to one of Davis's most significant artistic partnerships. Branford Marsalis and Bill Evans trade soprano saxophone duties on the album, underlining Davis's continued interest in showcasing new talent even as he leaned harder into synthesizers and programmed drums. Sitting between the more polished Star People and the pop-facing You're Under Arrest, Decoy is often viewed by critics as a transitional, moodier entry in Davis's 1980s catalog, and it earned a Grammy nomination for Best Jazz Fusion Performance. Its cool, brooding atmosphere and rhythm-forward writing helped cement the template Davis continued exploring through the rest of the decade, making it a key document of his evolution from acoustic hard bop pioneer to electric innovator.
albums.lpNotes: 1984 US Columbia FC 38991 original pressing - red 'walking eye' label, Masterdisk-cut AL/BL-38991-1B lacquers, gatefold jacket.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the standard 1984 red Columbia 'walking eye' label with catalog number FC 38991 and AL/BL-38991 matrix prefixes typical of Columbia's early-1980s in-house pressing scheme, under which titles were simultaneously stamped from Masterdisk lacquers at multiple CBS-owned plants (Pitman NJ, Terre Haute IN, Carrollton GA, Santa Maria CA) with differing stamper suffix letters. The -1B suffix on both sides places this among the earlier stamper generations cut shortly after the album's June 1984 release, though the multi-plant simultaneous release model makes precise plant identification from the matrix alone unreliable without a visible etched plant symbol. Columbia's 'walking eye' red label design was standard for the label throughout the late 1970s into the mid-1980s, so the label art itself only confirms the general era, not a specific pressing run. There is no meaningful first-pressing premium structure for this title as with rarer jazz LPs - all early-80s domestic Columbia pressings of Decoy trade in a narrow, low price band regardless of exact stamper letter.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Bob Ludwig at Masterdisk from the original 1984 mix; this era of Columbia pressings is generally well regarded for a clean, punchy cut of Davis's synth-heavy 1980s productions, though the studio mix itself (dense synths, programmed drums) limits ultimate sonic transparency compared to his acoustic-era Columbia LPs. Collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv generally treat the various early-80s domestic Columbia stampers (-1A through -1E) as sonically similar, with no consensus 'best' stamper commanding a premium. There is no audiophile reissue series (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, etc.) for Decoy, so this original Masterdisk-cut Columbia pressing remains the best commercially available vinyl fidelity reference for the album, ahead of later Sony/Legacy CD remasters for tonal warmth if not ultimate noise floor.
albums.generalNotes: 1984 Columbia FC 38991 - standard domestic US first-issue pressing. Red 'walking eye' Columbia labels with matching AL-38991-1B / BL-38991-1B Masterdisk matrix numbers on both sides confirm an early-stamper US pressing from Columbia's multi-plant simultaneous release run for this title. No club-edition text, promo markings, or foreign rim text are present, indicating a standard retail US copy rather than a Columbia House or export pressing. Barcode and copyright date (1984 CBS Inc.) on the jacket are consistent with a first-year pressing.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in Los Angeles in January 1965, E.S.P. documents the studio debut of Miles Davis's celebrated "Second Great Quintet" - Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, and Tony Williams - the first time this exact lineup appeared together on record following Shorter's arrival to complete the group. Almost the entire program consists of new originals contributed by the bandmembers themselves rather than standards, signaling a deliberate turn toward a freer, more abstract compositional and harmonic language. The album arrived at a pivotal juncture in Davis's career, following his mid-1960s live work and preceding the increasingly exploratory studio albums (Miles Smiles, Nefertiti, Sorcerer) that would follow through 1968. Its loosened rhythmic interplay and open harmonic frameworks, especially from Williams and Hancock, proved enormously influential on the development of post-bop and would help set the template for the
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing era (mono, 1965) - Columbia CL 2350; red 2-eye label with "Nonbreakable" text, Pitman plant etch in runout.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the classic red Columbia "2-eye" mono label - twin oval "eye" logos at 9 and 3 o'clock, "360 Sound" arced in white at the bottom, "MONO" and "Nonbreakable" text beneath the catalog number - the design Columbia used circa 1963-1966 before phasing out mono LPs around 1967-68. The catalog number CL 2350 with matrix XLP 79816-1B / XLP 79817-1A and a "P" etch confirms pressing at Columbia's Records Pressing Plant in Pitman, New Jersey, one of the East Coast plants used for early runs of this title. The rim reads "Printed in U.S.A." with no later orange-rim or 1-eye era text, and the presence of "Nonbreakable" (dropped from slightly later 2-eye pressings) supports placing this squarely in the earliest 1965 pressing run rather than the circa-1967 2-eye reissue that dropped that text.
albums.fidelity: This mono mix was mastered from the original 1965 Columbia session tapes; 2-eye era Columbia mono pressings of E.S.P. are well-regarded on forums.stevehoffman.tv for their punchy, immediate sound typical of mid-60s Columbia jazz mono cuts, though quality can vary somewhat between the Pitman and Terre Haute plants used for this title. This Pitman 2-eye mono pressing sits at the top of the fidelity hierarchy for E.S.P., ahead of the circa-1967 2-eye stereo-only reissue and the later 1-eye orange-rim stereo reissues; dedicated audiophile reissues of this specific title are scarce, so a clean vintage 2-eye mono copy like this remains the benchmark for collectors chasing the original sound.
albums.generalNotes: 1965 Columbia CL 2350 mono pressing in the red 2-eye label era (used c.1963-1966), consistent with an original first-pressing-run copy. Matrix XLP 79816-1B / XLP 79817-1A with a "P" etch confirms Pitman, New Jersey plant manufacture, one of the plants used for early East Coast pressings of this title. albums.albumStory: Recorded live over a Friday and Saturday night residency in April 1961 at the Blackhawk club in San Francisco, this album captures Miles Davis's working quintet with Hank Mobley on tenor in place of the departed John Coltrane, backed by the redoubtable rhythm section of Wynton Kelly, Paul Chambers and Jimmy Cobb. Columbia split the sprawling club tapes into two companion LPs, "Friday Night" (Volume I) and "Saturday Night" (Volume II), giving listeners an unusually intimate, in-the-room document of Davis on the bandstand rather than in the studio. The set leans on staples from his repertoire - "Walkin'," "Bye Bye Blackbird," "All Of You" - alongside the originals "No Blues" and the closing theme "Bye Bye," played with the loose, extended-solo freedom of a working club date. Mobley's presence has often been overshadowed by Coltrane's tenure, but the Blackhawk tapes are among the best surviving evidence of his stint with Davis and of a quintet quietly transitioning toward the more exploratory band Davis would assemble later in the decade. Critically, the album has long been regarded as a solid if secondary entry in Davis's vast Columbia discography - valued less for innovation than for its relaxed documentation of a great small group at work. It remains a touchstone for collectors of Davis's early-1960s Columbia period and of live hard-bop recording in general.
albums.lpNotes: 1st-era pressing (mono, 1961) - Columbia six-eye red label, CL 1669, matrix XLP 53548-1C/53549-1A.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the classic Columbia "six-eye" mono label: red field, "COLUMBIA" arched in white across the top, six small CBS-eye logos alternating with red/black flag panels around the rim, and the "LP" trademark medallion with "MARCAS REG. MADE IN U.S.A." at the bottom - the standard Columbia mono design used from roughly 1955 through 1962. CL 1669 was first issued in August/September 1961, squarely inside the six-eye label's production window, so a six-eye copy of this catalog number is consistent with (though not conclusive proof of) a first-pressing timeframe rather than the later two-eye or "360 Sound" redesigns that replaced it from 1962 onward. The mono CL-prefix and "NONBREAKABLE" text (no STEREO banner) confirm this is the mono edition, distinct from the parallel six-eye stereo CS 8469 issue. Matrix numbers XLP 53548/53549 with letter-suffix stampers (1C/1A) are period-correct Columbia lacquer/stamper codes for the original 1961 mastering rather than a later re-cut, though without a deadwax photo the precise stamper generation and deep-groove presence can't be confirmed beyond the label evidence.
albums.fidelity: The original 1961 Columbia mono cut was mastered from the Blackhawk club tapes recorded under producer Irving Townsend; as a live nightclub recording it has inherent room noise, imperfect balance and a warmer but narrower dynamic range than a studio date. Steve Hoffman-forum consensus generally favors the mono mix for cohesion on this title, though the stereo CS 8469 spreads the horns and rhythm section more distinctly. Six-eye era Columbia pressings are typically well-cut and reasonably quiet for the period, but this title has since been surpassed in fidelity by the expanded, newly-mastered 2003 Columbia/Legacy "Complete" box (engineered by Mark Wilder from the original tapes) and by the audiophile-grade 2021 Mosaic/Craft vinyl box of the complete Blackhawk sessions, both of which offer cleaner transfers and fuller unedited performances than the original single LP.

albums.albumStory: Jazz Track brings together two pivotal but very different Miles Davis dates: the improvised score he recorded in Paris on December 4-5, 1957 for Louis Malle's "Ascenseur pour l'échafaud," and three standards cut in New York on May 26, 1958 with the sextet that would soon record Kind of Blue. The Paris session is one of jazz's most celebrated instances of scoring to picture on the spot, with Davis and a mostly French pickup band reportedly improvising while watching projected footage, yielding a spare, atmospheric music that helped define the vocabulary of jazz film scoring. The New York side documents the first studio pairing of Davis with Bill Evans alongside Cannonball Adderley, John Coltrane, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb, the same lineup that would shortly make Kind of Blue, and its reading of "Stella By Starlight" is widely regarded by musicians and critics as among the finest on record. Arriving at the hinge between Davis's hard-bop years on Prestige and his modal breakthroughs of 1959, the album shows him working in two starkly different contexts within months of each other. Assembling a European film score alongside a domestic studio date made for an unusual pairing, but it preserved both performances for American audiences before the film's own soundtrack saw domestic release. Critically the record has often stood in the shadow of Davis's more unified statements, yet the Evans-Adderley-Coltrane tracks are prized as essential precursors to Kind of Blue and the Paris material remains a touchstone of jazz-and-film history.

albums.albumStory: Recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York across two sessions in March and April 1959, Kind of Blue grew out of Miles Davis's growing interest in modal composition, an approach he had begun testing on "Milestones" the year before, trading dense chord changes for simple scalar frameworks that opened up space for improvisation. Davis reportedly brought the band only brief sketches rather than fully written charts, asking his sidemen to improvise around scales and moods encountered largely for the first time in the studio, a method the original liner notes by pianist Bill Evans compared to the direct, unrevisable brushwork of Japanese ink painting. The sextet assembled for the date - Davis, John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb, with Wynton Kelly sitting in for "Freddie Freeloader" - represented an extraordinary concentration of talent, several of whom would soon lead their own historically important groups. The album arrived at a pivotal juncture in Davis's career, following his hard-bop and cool-toned work for Prestige and early Columbia, and it redirected jazz improvisation toward modality just as Ornette Coleman and others pushed the music toward free forms by a different route. Kind of Blue is widely regarded as the best-selling and most influential jazz album ever made, cited by generations of musicians across jazz, rock, and classical music as a foundational listening experience, and it remains a fixture of best-albums lists and jazz history curricula. Its restrained, spacious lyricism - epitomized by "So What" and "Blue in Green" - demonstrated that jazz improvisation could be harmonically simple and emotionally profound at once, cementing the album's legacy as a touchstone of twentieth-century American music.
albums.lpNotes: Early six-eye mono pressing (Columbia CL 1355) - deep groove label, XLP47324-1B / XLP47325-1C runout stampers, an early but not the absolute first (-1A/-1A) stamper generation.
albums.labelNotes: The label photos show Columbia's red "six-eye" design (six small "eye" logos around the rim, "Guaranteed High Fidelity" text at the top of the label field, deep groove visible around the spindle hole, and "NONBREAKABLE" printed under the catalog number) on both sides - a design Columbia used roughly 1958 into the early 1960s before switching to flat-edge (non-deep-groove) six-eye labels and, later, the 1968+ "360 Sound" text. The runout stampers, XLP47324-1B (Side 1) and XLP47325-1C (Side 2), are documented by LondonJazzCollector's matrix study as among the earliest lacquer generations used on the commercial mono release (1A/1B/1C being the earliest letters found), placing this copy just behind the true first -1A/-1A pairing. Combined, the deep-groove six-eye label and low-letter stampers place this copy firmly in the 1959-1961 first-issue manufacturing window, ahead of the later flat-edge six-eye pressings and far ahead of the 360 Sound reissues.
albums.fidelity: The mono mix of Kind of Blue is generally preferred by collectors and engineers over the original stereo master, since the stereo reels were affected by a tape machine running slightly fast/slow during the sessions, a flaw largely sidestepped on the mono tape; this six-eye mono pressing sits near the top of the album's fidelity hierarchy for that reason. Early six-eye Columbia pressings from this era used relatively high-quality lacquers and pressings by Columbia's own plants, and Steve Hoffman forum consensus generally rates original six-eye mono copies (especially early-stamper ones like -1B/-1C) as warmer and more three-dimensional than later reissues. Later benchmarks include the 1997 Mark Wilder Columbia/Legacy remaster, the 2009 Sony Legacy 50th-anniversary mono LP reissue (cut from analog tape), and the Analogue Productions/Classic Records audiophile stereo reissues; most forum listeners still rank an early six-eye mono original like this one above those later cuts for tonal warmth, even though the later audiophile stereo pressings offer superior surface noise and channel separation.

Deep groove labels, the "Guaranteed High Fidelity" six-eye design, and the "NONBREAKABLE" rim text all point to manufacture in the 1959-1961 window, before Columbia dropped the deep groove and years before the 1968 switch to "360 Sound" labels. The runout stampers, -1B on Side 1 and -1C on Side 2, indicate an early stamper generation close to (but one or two removed from) the true first -1A/-1A pairing prized by specialists. The jacket's misspelling of "Cannonball" Adderley's surname as "Adderly" and drummer Jimmy Cobb's name as "James Cobb" are consistent with the original-issue back cover text used on early copies of this title.

albums.albumStory: Miles Davis and Horns splices together two formative Prestige sessions: a January 17, 1951 date, Davis's first for the label and his first time recording alongside Sonny Rollins, and a February 19, 1953 session built entirely around compositions and arrangements by tenor saxophonist Al Cohn. The 1951 session paired Davis's trumpet with trombonist Bennie Green and pianist John Lewis in a three-horn front line, producing originals like Davis's own "Down" and Lewis's "Morpheus" alongside standards such as "Blue Room" and "Whispering." The 1953 date brought together Cohn and Zoot Sims, two tenor players closely associated with the Woody Herman "Four Brothers" sound, with trombonist Sonny Truitt and a rhythm section anchored by Lewis and Kenny Clarke, yielding tightly arranged pieces like "Tasty Pudding" and "Willie The Wailer." Together the sessions capture Davis moving beyond his bebop apprenticeship and the Birth of the Cool dates toward the leaner, more blues-rooted voice that would soon define hard bop. Prestige compiled the material into this 12-inch LP in 1956, just as Davis's first great quintet was establishing him as a major bandleader, making the record a valuable document of his pre-stardom collaborations with Rollins, Cohn, Sims, and Lewis.

Because the underlying 1951 and 1953 sessions predate Prestige's regular contemporary Van Gelder engineering, the sound has somewhat limited dynamic range and added period reverberation compared to a full mid-1950s Van Gelder session tape, but this remains the most immediate and collectible cut of the material. Later Bergenfield-era fireworks pressings can still draw on related Van Gelder metal and sound respectable, while the 1980s OJC reissue is a serviceable but lower-fidelity budget alternative; there is no dedicated Tone Poet, Music Matters, or Analogue Productions audiophile edition of this specific title.

albums.albumStory: Recorded live on the evening of May 19, 1961, this album documents a benefit concert at Carnegie Hall that marked a unique convergence in Miles Davis's career: his working quintet, featuring Hank Mobley on tenor sax alongside the rhythm section of Wynton Kelly, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb, performing both standalone and backed by a 21-piece orchestra arranged and conducted by Gil Evans, Davis's most important large-ensemble collaborator. The program mixed hard-bop quintet vehicles like "So What" and "No Blues" with orchestral reworkings drawn from the Miles Ahead/Sketches of Spain vein, including Ahmad Jamal's "New Rhumba" and "The Meaning of the Blues," giving listeners a rare live document of the Evans-Davis orchestral sound performed in concert rather than assembled in the studio. Coming at a transitional moment for Davis - between the classic quintet years and his later shift toward Wayne Shorter and a more modal, exploratory direction - the record captures him at a peak of technical and expressive command, with contemporary critics singling out the trumpet's tone and the drama of the evening. Critical reaction at the time, excerpted on the original jacket from the New York Times, New York Herald Tribune, and Down Beat, was enthusiastic, with reviewers noting Davis's shift from restraint to an impassioned, brassy exuberance over the course of the performance. The album stands as an important entry in the Davis-Evans discography, valued both as a rare live big-band jazz recording and as a document of Davis's showmanship and interpretive range mid-career, and it remains a touchstone for listeners tracing the arc from Miles Ahead and Sketches of Spain through his live performance practice of the early 1960s.

Because promotional copies were drawn from the same early pressing runs sent to press and radio ahead of/at general release, the 6-eye demo label indicates this is a first-pressing-era pressing, distinguished from a general commercial 6-eye copy only by its promotional overprint and lack of a for-sale designation.

As a promotional pressing drawn from early stampers, sound quality should be comparable to a standard 6-eye commercial mono copy of similar vintage, i.e., among the better-sounding versions of this title. No audiophile remaster (Mobile Fidelity, Analogue Productions, Music Matters, etc.) of this specific live album is known to exist, so within the album's fidelity hierarchy this 6-eye mono pressing sits at or near the top, well above the electronically re-channeled stereo pressings and later 2-eye/orange-label reissues.

albums.albumStory: Porgy and Bess was the second full orchestral collaboration between Miles Davis and arranger-conductor Gil Evans, recorded over four sessions at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in July and August 1958, with Davis's trumpet and flugelhorn taking the vocal roles of George and Ira Gershwin's 1935 folk opera (book and lyrics co-written by DuBose Heyward). Evans reworked the opera's songs into dense, brooding voicings for a large ensemble of brass, reeds, and French horns built specifically around the color and phrasing of Davis's horn rather than a conventional big-band chart, pushing jazz orchestration into new territory. The record arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, sandwiched between the hard-bop small-group work of his mid-50s quintet/sextet and the modal breakthroughs of Kind of Blue, recorded only months later, and its spacious, harmonically open writing is widely heard as a direct precursor to that watershed album. Alto saxophonist Cannonball Adderley appears on the sessions though he went uncredited on the original jacket, a detail that has fed decades of critical and fan discussion. Porgy and Bess has been consistently ranked among the finest Davis-Evans collaborations and among the great orchestral jazz albums of its era, prized for its emotional depth on a program built entirely of other composers' material, and it remains a cornerstone in assessments of both Davis's interpretive genius and Evans's arranging artistry; it was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2000.

As a deep-groove 6-eye pressing this sits at or very near the top of the vintage fidelity hierarchy for CL 1274, just below only the earliest-stamper commercial copies in strict collector terms since promo copies were cut and pressed from the same early metalwork as initial retail runs. The 2020 Mobile Fidelity 45RPM 2xLP is a more recent audiophile alternative praised for openness and detail but derives from later-generation tape sources rather than the original mono cut, so mono purists still favor a clean original 6-eye pressing like this one.

albums.albumStory: Round About Midnight was Miles Davis's debut for Columbia Records, cut at Columbia's New York studios in sessions spanning October 1955 and June and September 1956 while Davis was still technically finishing out his Prestige contract. It introduced his first great quintet - John Coltrane, Red Garland, Paul Chambers and Philly Joe Jones - a working band whose telepathic interplay reshaped small-group jazz and set Coltrane on the path to his own landmark career. Anchored by a moody reworking of Thelonious Monk's title tune, the program mixes standards ('All of You,' 'Bye Bye Blackbird') with bebop repertoire (Charlie Parker's 'Ah-Leu-Cha,' Tadd Dameron's 'Tadd's Delight'), spotlighting Davis's newly matured, harmon-muted lyricism against Coltrane's harder-edged tenor attack. The record marked Davis's leap from Prestige's hard-bop scene to a major label's resources and promotional reach, opening the decade of landmark Columbia albums that followed. It is widely regarded as a cornerstone of hard bop and one of the defining quintet statements of the mid-1950s, later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. Its blend of restraint, harmonic sophistication and controlled intensity has kept it a fixture on best-jazz-album lists and an essential document of Davis's transformation from bebop sideman to major bandleader.

Discogs documents several sub-variants of this 6-eye deep-groove issue distinguished mainly by stamper suffix (1A through 1K observed on side A) rather than by a differently laid-out label; this copy's stamped runout (XLP39109-1A / XLP39110-1A) matches the lowest, earliest-documented stamper pair for the catalog number. Within the album's overall fidelity hierarchy this early six-eye deep-groove mono sits at or near the top, ranked above the later 2-eye 'Guaranteed High Fidelity' mono, the 1970s orange-label reissue, and the stereo/rechanneled CS 8649 pressings. It is generally considered comparable to, and by some vintage-mono purists preferred over, the 2013 Sony Legacy/Kevin Gray-mastered 180g mono reissue and the Mobile Fidelity SACD, which are praised for added clarity but not universally judged to surpass the original six-eye pressing's tonal character.

albums.albumStory: Recorded across two sessions in Hollywood and New York in the spring of 1963, Seven Steps To Heaven captures Miles Davis at a pivotal transitional moment, moving away from the classic quintet sound of the late 1950s toward the more exploratory group that would soon feature Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter and Tony Williams alongside Wayne Shorter. The Hollywood tracks feature a short-lived West Coast lineup with Victor Feldman and Frank Butler, while the New York sessions introduced the teenage Tony Williams and a young Herbie Hancock, both of whom would become central to Davis's mid-1960s quintet. The album blends standards like 'Basin Street Blues' and 'I Fall in Love Too Easily' with the original title track, co-written by Feldman and Davis, which became a modern jazz standard in its own right. Critically, the record is viewed as a bridge album, less unified than the classic quintets that preceded and followed it, but historically important as the first appearance on record of the rhythm section that would soon revolutionize jazz. Its significance lies less in stylistic innovation on this particular record and more in personnel: it is the recorded birth certificate of the Hancock-Carter-Williams rhythm section under Davis's leadership. The album has remained a respected, if sometimes overlooked, entry in Davis's vast catalog, valued by historians for its transitional role between the hard-bop era and the more abstract, interactive small-group jazz Davis would pioneer through the mid-1960s.
albums.lpNotes: 1963 mono first pressing - Columbia CL 2051, red 2-eye 'Guaranteed High Fidelity' label, Pitman (P) plant stamper.
albums.labelNotes: The label photo shows a red Columbia label with a two-eye logo (one 'eye' block at 9 o'clock, one at 3 o'clock), 'GUARANTEED HIGH FIDELITY' arcing along the bottom rim, 'NONBREAKABLE' printed near the spindle, and 'PRINTED IN U.S.A.' with the Columbia trademark notice — no '360 SOUND' arc or gold/six-eye elements are present. Per bsnpubs' Columbia label timeline, this two-eye red mono design was standard from roughly 1961 through 1965, before Columbia shifted to the 'CBS/360 Sound' and later red/gold six-eye designs beginning c.1965-66. The catalog number CL 2051 (mono) versus CS 8851 (stereo, printed on the jacket) confirms this specific copy is the mono issue from the album's original 1963 release window. The matrix suffixes XLP-59702-1D and XLP-59703-1F with a 'P' plant stamp point to a Columbia Pitman, NJ pressing, one of several plants (also Terre Haute, Carrollton) used interchangeably for this high-demand title, which does not diminish first-pressing status since Columbia ran shared lacquers across plants simultaneously. Together, the label design and catalog configuration place this disc squarely in the first-issue mono pressing run.
albums.fidelity: This is a mono cut from the original 1963 Columbia analog masters; Columbia's early-1960s in-house mastering for Davis titles is generally well regarded by collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv, though not in the audiophile-legend tier of some Blue Note or Van Gelder jazz cuts. Pitman pressings from this era are generally solid, flat, quiet vinyl, comparable to Columbia's other major plants (Terre Haute, Carrollton) of the period. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy, this 2-eye mono original sits above later 1965+ six-eye/360 Sound reissues and generic budget reissues, but below modern audiophile treatments such as the Analogue Productions 45 RPM 2xLP stereo reissue, generally considered the sonic reference for this title. Mono collectors specifically prize the original CL 2051 pressing for its focused, punchy horn presence compared to the wider but sometimes thinner-sounding stereo mix of the era.

albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain grew out of Miles Davis's fascination with Spanish and Andalusian folk and classical music, sparked in part by hearing Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez and by flamenco encountered around the time of his marriage to Frances Taylor. Recorded across sessions in November 1959 and March 1960, it was the third and most ambitious of Davis's large-scale orchestral collaborations with arranger Gil Evans, following Miles Ahead and Porgy and Bess. Rather than a conventional jazz combo date, the album places Davis's trumpet and flugelhorn as a singular, vocal-like voice floating over Evans's dense, classically inflected orchestrations for woodwinds, brass, and percussion, with almost no traditional swing rhythm section driving the music. The adagio movement from the Concierto became one of the most recognized themes in the jazz repertoire. The record arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, sandwiched between the modal breakthroughs of Kind of Blue and his subsequent quintet work, and it cemented his reputation as an artist unafraid to reshape jazz's boundaries. Critically it was hailed on release as a bold, atmospheric triumph and has remained one of the most acclaimed and influential orchestral jazz albums ever made, frequently cited alongside Kind of Blue and Miles Ahead as a high-water mark of the Davis-Evans partnership.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1960) - Columbia 6-eye deep-groove label, no CBS text, matrix XLP 49956/49957-1A.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries Columbia's earliest "6-eye" red label design: "COLUMBIA" arched across the top in white, six small eye-in-triangle logos ringing the label (three per side), a circled "LP" logo at bottom center, no "CBS" branding anywhere, and the abbreviated credit "Orch. arranged and conducted by Gil Evans." This design, paired with a deep-groove ring pressed near the label edge, was Columbia's standard label from the mid-1950s until it was phased out for the two-eye and later "Guaranteed High Fidelity" black-label styles around 1961-62. Discogs documents numerous stamper variants for CL 1480 (1A through the 1AK+ range, plus Hollywood "H" and Terre Haute "T" plant suffixes); the -1A suffix on both sides here places this pressing among the earliest stamper generations run at the outset of production, i.e., very near the front of the original mono pressing run rather than a later reground stamper. No plant letter (H/T) appears in the transcribed runout, so the specific pressing plant cannot be confirmed from the data provided.
albums.fidelity: This is an original 1960 Columbia mono cut, mastered from the analog session tapes at the dawn of Columbia's in-house mastering era; 6-eye deep-groove pressings are widely regarded by collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv as the most natural, warm, and dynamically alive versions of this recording, especially in mono, which best represents Gil Evans's dense orchestration without the phasing artifacts of the era's stereo mixdowns. Later 2-eye and black-label Columbia reissues (mid-1960s onward) are generally considered a step down in vinyl quality and mastering freshness. Modern audiophile reissues - Mobile Fidelity's 2013 MFSL 1-375 (mono/stereo) and the more recent MoFi UHQR/standard 2025 pressing - are praised for quietness and clarity but some forum listeners find them slightly more polite or bass-heavy than the vintage 6-eye cut; among vintage and modern options, a clean original 6-eye mono like this one remains the benchmark reference pressing for many collectors, with the best modern reissues competing closely but not universally preferred.

albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain (1960) was the third and most ambitious orchestral collaboration between Miles Davis and arranger Gil Evans, following Miles Ahead and Porgy and Bess. Davis brought Evans a classical guitar recording of Joaquín Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, and Evans built an entire suite around it plus original and traditional Spanish- and flamenco-inflected material, scoring for a large studio orchestra of brass, woodwinds, harp and percussion rather than a conventional jazz combo. Recorded across sessions in late 1959 and early 1960 at Columbia's 30th Street Studio, the sessions were famously arduous, requiring extensive splicing and studio craft from Evans and producer Teo Macero to assemble the finished performances. The album arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, between the modal breakthrough of Kind of Blue and his later 1960s quintet work, showcasing his ability to function as a lyrical soloist within dense, painterly orchestral textures rather than a small-group improviser. It is widely regarded as a landmark of Third Stream and orchestral jazz, prized for Evans's lush, dissonant voicings and Davis's aching, vocal-like trumpet and flugelhorn tone on pieces like Saeta and Solea. Critically acclaimed on release and ever since, it remains one of the most celebrated fusions of jazz improvisation with classical and Spanish folk idioms, cited by generations of critics and musicians as a high-water mark for both Davis and Evans.
albums.lpNotes: 1998 Classic Records CS 8271-200g reissue — white-label, unnumbered TEST PRESSING in generic Classic Records jacket, not a retail copy.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries plain white Classic Records 'TEST PRESSING' labels with no printed catalog or track text, housed in a generic Classic Records white jacket bearing a typed sticker reading 'Classic Records CS 8271-200g A/B CRWH.' Classic Records began its 200-gram Quiex SV-P audiophile reissue program licensing Columbia/Sony masters in the late 1990s, with Bernie Grundman cutting new lacquers for titles including this one, Kind of Blue, and other Columbia jazz staples; the BG etch (CS 8271-A BG / CS 8271-B BG) confirms this pedigree. As a pre-release test pressing it sits ahead of and outside the normal retail run in the pressing hierarchy, representing the mastering/plant quality-check stage rather than the standard-issue copy with printed Classic Records labels. The blank white labels and hand-typed jacket sticker match documented Classic Records test-pressing practice, which typically produced small, unnumbered runs distributed internally or to select accounts.
albums.fidelity: Bernie Grundman remastered this edition from analog Columbia tapes for Classic Records' 200-gram Quiex SV-P Super Vinyl Profile, and collector consensus on forums.stevehoffman.tv generally rates this cut as a strong, dynamic all-analog alternative to vintage Columbia pressings, praised for bass weight and clarity though occasionally noted as slightly forward in the upper midrange, a trait sometimes associated with Grundman's Classic Records work. As a test pressing, this copy represents the mastering chain ahead of any later-stamper drift, theoretically offering the most faithful transfer of Grundman's cut. In the album's overall fidelity hierarchy it ranks below a pristine original 1960 Columbia 6-eye stereo pressing (the tape-fresh benchmark most Steve Hoffman forum members prefer) but above later Columbia reissues, and is generally considered comparable to or slightly favored over the 2013 Mobile Fidelity 180g half-speed remaster by fans of heavier, all-analog cuts, though MFSL is often cited as quieter and more refined by others.

The plain white 'TEST PRESSING' labels (no track/catalog text) and the generic Classic Records jacket with a typed 'CS 8271-200g A/B CRWH' sticker are consistent with pre-production quality-control copies made ahead of the commercial run. Runout etchings CS 8271-A BG / CS 8271-B BG confirm Bernie Grundman as mastering engineer, matching the documented 1998 200g Quiex SV-P edition. albums.albumStory: Recorded in 1984-85 at the Record Plant in New York, You're Under Arrest was Miles Davis's penultimate studio album for Columbia and the third of his 1980s comeback releases following The Man with the Horn and Decoy. Working closely with co-producer and keyboardist Robert Irving III, Davis folded contemporary pop material into his electric fusion sound, reworking Michael Jackson's "Human Nature" and Cyndi Lauper's "Time After Time" as vehicles for his muted trumpet alongside politically charged originals touching on apartheid, nuclear anxiety and police surveillance. The sessions marked guitarist John McLaughlin's return to a Davis record for the first time since 1972's On the Corner, while bassist Darryl Jones's connections brought in a young Sting to voice a menacing police interrogator on the title-referencing opener. The record stands as a document of Davis reasserting commercial relevance in the MTV era, pairing drum-machine grooves and synthesizers with jazz improvisation in a way that polarized critics and longtime followers who felt the pop covers marked a departure from his acoustic legacy. It reinforced Davis's late-career reputation as an artist willing to court mainstream pop audiences on his own terms, and remains a key touchstone in discussions of his controversial 1980s output.

albums.albumStory: Walkin' brings together two April 1954 sessions recorded by Rudy Van Gelder at his Hackensack home studio, pairing two different Davis groups on one LP. Side one preserves the all-star sextet date built around extended blues performances, while side two features the quieter, harmonically searching quintet session with Davey Schildkraut. The thirteen-minute title track became a defining early Davis statement, its patient, blues-soaked momentum helping steer modern jazz from crowded bebop virtuosity toward the emerging hard-bop language, and it became a durable concert anthem for Davis. 'Solar' became one of the most frequently played Davis-associated compositions, though later research tied it closely to Chuck Wayne's earlier tune. Horace Silver, Percy Heath and Kenny Clarke form an exceptionally sympathetic rhythm section across both dates, while Schildkraut's poised alto playing remains one of the album's most underappreciated pleasures. Critics immediately regarded the set as a significant Davis release, and it has continued to rank among the finest modern jazz recordings of its era. The album captures Davis at a pivotal transitional moment, following his early-1950s struggles and just before the 1955 Newport appearance and first great quintet brought him wider fame.
albums.lpNotes: 1st-label early press (mono, 1957) - Prestige 446 W. 50th St. NYC fireworks DG labels; typed RVG + AB dead-wax codes.

Prestige used this 446 West 50th Street address on its 12-inch LPs from roughly 1955 into 1958, up to about PRLP 7141, before relocating to 203 South Washington Avenue, Bergenfield, New Jersey starting with PRLP 7141 in 1958. The jacket carries the matching 447 West 50th Street company address, the normal first-issue pairing with this label. Typed dead-wax codes RVG (Van Gelder) and AB (Abbey Record Manufacturing) with E/D metal letters place this within the original NYC-address pressing run, ahead of all Bergenfield-label and later Prestige reissues, though the letters alone don't confirm the earliest possible stamper.
albums.fidelity: This is a Rudy Van Gelder recording and original Van Gelder mono cut, pressed by Abbey Record Manufacturing; the RVG/AB dead-wax combination preserves the close, immediate horn sound typical of mid-1950s Prestige. Original Prestige pressings can carry more surface noise and less refined vinyl than contemporaneous Blue Note pressings due to economical manufacturing, but a clean deep-groove RVG copy offers the most period-correct presence and tonal density. Later 1960s Bergenfield-label pressings can still sound strong from RVG-derived metal, while 1980s OJC copies are typically cleaner but somewhat brighter and less authoritative. The 2009 RVG Remaster and the newer Kevin Gray/Craft all-analog RTI edition are quieter and more polished, with Gray's cut the strongest modern-fidelity option, though neither displaces an original NYC-label RVG/AB pressing for historical and collector priority.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in a single session at Rudy Van Gelder's Hackensack home studio on June 7, 1955, The Musings of Miles was Miles Davis's first 12-inch LP, arriving as Prestige began issuing full-length albums instead of 10-inch discs. It captures Davis fronting a quartet with Red Garland, Oscar Pettiford, and Philly Joe Jones - the same rhythm-section chemistry (minus Coltrane) that would soon anchor his celebrated First Great Quintet. The material mixes standards like "Will You Still Be Mine?" and Dizzy Gillespie's "A Night in Tunisia" with Davis originals "I Didn't" and "Green Haze," showcasing his increasingly lyrical, harmonically spare trumpet approach in the years just before his major-label breakthrough. The album arrived at a pivotal career moment, as Davis rebuilt momentum that culminated later that year in his triumphant appearance at the 1955 Newport Jazz Festival. It is valued as an important document of Davis's mid-1950s transitional style and the formation of his rhythm-section partnerships, and remains a touchstone for collectors tracing the emergence of hard bop out of bebop.

albums.albumStory: Cookin' With the Miles Davis Quintet was assembled from two marathon single-day sessions, May 11 and October 26, 1956, that Davis booked to fulfill his Prestige contract before moving to Columbia Records. Rather than a carefully planned studio project, producer Bob Weinstock simply had the working quintet - Davis, John Coltrane, Red Garland, Paul Chambers, and Philly Joe Jones - run through its live club repertoire in one or two takes with no overdubs, capturing the band's road-tested interplay at its peak. The results, later parceled across four LPs (Cookin', Relaxin', Workin', Steamin'), are prized as some of the most unguarded, natural small-group jazz of the era, pairing standards like the ballad feature with hard-swinging vehicles by Sonny Rollins and Davis himself. This was the first great Miles Davis Quintet with Coltrane, a group whose brief run reshaped both men's careers and became a cornerstone of hard bop small-group vocabulary. Critics and historians have long ranked the quintet's chemistry here among the most influential in jazz, and the album is consistently cited among the essential entries in the Davis-Coltrane discography.

The back cover's "447 West 50th Street" address is a minor, well-documented in-house discrepancy on original-era Prestige jackets and does not indicate a later pressing. Modern audiophile cuts such as Analogue Productions' 200g APRJ 7094 (Kevin Gray) offer quieter, high-fidelity surfaces but are generally regarded as smoother and less raw than this original. The Abbey Record Mfg. pressing here is a solid, standard-quality period plant job rather than a premium pressing, but the early metal generation is the decisive factor for sound quality.

albums.albumStory: Louis Malle's 1958 film noir Ascenseur Pour L'Échafaud became a landmark of jazz-and-cinema collaboration when Miles Davis, in Paris in December 1957, improvised the score overnight with a pickup quintet of Barney Wilen, René Urtreger, Pierre Michelot and Kenny Clarke, reacting spontaneously to the film's projected rushes without written charts. The spare, modal result is widely regarded as the first great jazz film score and a key stepping stone toward the modal explorations Davis pursued the following year on Kind of Blue. This compilation pairs that soundtrack with two related French scores: Art Blakey and The Jazz Messengers' music for Édouard Molinaro's Des Femmes Disparaissent (1958), featuring the classic Golson-Morgan-Timmons-Merritt lineup, and Barney Wilen's score for Molinaro's Un Témoin Dans La Ville, played by a quintet with Kenny Dorham and Duke Jordan. Together the sessions capture a vivid transatlantic moment when touring American beboppers collided with the French Nouvelle Vague, producing mood-driven, largely improvised jazz that shaped the sound of European crime cinema. The Davis score has been repeatedly cited by critics as a model of economical, atmospheric jazz composition, remaining one of his most celebrated non-album works and reinforcing his stature as a restless innovator outside his regular Columbia output. Blakey's contribution is a lesser-known but well-regarded entry in the Jazz Messengers discography, capturing the group just before Wayne Shorter's arrival reshaped the band.

albums.albumStory: Relaxin' with the Miles Davis Quintet was drawn from two marathon 1956 sessions - May 11 and October 26 - cut so Davis could fulfill his Prestige contract before departing for Columbia Records, yielding enough material for four LPs alongside Cookin', Workin', and Steamin'. The quintet paired Davis with a young John Coltrane, whose tenor was still developing the harmonic aggression that would later define him, atop the tight, blues-rooted rhythm section of Red Garland, Paul Chambers, and Philly Joe Jones. Producer Bob Weinstock and engineer Rudy Van Gelder favored mostly first or near-first takes of standards and a couple of jazz staples, capturing the band's remarkable in-the-moment interplay, including studio patter that became part of the record's charm. This unit is widely regarded as Davis's First Great Quintet, a pivotal group bridging his cool-toned early work and the harder-driving, blues-inflected hard bop he refined through the late 1950s. The relaxed-tempo readings of ballads like "You're My Everything" alongside the incisive swing of "Oleo" and "Woodyn' You" showcase the group's dynamic range and remain touchstones of the hard bop repertoire. The album and its sister releases are viewed as essential documents of a band at peak chemistry just before Coltrane's departure and Davis's move to a larger label, cementing its lasting stature in the jazz canon.

albums.albumStory: Steamin' with the Miles Davis Quintet is the last-released of the four classic Prestige albums (Cookin', Relaxin', Workin' and Steamin') assembled from two marathon studio dates - May 11 and October 26, 1956 - that Davis's celebrated "First Great Quintet" recorded to fulfill its Prestige contract before the trumpeter's move to Columbia Records. Having road-tested most of this material on tour, Davis, John Coltrane, Red Garland, Paul Chambers and Philly Joe Jones cut the sessions essentially live in the studio, often in a single take, capturing the loose, blowing-session spontaneity that became legendary. The program balances Tin Pan Alley and Broadway standards with bebop staples and a Monk composition, showcasing Coltrane's rapidly maturing improvisational voice alongside Davis's understated lyricism. These sessions mark a pivotal moment in Davis's career, the closing chapter of his first great working band just before he assembled the sextet that would record Milestones and Kind of Blue. The quintet's telepathic interplay and the rhythm section's effortless swing made these Prestige dates a cornerstone of hard bop, influencing how small-group jazz combos approached repertoire and pacing for years afterward. Critically, the four Prestige LPs drawn from these sessions are regarded as among the finest examples of mid-1950s modern jazz, and Steamin' in particular is prized for the ballad performances and the burning tempo of "Salt Peanuts." Its lasting legacy rests on documenting, in real time, the sound of a band operating at the peak of its collective chemistry just before disbanding.

albums.fidelity: Mastered and engineered by Rudy Van Gelder at his Hackensack studio directly from the 1956 quintet sessions; this deep-groove yellow-label mono pressing with RVG stamp represents Van Gelder's own original lacquer cut, prized by collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv for its warmth and immediacy compared to later Fantasy-era repressings sourced from generation-removed tapes. Pressing quality on these early Bergenfield-era Prestige mono LPs is generally very good, though slightly more prone to surface noise than contemporary Blue Notes due to Prestige's more modest vinyl stock. In the album's fidelity hierarchy this original mono first press sits at the top alongside early gold-trident mono repressings, well above later stereo Fantasy reissues, with the 2014 Analogue Productions APRJ 7200 200g mono LP (mastered from the original tapes, pressed at QRP) representing the modern audiophile-grade alternative most Steve Hoffman forum members consider the best-sounding modern option.

albums.albumStory: Jazz On The Screen pairs the ten-track score Miles Davis improvised in Paris for Louis Malle's 1958 thriller Ascenseur pour l'échafaud with three cues Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers, featuring Benny Golson's arrangements, recorded for the French film Les Femmes Disparaissent. Davis cut his side of the music in a single overnight session on December 4-5, 1957, with a quartet of French and expatriate musicians - Barney Wilen, René Urtreger, Pierre Michelot and Kenny Clarke - largely improvising to the projected film, an approach later celebrated as an early landmark fusion of modal jazz and cinema. The Blakey/Golson material, cut in Paris with the classic Golson-era Jazz Messengers lineup of Lee Morgan, Bobby Timmons and Jymie Merritt, showcases the harder-driving, hard-bop side of the group in contrast to Davis's spare, atmospheric mood pieces. The Davis soundtrack arrived at a pivotal turning point in his career, just before he assembled the sextet that would record Milestones and Kind of Blue, and it is now regarded as a foundational work of modal jazz and film-scoring craft. Critics of the day, including Martin Williams and Ralph Gleason, praised the Davis score for elevating film music beyond mere mood-setting into fully realized, self-sufficient jazz, while the Blakey/Golson cuts are valued for their concentrated bop firepower. Decades on, Ascenseur pour l'échafaud is cited as a landmark that legitimized jazz composed specifically for cinema, and this compilation remains a compact, historically important document of that moment for both bandleaders.

albums.fidelity: The Davis material was recorded quickly to a projected film image in a Paris studio in December 1957, giving an intimate, close-mic'd character rather than pristine hi-fi polish; the Blakey/Golson cuts, recorded separately, are tighter and punchier. This Fontana US mono pressing is a straightforward transfer with no evidence of alternate audiophile mastering; collector discussion (Steve Hoffman forums) tends to favor the original French Fontana/Barclay pressings of the Davis score and later audiophile-grade reissues (e.g. Speakers Corner, Universal/Verve remasters of Ascenseur pour l'échafaud) for critical listening over this US compilation cut, which is valued more for rarity and historical packaging than absolute sonic fidelity.

albums.albumStory: Miles Ahead launched Davis's landmark series of large-ensemble collaborations with arranger Gil Evans, recorded in 1957 soon after Davis signed with Columbia while his working quintet remained active elsewhere. Rather than leading a combo, Davis appears here purely as a soloist on trumpet and flugelhorn, floating over Evans's meticulously voiced 19-piece orchestra built around unconventional colors like French horns, tuba and bass clarinet in place of standard big-band brass and reeds. Evans and producer George Avakian conceived the record as a continuous suite, splicing the individual pieces together with tape edits so one flows into the next without pause - an unusually ambitious production choice for a jazz LP of its time. The repertoire blended originals by Evans, Davis and John Carisi with reworked material by Dave Brubeck, Léo Delibes, Kurt Weill and others, all refracted through Evans's distinctive harmonic palette rather than played as straight charts. The album announced Davis's arrival at Columbia as a major artistic and commercial force and established the Davis-soloist/Evans-orchestra format later refined on Porgy and Bess and Sketches of Spain. It remains a touchstone of Third Stream writing and large-ensemble jazz orchestration, praised for Davis's lyrical, unhurried playing and for Evans's arranging, and it endures as a canonical entry in both men's discographies.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press-era (mono, 1957) - Columbia 6-eye deep-groove Sailboat Cover, DEMONSTRATION/NOT FOR SALE promo labels, early XLP41762/41763-1G stamper family.
albums.labelNotes: Both labels show Columbia's 1957 "6-eye" design - a ring of six red pinwheel/eye graphics around a white field, with the deep-groove ring visible near the label edge - the format Columbia used circa 1955-1961 before the 2-eye/360 Sound redesign documented on bsnpubs.com. Here the fields are overprinted "DEMONSTRATION" above the title and "NOT FOR SALE" beside the track list, marking this as a promotional pressing sent to radio/press rather than retail stock, though cut from the same early stamper family as first commercial copies. The XLP41762-1G/XLP41763-1G matrix suffixes match the earliest documented stamper generation for the original sailboat-cover CL 1041, per Discogs variant listings, placing this pressing at the front of the mono production run rather than a later re-stamped or 2-eye repress. Paired with the sailboat-cover jacket - withdrawn within the LP's first year in favor of a portrait cover - this promo/deep-groove/6-eye combination sits at the top of the CL 1041 collector hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: This is an original-era Columbia mono cut mastered from the 1957 session tapes with no evidence of electronic reprocessing, unlike the 1961 "stereo" CS 8633 issue, which Steve Hoffman forum consensus generally regards as an artificially widened, inferior-sounding rechannel. Collectors rate the 6-eye mono pressing as definitive, prizing Columbia's clean, detailed late-1950s cutting and the warmth needed for Evans's dense orchestral voicings; promo copies like this typically share lacquers/stampers with early retail pressings, so sonics should match a standard first pressing modulo vinyl wear. Later 2-eye/360 Sound mono reissues used closely related masters into the 1960s with solid but slightly less immediate results, while 1970s-80s orange-label reissues are considered noticeably flatter. Modern audiophile reissues (Columbia/Legacy, Speakers Corner) offer quieter surfaces and updated mastering but are generally ranked below a clean original 6-eye mono for tonal character.

albums.albumStory: Recorded on August 5, 1955 at Rudy Van Gelder's Hackensack studio, this session paired Miles Davis with vibraphonist Milt Jackson for a one-off all-star date drawing on none of Davis's regular working-group members of the period. The billed "quintet/sextet" credit reflects the addition of a young Jackie McLean, who sits in on alto sax for his own two compositions, "Dr. Jackle" and "Minor March," while the remaining tracks feature the core quintet of Davis, Jackson, pianist Ray Bryant, bassist Percy Heath, and drummer Arthur Taylor. The record arrived during Davis's prolific mid-1950s run of Prestige sessions that preceded his signing to Columbia, capturing him at a pivotal moment just before he assembled his classic quintet with John Coltrane. Thad Jones's "Bitty Ditty" and Bryant's blues-based closer "Changes" round out a compact, blowing-session program that showcases the interplay between Davis's understated lyricism and Jackson's fluid, blues-drenched vibraphone lines. The album has long been valued by hard-bop collectors as an early, informal document of two major voices of the era working together outside their usual bandstands, and it remains a minor but respected entry in Davis's vast Prestige discography.

It ranks above the later Bergenfield-address and silver-label Prestige repressings, the 1968 "Odyssey!" reprocessed-stereo reissue, and the OJC vinyl/CD reissues, none of which carry the same first-generation Van Gelder lacquer; there is no widely noted audiophile remaster of this specific title to compare against.

albums.albumStory: Dig collects the bulk of a single October 5, 1951 session, one of the first jazz dates conceived with the new long-playing format in mind, letting the musicians stretch beyond three-minute 78 constraints. It documents the first extended studio partnership between Miles Davis and Sonny Rollins, alongside a teenaged Jackie McLean still deep in his Charlie Parker apprenticeship; Parker himself reportedly visited the studio during the date. 'Dig' and 'Denial' are Davis contrafacts built on 'Sweet Georgia Brown' and 'It's Only a Paper Moon' changes respectively, 'Bluing' is an extended blues meditation, and 'Out of the Blue' went on to become a jazz staple. The session falls in Miles's early-1950s Prestige years, after Birth of the Cool but before his mid-decade heroin struggles and his celebrated 1954-55 comeback dates, capturing him consolidating a harder, more driving post-bop language against Art Blakey's explosive drumming. The two remaining performances from the date, 'Conception' and 'My Old Flame,' appeared on the companion LP Conception (PRLP 7013). Ira Gitler's original liner notes frame the record as a landmark in the Davis-Rollins relationship, and it has since been recognized as a foundational hard-bop document and an early showcase for Rollins's emerging voice.

Prestige occupied the 446 W. 50th St. address from 1955 until moving to Bergenfield, N.J. around 1958, so this address places the pressing squarely in the 1955-58 window and, combined with the '447 West 50th Street' catalog address on the jacket, into the 1955-56 first-issue period specifically. The typed runouts show hand-etched RVG with AB (Abbey Record Mfg.) plant stamps and a first-lacquer 'PRLP-7012-A-1' marking on side 1, consistent with an original 1955 Van Gelder-remastered pressing rather than a later Bergenfield-era repress on the same metal.
albums.fidelity: Cut and remastered for LP by Rudy Van Gelder (hand-etched RVG in the deadwax and back-cover credit) from the October 1951 session tapes, pressed at Abbey (AB stamps). Original mono deep-groove copies like this are the benchmark for the title among collectors on forums such as Steve Hoffman's, offering a warm, present midrange typical of Van Gelder's early remastering work, though the underlying 1951 recording predates his Hackensack studio and lacks the bloom of his later sessions. Later Bergenfield-address pressings share the same stampers and sound very close; OJC/Fantasy reissues and modern audiophile reissues are competent but sit a generation removed from this first-cut pressing.
