albums.albumStory: Pennywise formed in Hermosa Beach, California in 1988, part of the tight-knit South Bay scene that also produced Black Flag, the Descendents, and the Circle Jerks. They cut their self-titled debut in 1991 at West Beach Recorders in Hollywood, the studio run by Bad Religion guitarist and Epitaph founder Brett Gurewitz, who co-produced. Released on Epitaph, it was one of the key early records - alongside Bad Religion's own catalog - in the wave of fast, melodic Southern California hardcore that would define 1990s skate punk and eventually carry labelmates like The Offspring and Rancid to platinum success. Fourteen songs in under half an hour, it pairs breakneck anthems of self-reliance ('Rules,' 'Wouldn't It Be Nice') with socially barbed material like 'Homeless' and the self-mythologizing title track. Its closing song, 'Bro Hymn,' became the band's signature anthem; after bassist Jason Thirsk's death in 1996, the band re-recorded it as 'Bro Hymn Tribute' on Full Circle, and it remains a staple of their live set and of sports arenas worldwide. The album established the classic lineup of Jim Lindberg, Fletcher Dragge, Jason Thirsk, and Byron McMackin and is widely regarded as one of the band's best records and a cornerstone of the Epitaph sound. Its influence on the melodic hardcore and skate-punk scenes of the 90s and beyond is difficult to overstate.
albums.lpNotes: Modern Epitaph reissue (undated, c. 2018-2024) - replicates the 1991 label/jacket art; 'LIVERMORE A/B' runout etchings = the current in-print reissue variant (Discogs r26866220), not the 1991 Rainbo first press ('E-86412-1-A / L-37929', no S-numbers).

UNLAWFUL DUPLICATION MAY BE HAZARDOUS TO YOUR HEALTH!' - the classic early-90s Epitaph design. Epitaph was founded by Bad Religion's Brett Gurewitz out of the West Beach Recorders operation, and the Sunset Blvd. address was the label's home through its mid-90s punk explosion, so the address dates the artwork, not the pressing: this reissue faithfully replicates the 1991 label art including the original copyright line. The typed runouts 'PENNYWISE S/T (EPITAPH) 86412-1 LIVERMORE A/B' are the decisive evidence - they match the undated modern Epitaph reissue variant (Discogs r26866220), not the 1991 Rainbo original ('E-86412-1-A / L-37929', no S-numbers) or the 1994 Rainbo repress (S-numbers added). This copy therefore sits at the bottom of the pressing hierarchy as the current in-print reissue.
albums.fidelity: Reissue cut, almost certainly from a digital source/remaster rather than the original analog tapes; pressing quality is standard modern Epitaph fare - serviceable but not audiophile-grade. For sonics the 1991 Rainbo original (and its 1994 repress from the same Greg Lee Processing metal) remains the reference analog-era cut. The 2014 clear-vinyl Epitaph-store exclusive (500 copies) and 2021 30th-anniversary splatter editions share the later reissue source. No dedicated audiophile edition of this title exists, so the fidelity hierarchy is simply: original 1991 pressing on top, all reissues a step below.

albums.albumStory: This album gathers four cornerstone works of Samuel Barber in landmark performances by Howard Hanson and the Eastman-Rochester Orchestra, tireless champions of American orchestral music. The Symphony No. 1, Op. 9, a compressed one-movement work whose scherzo, slow movement and finale grow organically from the opening themes, premiered in Rome in 1936 and was revised for its 1944 New York Philharmonic premiere under Bruno Walter, announcing Barber as a major symphonist in his twenties. The Overture to 'The School for Scandal,' Op. 5, was Barber's Curtis Institute graduation piece, written at 21 and winner of the 1933 Bearns Prize, becoming his first work to enter the standard repertoire. The Medea Suite, Op. 23, derives from the 1946 ballet commissioned by Martha Graham, later revised as 'Cave of the Heart,' and reveals Barber's more astringent, dramatic side across seven mythological episodes. The Adagio for Strings, arranged from the slow movement of the String Quartet, Op. 11, received its immortal 1938 premiere under Toscanini and the NBC Symphony and has become the defining American elegy of mourning. Hanson, longtime director of the Eastman School of Music, premiered and recorded more American music than any conductor of his generation, and his Mercury Living Presence recordings with the Eastman-Rochester Orchestra remain a reference document of mid-century American orchestral art. These performances, among the earliest and most authoritative documents of these Barber works, helped fix the Barber canon for the LP era and remain interpretive touchstones.
albums.lpNotes: Budget reissue (1974) - Dutch Mercury Golden Imports SRI 75012 lilac label; electronic stereo (Medea Suite genuine stereo), Phonogram Baarn stampers.
albums.labelNotes: This copy shows the lilac/light-purple Mercury 'Golden Imports' label: oval Mercury logo at top, 'Golden Imports' script banner beneath it, a boxed ELECTRONIC STEREO field, and 'MADE IN HOLLAND' printed under the catalog number SRI 75012, with standard 1970s Phonogram International rim text. Golden Imports was Phonogram Holland's mid-1970s budget line (SRI-75xxx, c. 1973-78) licensing US Mercury Living Presence recordings for European distribution, making this a Dutch reissue rather than a US Mercury pressing. The 'STEREO*' asterisk tied to 'Medea Suite, Op. 23*' flags that only the Medea is genuine stereo, the rest electronically reprocessed from mono, confirmed by the back-cover disclaimer and the credit line noting prior release as SR 90428, MG 50148, and MG 50075. This places the copy two generations below the 1955/1958 US Living Presence originals in the pressing hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: The sources are the celebrated Mercury Living Presence Eastman Theatre sessions, single-point recordings engineered by C. Robert Fine under producer Wilma Cozart, but this pressing presents three of four works in electronically simulated stereo, smearing the clean mono Living Presence imaging; only the Medea Suite is genuine stereo. Dutch Phonogram/Baarn pressing quality is quiet and well-centered for the era, and collectors regard Golden Imports as among the better-sounding budget reissue lines, but it remains a reprocessed budget cut. It sits well below the US mono originals (MG 50075/MG 50148) and the 1958 stereo SR 90428, and below modern Mercury Living Presence audiophile reissues (Speakers Corner, Analogue Productions) where applicable. Buy this copy for the repertoire, not for reference sound.
albums.generalNotes: 1974 Dutch Mercury Golden Imports SRI 75012, a licensed European budget reissue of 1955/1958 US Mercury Living Presence masters, not an original pressing. Decisive evidence: lilac Golden Imports labels with 'MADE IN HOLLAND' and Phonogram rim text; back-cover disclaimer 'Electronically altered to simulate stereo' plus 'Previously released as SR 90428, MG 50148, and MG 50075'; Phonogram Baarn matrix format (SRI 75 012 1Y/2Y ... 670) in the runouts. The 'STEREO*' flag on the label confirms only the Medea Suite is true stereo.

albums.albumStory: The Cranberries taped their MTV Unplugged set on February 14, 1995 at the Howard Gilman Opera House in Brooklyn, at the commercial height of their breakthrough second album No Need to Argue, which had turned the Limerick quartet fronted by Dolores O'Riordan into one of the biggest alternative rock acts in the world. Stripped of the layered electric guitars that defined the studio records, the acoustic format - the core trio of Noel Hogan, Mike Hogan and Fergal Lawler joined by supplemental strings - threw O'Riordan's keening, ornamented vocal delivery into sharp relief, giving "Linger," "Ode to My Family" and a hushed, harrowing "Zombie" a fragile intimacy the studio versions didn't have. The broadcast aired on MTV in April 1995 and quickly became beloved among fans, but the audio was never given an official release, leaving it to circulate for decades as a heavily traded and treasured bootleg. It captures the band at its commercial and artistic peak, just before the pressures of global fame and O'Riordan's own struggles began to complicate the group's trajectory, and it stands as a vivid document of how completely her voice could carry a song without a wall of sound behind it. Critics and longtime fans have long regarded this taping as among the strongest entries in the entire MTV Unplugged series, prized for its emotional directness and the acoustic reinvention of songs that were already era-defining on record. Its eventual full release became one of the emotional touchstones of the archival campaign the surviving members undertook following O'Riordan's death in January 2018, cementing the performance's status as an essential, career-spanning companion piece to the band's studio catalog.
albums.lpNotes: 1st standalone vinyl press (stereo, 2025) - US Island/UMe black LP, catalog 602478707520, Mexico-pressed, gatefold jacket with hype sticker intact in shrink.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the 2025 Island Records/UMe picture labels (MTV Unplugged logo, Island palm-tree logo, rim text crediting "An Island Records release... under exclusive license to UMG Recordings, Inc., \u00a92025 UMG Recordings, Inc."), the standard US configuration rather than the Europe/Czech variant, which carries its own "Made in Czech Republic" sticker and separate mastering credit. The printed catalog/barcode is 602478707520, while the deadwax embeds an internal Universal reference (00602475914693 E/F) that Universal reuses across formats of this title; the printed catalog is the correct identifier for cataloging purposes. Discogs documents this exact pressing (matrix 00602475914693E/F, barcode 602478707520, gatefold jacket) as release r35599996, "Made in Mexico," distinguishing it from the Europe/Czech pressing and the Complex-exclusive alabaster-white edition (r35618833). As the first-ever standalone vinyl release of this 1995 performance, this Mexico-pressed black LP represents the baseline first standalone pressing in the release hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: Mastered from the archived 1995 MTV broadcast tapes for this 2025 release, the first officially sanctioned audio treatment of a recording previously known only through bootlegs; the standalone US Unplugged mastering credit is not clearly documented on this variant, unlike the Europe/Czech pressing which credits Mystery Room Mastering & Recording Co. Early collector reports on Discogs are mixed-to-positive, generally describing the pressing as full-bodied and clean with O'Riordan's vocal well separated from the strings and acoustic guitars, though some buyers note surface noise or off-center pressing issues on individual copies. As an in-print, mass-manufactured modern reissue there is no meaningful vintage fidelity hierarchy to rank against - the alabaster-white Complex-exclusive edition and the Europe/Czech pressing are contemporaries pressed from the same digital transfer rather than superior audiophile alternatives, with buyer reports suggesting the alabaster-white edition may have a slight edge in perceived clarity.
albums.generalNotes: 2025 Island/UMe 602478707520 stereo LP is the first-ever standalone pressing of this 1995 performance, released November 2025. Matches Discogs release r35599996, documented as "Made in Mexico," gatefold jacket, matrix 00602475914693E/F, distinguishing it from the separately manufactured Europe/Czech pressing (Mystery Room mastering, Czech Republic sticker) and the Complex-exclusive alabaster-white alternate-cover pressing (barcode 602478853487). The only earlier vinyl appearance of this performance was inside the 2024 No Need to Argue 30th-anniversary box set. Hype sticker text ("First Time Released In Its Entirety") and standard black vinyl confirm this is the regular retail edition rather than the colored-vinyl exclusive.

albums.albumStory: To the Faithful Departed (1996) is the Cranberries' third album, recorded in a burst of activity in November-December 1995 at Windmill Lane in Dublin and Mushroom Studios in Vancouver with producer Bruce Fairbairn, whose stadium-rock pedigree with Aerosmith and AC/DC pushed the band toward a harder sound than the jangle of their first two records. The album is steeped in grief, dedicated to two men who died in 1995: Dolores O'Riordan's grandfather Joe, mourned in 'Joe', and Denny Cordell, the Shelter Records co-founder who had championed the Limerick band from their earliest days, elegized in 'Cordell'. Elsewhere O'Riordan confronts heroin addiction in 'Salvation', press intrusion in 'Free to Decide', the Bosnian war in 'Bosnia', and gun violence in 'I Just Shot John Lennon', while the love song 'When You're Gone' took on a haunting second life after O'Riordan's own death in January 2018. Arriving on the heels of 'Zombie' and the multi-platinum No Need to Argue, the album topped charts in six countries and reached number 2 in the UK, becoming the band's highest US chart placing and selling over six million copies worldwide. Critics were cooler than the public, finding Fairbairn's arena-rock production strident against the band's earlier delicacy, though some outlets called it their best work. It remains the Cranberries' most debated record, its raw mourning and O'Riordan's singular voice aging well under reassessment, closing out the band's imperial commercial run as the biggest Irish alternative act of the 1990s after U2.
albums.lpNotes: 2023 European deluxe 2LP reissue (Island/UMe 5570947) - John Dent/Metropolis remaster, dual 1996/2023 copyright labels, sits behind the 1996 Island 524 314-1 original single LP.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show a modern grey Island design with a single circular palm-tree logo at the bottom, LC 00407 box, BIEM/SDRM rights numbers, and dual '(c) 1996 / (c) 2023 UMG Recordings, Inc.' copyright lines, with rim text citing Universal International Music B.V., Hilversum, Netherlands - the standard 2020s UMe/Universal catalog-reissue label template, not any period Island design. Island has been a UMG (formerly PolyGram) property since 1989, and its 1990s catalog is now administered by UMe, explaining why a 1996 copyright sits alongside a 2023 one. The 'Universal Music Recordings' signature box and 557####/006024557##### numbering are current Universal EU catalog conventions, placing this copy unambiguously in the 13 October 2023 deluxe reissue campaign - two label-design generations removed from the 1996 Island 524 314-1 original single LP.
albums.fidelity: All tracks remastered from the original audio by John Dent at Metropolis (the jacket's 'John Davis' credit is a misread, consistent with the 'JD' deadwax etch on side A), pressed in Germany with typically flat, quiet, well-centered EU vinyl. As with most UMe catalog remasters it is cut from a high-resolution digital transfer rather than an all-analog chain, yielding a louder, denser modern master than the 1996 cut. A genuine advantage is that the roughly 55-minute program is spread across three album sides here rather than crammed onto one 1996 LP, easing inner-groove distortion. No audiophile edition (MoFi, Analogue Productions, Speakers Corner) exists for this title, so the fidelity hierarchy is essentially the scarce 1996 Island original single LP (favored for period dynamics) versus this 2023 deluxe (favored for quiet surfaces, generous groove spacing, and the exclusive Paris demos).
albums.generalNotes: 2023 Island/UMe European deluxe 2LP reissue/remaster (released 13 October 2023), not a 1996 original pressing. The 'Made in Germany' sticker and typed deadwax job numbers 62082/62083 confirm an EU pressing, and the 'JD' etch on side A marks remastering engineer John Dent of Metropolis. The true original is the 1996 Island single LP 524 314-1 with period labels and no bonus side.

albums.albumStory: Francis Coppola conceived One from the Heart as an intimate, stylized romance following Apocalypse Now, and commissioned Tom Waits to write a song cycle charting a couple's breakup and reconciliation in a neon-lit Las Vegas. Waits spent nearly two years on the project, writing every song and recording with longtime producer Bones Howe and arranger Bob Alcivar, whose lush, string-and-brass orchestrations gave the material a Nelson Riddle-era romanticism unlike anything else in Waits's catalog. Crystal Gayle was brought in to voice the female half of the story - reportedly at the suggestion of Waits's wife Kathleen Brennan - and the pairing of her polished country-pop voice with Waits's ragged, whiskey-soaked delivery became the record's defining device, most vividly on the duets. The film was a lavish, expensive flop that helped sink Coppola's Zoetrope Studios, and the soundtrack's release was delayed by the ensuing turmoil before finally appearing in 1982. Waits earned an Academy Award nomination for the score, and critics came to regard the album as the most sophisticated, orchestrated statement of his early songwriting period. It effectively closed out his Asylum-era lounge-jazz balladeer persona; within a year he had reinvented his sound entirely on Swordfishtrombones, making this soundtrack a singular, beloved outlier in his body of work.

albums.labelNotes: The label photos show the red Columbia design with 'COLUMBIA' repeated around the rim interspersed with CBS note logos, 'PRINTED IN U.S.A.' rim text, and '(c) 1982 CBS Inc.' - the layout Columbia introduced c. 1981 alongside the FC catalog prefix for full-price pop, replacing the earlier JC-era design. The AL/BL 37703 side-specific numbers are standard Columbia practice for this era. The typed matrix transcription shows an etched 'T1' before the KDISK mark, which Discogs and collector references confirm is Columbia's Terre Haute, Indiana pressing plant designation (distinct from Pitman's 'P' stamp), so this copy is a Terre Haute pressing rather than Pitman. Both plant variants are equal-status original 1982 first issues cut from Kendun Recorders, Burbank ('KDISK') lacquers.
albums.fidelity: Mastered at Kendun Recorders, Burbank (the 'KDISK' etching) and pressed at Columbia's Terre Haute, Indiana plant - generally viewed by collectors as a slightly less consistent presser than Pitman but capable of clean, quiet copies. The Bones Howe production, tracked at Wally Heider's in Hollywood, is a big, polished analog studio recording, and the original Kendun cut is warm and dynamic. In the album's fidelity hierarchy, the 2016 Mobile Fidelity Original Master Recording LP (MFSL 1-448) is the acknowledged top tier, praised by audiophile reviewers for a deeper, more three-dimensional presentation; a clean original 1982 US pressing like this one is the reference vintage alternative, while the recent colored-vinyl reissue and the CD editions sit below both for pure analog sonics.

albums.albumStory: Wild Bill Moore (1918-1983) was a Houston-born tenor saxophonist who became one of the great R&B 'honkers' of the late 1940s, scoring one of the earliest proto-rock'n'roll hits with "We're Gonna Rock, We're Gonna Roll" on Savoy in 1947. After a decade of hard-blowing singles and a stretch in Detroit, he was signed by Orrin Keepnews to Riverside's Jazzland subsidiary for a surprising late-career reinvention as a straight-ahead soul-jazz leader. Bottom Groove, recorded July 5, 1961 at Plaza Sound Studios in New York, was his second and final Jazzland LP, following Wild Bill's Beat (JLP 38) from earlier that year. Where the first album featured Junior Mance's piano, this session substitutes the earthy organ of Johnny 'Hammond' Smith, borrowed from Prestige, and adds Ray Barretto's conga for a down-home, Latin-tinged groove. The program mixes blues-drenched Moore originals with Nat Adderley's "Sister Caroline" and the Ellington-Tizol standard "Caravan." Though it made little commercial noise, the album is now prized by organ-combo and soul-jazz collectors as a rare document of a rock'n'roll sax pioneer sitting comfortably inside the early-60s groove movement, alongside one of Johnny Hammond Smith's finest sideman appearances.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1961) - yellow Jazzland JLP 54 label, Bill Grauer Productions NYC rim text, 235 W. 46th St. jacket; matrix JLP-54-A/B.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the original yellow Jazzland label with the black rectangular 'JAZZLAND' banner logo, 'long playing microgroove' banner text, and 'BILL GRAUER PRODUCTIONS INC. NEW YORK CITY' rim text; the back cover gives the 235 West 46th Street, New York 36 address. Jazzland was founded in 1960 by Bill Grauer and Orrin Keepnews as Riverside's jazz subsidiary, and this yellow-label/Bill Grauer Productions configuration is the label's only original-era design, in use from 1960 until Grauer's death and the company's bankruptcy in 1964. The mono catalog number JLP 54 (versus JLP 954S for the stereo edition, advertised on the back cover) and the typed matrix JLP-54-A/B confirm this is a mono first pressing from the album's 1961 release. Later catalog activity was limited to ABC-leased reissues (1967-71) and Fantasy-era product after 1972, none of which carried this label design.
albums.fidelity: Recorded and mastered at Plaza Sound Studios with Ray Fowler engineering, the house team for Grauer/Keepnews productions, generally well-regarded for warm, present mono sound. Original 1961 mono and stereo pressings are the only vintage analog cuts of this album; there are no audiophile reissues (no OJC/Analogue Productions/Tone Poet-style treatment), so the originals define the fidelity hierarchy. Forum discussion of the title is sparse, but the mono fold of this session is the more common collector's choice, and clean originals like this one are the best-sounding way to hear it - the only significant alternative is the 2002 Milestone CD two-fer with Wild Bill's Beat.
albums.generalNotes: 1961 Jazzland JLP 54 mono - original US first pressing. Yellow label with black banner logo and 'Bill Grauer Productions Inc. Recorded July 5, 1961 at Plaza Sound Studios, produced by Orrin Keepnews, engineered by Ray Fowler.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in Paris in March 1986 for the French OWL label, Music Makers finds veteran American jazz singer Helen Merrill deep into her European period, pairing her with longtime pianist Gordon Beck in two contrasting stripped-down trios - one with soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy, the other with violinist Stéphane Grappelli. The unusual, largely piano-and-single-horn instrumentation forces an intimate, conversational reading of standards such as "Round About Midnight," "Laura," "As Time Goes By" and "Solitude," alongside Django Reinhardt's "Nuages" and the Beck/Merrill original title track. Merrill, who first made her reputation with her 1954-55 Clifford Brown collaboration, had by the mid-1980s become something of an expatriate favorite in France, and this Owl session is emblematic of the low-key, chamber-jazz vocal dates she pursued abroad when major-label American work had dried up. Lacy's spare, probing soprano and Grappelli's lyrical violin each give the two sides a distinct color, and Leonard Feather's liner notes situate the record within Merrill's four-decade career as one of jazz singing's most harmonically sophisticated and understated stylists. Critical response, including a later four-star AllMusic review, praised the album's freshness, attributing it to both the unconventional instrumentation and the inventiveness of the players. The record stands as a late-career highlight showing Merrill's interpretive artistry undimmed, working in a minimalist setting that showcases the voice against sparse, harmonically alert accompaniment rather than a full rhythm section.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in two separate sessions - December 1957 in Chicago with a working local rhythm section, and February 1958 in New York with an all-star sextet including Bill Evans, Bobby Jaspar, Oscar Pettiford and Jo Jones - The Nearness of You was Helen Merrill's fifth studio album and her final release on the EmArcy label before she relocated to Italy and later Japan. Merrill had already established herself with her acclaimed 1954 self-titled album (featuring Clifford Brown) as one of the most distinctive vocal stylists in jazz, prized for her breathy, intimate delivery and unconventional phrasing on standards. This record leans into a warmer, more relaxed mood than her earlier, more dramatic outings, pairing familiar songbook fare - Porter, Gershwin, Arlen, Kern - with a set of top-tier sidemen who give the date real jazz weight, particularly the New York quartet tracks where Evans's harmonic sensibility is already audible just before his rise to fame with Miles Davis. Critics have long treated Merrill as a singer's singer whose readings of standards prioritize mood and space over technical display, and this album is generally viewed as a solid, late-period entry in her formative EmArcy run rather than a landmark on the order of her 1954 debut. It remains valued chiefly for the rare studio pairing of Merrill with Evans and for its place capping her important, if commercially modest, late-1950s American output before her long expatriate period.

albums.albumStory: Recorded over two sessions in late December 1954 at Fine Sound Studios in New York, this debut studio album introduced vocalist Helen Merrill to the jazz world in the company of trumpet prodigy Clifford Brown, with arrangements and conducting by a young Quincy Jones making one of his earliest marks on record. Merrill, whose hushed, breathy, deeply intimate delivery set her apart from the more forceful jazz singers of her era, found in this quiet, spacious date the ideal showcase for her phrasing, particularly on the ballads "Don't Explain" and "What's New," the latter later singled out by Jones as one of the most compelling vocal performances he had arranged. Brown, only months away from his death in a 1956 car accident, plays with the lyrical warmth and melodic invention that made him one of the defining trumpet voices of hard bop, and his obbligato lines behind Merrill's vocals are treated as equal partners in the conversation rather than mere accompaniment. The album occupies a pivotal place in Merrill's career as the record that established her reputation as a singer's singer, prized by musicians and cognoscenti for her restraint and intonation rather than for pop crossover appeal. Within the vocal jazz canon, the record is often cited alongside the best work of the era's ballad singers for its unhurried intimacy and its integration of top-tier instrumental soloists into a vocal date. Critical reception over the decades has been consistently glowing, with the session's chemistry between Merrill and Brown frequently singled out as one of the great vocalist-instrumentalist pairings in jazz history, securing the album's lasting stature as an essential and influential title.

The 2020 Analogue Productions APJ 127 200g reissue, mastered by Kevin Gray from the analog tapes, is well regarded for quiet, clean surfaces and improved bass extension but is generally viewed by purists as a fine modern alternative rather than a replacement for a good first pressing. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy, this deep-groove YMG first pressing sits at the top, ahead of later 1950s/60s Mercury reissues, 1970s Japanese pressings, and CD editions, with only the Analogue Productions LP as a serious modern competitor for those unconcerned with owning an original.

albums.albumStory: Recorded over two December 1954 sessions for Mercury's EmArcy imprint, this eponymous debut introduced 24-year-old Helen Merrill to the jazz world alongside trumpeter Clifford Brown, then at the height of his tragically brief career, and bassist/cellist Oscar Pettiford, with arrangements by a 21-year-old Quincy Jones in one of his earliest professional credits. Merrill's hushed, breathy, deeply intimate delivery on ballads such as "Don't Explain" and "What's New" distinguished her from the more extroverted vocalists of the day, and Brown's tender obbligato lines behind her voice stand among the most affecting recorded examples of his artistry before his death in a 1956 car accident. The session favored relaxed tempos and close small-group interplay, with Jones's spare charts framing Merrill's phrasing rather than crowding it. Produced by Bob Shad for EmArcy, the album is now considered a landmark of 1950s vocal-jazz intimacy and one of the definitive pairings of a singer with a major horn soloist. It never delivered Merrill mainstream pop success, but it secured her lasting reputation among serious jazz listeners and critics, and remains the recording most identified with both her early career and Clifford Brown's brief but luminous discography as a sideman-collaborator.

albums.albumStory: Aretha Live at Fillmore West captures Franklin's three-night stand of March 5-7, 1971 at Bill Graham's San Francisco rock palace, a booking producer Jerry Wexler pursued to bridge the Queen of Soul to the Fillmore's rock audience. Wexler paired her with King Curtis and the Kingpins - Cornell Dupree, Bernard Purdie, Jerry Jemmott and Billy Preston - augmented by the Memphis Horns and her own Sweethearts of Soul, yielding one of the hardest-driving bands she ever recorded with. The set straddled worlds deliberately: signature hits like "Respect" and "Dr. Feelgood" alongside radical soul reworkings of Stephen Stills, Simon & Garfunkel, the Beatles and Bread. Its legendary, unplanned highlight came when Ray Charles, sitting in the audience, was called onstage for an extended jam reprising "Spirit in the Dark." Released in May 1971 on Atlantic, the album topped the Billboard R&B chart, reached #7 pop, and became Franklin's first gold album since 1968's Aretha Now. It is routinely ranked among the greatest live soul albums ever made, capturing Franklin at her creative peak, and carries added poignancy as one of saxophonist King Curtis's final recorded triumphs before his murder later that year.

albums.albumStory: Modern Art captures the Art Pepper Quartet at a pivotal early moment in the alto saxophonist's rise on the West Coast scene, recorded across two Los Angeles sessions - December 28, 1956 at Radio Recorders and January 14, 1957 at Master Recorders. The program balances four Pepper originals against four standards: the blues frames 'Blues In' and 'Blues Out' plus 'Cool Bunny' and 'Dianne's Dilemma,' alongside Rodgers and Hart's 'Bewitched,' 'When You're Smiling,' 'Stompin' at the Savoy,' and Cole Porter's 'What Is This Thing Called Love.' Don Clark's original liner notes made the era's pitch plainly, billing Pepper as playing among the most modern jazz on the scene. Pepper stands as one of the defining alto voices of 1950s West Coast jazz - lyrical, vibrato-rich, rhythmically supple, a cooler counterweight to the East Coast hard-bop mainstream - even as addiction and incarceration repeatedly interrupted his career in the decades that followed. Cut just before his celebrated 1957 Contemporary date Art Pepper Meets the Rhythm Section, the album documents his own working-quartet concept in full flower: relaxed, unhurried interplay rather than uptempo display. Its compact, front-to-back coherence has kept it a touchstone of the intimate small-group side of the cool school and an enduring entry in Pepper's catalog.

albums.albumStory: Betty Davis's self-titled 1973 debut was the culmination of a persona she had spent years shaping as a songwriter, model, and tastemaker in the late-1960s New York and San Francisco scenes, a period that included her brief marriage to Miles Davis. Recorded at Wally Heider Studios in San Francisco with an all-star cast drawn from Sly and the Family Stone, Santana, and the Bay Area session scene, the album was produced by former Sly and the Family Stone drummer Gregg Errico, who built dense, syncopated funk-rock arrangements around Davis's raw, unapologetically sexual vocal delivery. Every song was written and arranged by Davis herself, an unusual degree of creative control for a Black woman artist in 1973, and the record's frank eroticism and swaggering persona set her apart from the polished soul divas of the era. The album arrived as a bold, uncompromising statement of Black female sexuality and rock-funk fusion, predating and arguably paving the way for later funk and proto-punk provocateurs. Commercially the record struggled against radio and retail resistance to its explicit content, and Davis's career remained a cult phenomenon during her lifetime rather than a mainstream success. In later decades critics and musicians reassessed the album as a visionary, era-defining work, and Davis herself came to be regarded as a foundational, if undersung, figure linking funk, rock, and proto-punk sensibilities. The record's reputation has grown steadily, cited by generations of funk, rock, and hip-hop artists as an influence and a landmark of uncompromising artistic and sexual self-expression.

albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the cream/tan Just Sunshine Records label with orange rim text reading "JUST SUNSHINE RECORDS," a single sunburst/swirl logo at bottom center, orange floral-vine graphics around the lower perimeter, "STEREO" (not "Stereophonic") above the catalogue number, and a three-line production/publishing credit block beneath the track list - matching Discogs' standard first-run JSS-5 label rather than the Monarch "Stereophonic"/six-line-credit variant or the Sonic Recording Products variant (JSS-5 at left, embossed jacket). Just Sunshine was a short-lived boutique label (1973-74) distributed by Famous Music/Gulf+Western that farmed pressing out simultaneously to several contract plants (Monarch, PRC Richmond, Sonic, and others), so multiple dead-wax variants exist under this identical catalog number and label face. The collector's runout (JSS-5-A1/JSS-5-B-1) matches the PRC Richmond variant's documented etch style, consistent with an early-stamper first pressing, though a dead-wax photo would be needed to confirm the specific PRC plant stamp with certainty. Regardless, the label face itself places this copy firmly within the original 1973 first-issue pressing run, prior to any reissue.
albums.fidelity: The original 1973 Just Sunshine pressing was cut from analog masters and farmed across several contract plants (Monarch, PRC Richmond, Sonic Recording Products), so sound quality varies somewhat copy to copy; collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv generally describe clean originals as warm and punchy with surface-noise variability tied to plant/stamper generation. The 2007 Light in the Attic CD/LP and especially the 2017 Vinyl Me Please 180g reissue (remastered from the original tapes) are regarded as sonic upgrades with tighter low end and quieter surfaces, though purists still prize a clean original for its immediacy and closeness to the analog source. This PRC Richmond-pressed original sits below the modern audiophile remasters for outright surface quiet but above later reissues in tonal authenticity as a first-generation cut; a well-preserved copy like this one (VG+ vinyl) should still sound excellent, with any noise more a function of the pressing plant than the mastering.

albums.albumStory: Big Bill Broonzy was the great bridge figure of the blues: a prolific songwriter, commanding singer, and hugely influential guitarist who linked the prewar Chicago scene to the postwar folk-blues revival. Mercury recorded him on November 8-9, 1951, at Bill Putnam's Universal Recording Studios in Chicago, in two sharply contrasting settings. The first day strips the music to Broonzy's voice and guitar with only Ransom Knowling's bass, showcasing his rhythmic attack and direct, conversational storytelling. The second day adds a small horn-and-rhythm band, connecting his country-blues vocabulary to the sound of a postwar club combo. The tapes then sat unissued in Mercury's vaults until 1958, when they finally appeared with liner notes by Studs Terkel. By then Broonzy had become an ambassador of the blues to European and folk-revival audiences, and this set reveals the deep, hard blues foundation beneath that troubadour image. The songs, nearly all Broonzy originals, move through travel, separation, jealousy, hard labor, and resilience. Broonzy died of throat cancer in August 1958, just weeks before the LP's release, and it stands today as a vivid late-career portrait of an artist whose influence runs from Muddy Waters through the folk revival to the blues-rock generation that followed.
albums.lpNotes: 1st US press (mono, 1958) - blue EmArcy David Stone Martin drummer labels, deep groove; etched MG-36137A-1/B-1 plus M MS1, matching the earliest documented runout variant.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries EmArcy's first-generation blue-and-silver label with the white David Stone Martin drummer illustration, curved 'LONG PLAYING HIGH FIDELITY' rim text, 'Mercury Record Corporation / Made in U.S.A.' attribution, and a pronounced deep groove. Mercury launched EmArcy in 1954 as its jazz subsidiary (the name phonetically spells 'MRC'), and this no-address drummer-label style covers the imprint's roughly 1954-60 LP era before the early-1960s redesigns. MG-36137 sits near the end of the 36000 series, which wound up around MG-36150 in 1958-59. The etched MG-36137A-1 / MG-36137 B-1 masters with M MS1 markings match the earliest documented runout configuration on Discogs, so this is first-run 1958 stock, not one of the mid-1960s Mercury/EmArcy repressings that appear without the deep groove or with the plain 'Mercury EmArcy Jazz' logo sticker variant.
albums.fidelity: Mono cut from the 1951 Universal Recording Studios masters engineered by Bill Putnam, one of the finest rooms and engineers of the era; no mastering engineer is separately credited, and the M MS1 deadwax marking cannot be securely tied to a specific cutting engineer or plant. Mercury's 'Custom High Fidelity / Sound Margin Control' branding denotes its period in-house mastering chain rather than a later remaster. Clean deep-groove originals sound full-bodied and immediate, with the four combo tracks naturally denser than the eight sparse voice-guitar-bass performances. No Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, Classic Records, or Speakers Corner audiophile edition of this title is known, so this US original sits at the top of the album's fidelity hierarchy, ahead of the later Mercury/EmArcy reissues and any CD transfers.
albums.generalNotes: 1958 EmArcy MG-36137 mono - original US first pressing. The jacket dates the sessions to November 8-9, 1951 and notes the tapes surfaced in spring 1958, corroborating the issue year; the LP appeared just weeks before Broonzy's death in August 1958.

albums.albumStory: Recorded April 29, 1966 at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio, Got a Good Thing Goin' captures organist Big John Patton at the height of his mid-1960s soul-jazz run for Blue Note, reunited once more with guitarist Grant Green in what proved to be their final recorded collaboration. The program pairs two extended Patton-Green originals, "The Yodel" and "Soul Woman," with three contemporary R&B covers - Marvin Gaye's "Ain't That Peculiar," Sam Cooke's "The Shake," and Duke Pearson's "Amanda" - reflecting Blue Note's mid-60s push toward a groovier, jukebox-friendly soul-jazz sound. Patton, a Kansas City-raised organist who cut his teeth in R&B bands before joining Lou Donaldson and later leading his own Blue Note dates, was among the most rhythmically direct and unpretentious organists in the label's stable, and this session is frequently cited as a high point of his catalog. Drummer Hugh Walker and conguero Richard Landrum push the record into a percussive, dance-oriented groove that helped define mid-60s organ-combo soul jazz alongside contemporaries like Grant Green's own leader dates and Lou Donaldson's records of the era. AllMusic's retrospective review awarded the album four and a half stars, and it remains a favorite among soul-jazz collectors for its hot, unfussy grooves, even as some listeners find the material simpler than Patton's more exploratory work. The session stands as a snapshot of Blue Note on the eve of its sale to Liberty Records, closing out a fruitful and influential chapter in both Patton's and Green's careers.
albums.lpNotes: 1966 stereo first pressing - Blue Note NY USA label (BST 84229), Van Gelder-stamped runout, catalog number falls inside the NY USA design window that closed later that year.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are the light-blue and white design reading "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC · NEW YORK, USA" with no Liberty Records credit, the fifth Blue Note label style used roughly 1962-1966 across the BLP/BST 4081-4247 catalog run. Blue Note was sold to Liberty Records in mid-1966, after which remaining NY USA-labeled stock was used briefly before the imprint was updated to read "A Division of Liberty Records, Inc." Because BST 84229 falls within the NY USA catalog window and this copy retains the unmodified New York address text, it represents the label's last independent-era design for this title, pre-dating the Liberty-credited pressings that followed later in 1966. The typed runout (BNST 84229 A/B, Van Gelder stamp, matrix 114) matches Discogs-documented Van Gelder-cut lacquers for this pressing; no Plastylite ear was noted in the transcription, which is common in casual write-ups and does not itself rule out a first-pressing plant.
albums.fidelity: Engineered by Rudy Van Gelder direct to the original stereo masters, this NY USA pressing sits at or near the top of the fidelity hierarchy for this title, ahead of the thinner-sounding Liberty and United Artists-era pressings from roughly 1967-1973. Collectors on forums such as Steve Hoffman generally favor these mid-60s Van Gelder-cut Blue Note stereo pressings for their warmth and immediacy over later reissues. No audiophile remaster (Music Matters, Analogue Productions, Tone Poet, etc.) of this specific title is documented, so this original pressing represents the best commonly available sonic option; a 2000s CD reissue exists but is a digital, not vinyl, alternative.
albums.generalNotes: 1966 Blue Note BST 84229 stereo - original first pressing. Label reads "Blue Note Records Inc, New York, USA" with no Liberty Records text, placing it before the mid-1966 ownership-change relabeling; runout shows the expected BNST 84229 A/B etchings with matrix number 114 and a Van Gelder stamp, matching Discogs-documented lacquers for this release. No Plastylite ear was noted in the collector's transcription, which does not by itself rule out a first-pressing plant. Reid Miles cover design and back-cover ad art for contemporaneous Patton titles (Along Came John, Blue John, The Way I Feel, Oh Baby!) support a mid-1966 release window.

albums.albumStory: On August 14, 1954, EmArcy A&R chief Bob Shad staged a public jam-session concert in Hollywood, drawing on musicians already in town for a Clifford Brown/Max Roach recording date, and rolled tape on an ad-hoc all-star band for a free-admission crowd. Three of the era's most exciting trumpeters - the meteoric young Clifford Brown, high-note specialist Maynard Ferguson, and the soon-to-be Ellington sideman Clark Terry - traded extended choruses over a rhythm section led by Max Roach, joined by reedmen Harold Land and Herb Geller; Dinah Washington, whose own portion of the concert became the companion LP "Dinah Jams," contributes a luminous guest vocal on "Darn That Dream." The record captures Brown at the very start of his ascent, only two years before he would be recognized as the most influential trumpet voice since Dizzy Gillespie, and less than two years before his death at 25 in a car accident in June 1956 cut short a career already reshaping the instrument. "Move" stands as one of the great trumpet-battle performances in the jam-session idiom, while the closing ballad medley shows Brown, Terry, Geller and pianist Richie Powell at their most lyrical and unguarded. The album was praised on release in early 1955 as a showcase for its trumpet section, and it has since been championed by critics as an essential and unusually well-realized document of the informal jam-session format. It remains a landmark in Brown's brief discography and a touchstone recording of 1950s West Coast-adjacent hard bop.

The back jacket is printed in blue ink rather than black. albums.fidelity: Recorded live-to-mono in Hollywood in 1954 under Mercury/EmArcy's 'Fine-Fairchild Margin Control' process and mastered/pressed through Mercury's Chicago operation; original deep-groove blue-label pressings like this one are considered the sonic benchmark for the title, with vivid, upfront brass and audible room ambience typical of a well-run live-to-tape jazz date. The 1975 Trip Jazz reissue is a thin, budget-grade cut, and the 1980s EmArcy/Polygram reissue series, while competently mastered, sounds noticeably cooler and more compressed than the original. No modern audiophile remaster (Tone Poet/Analogue Productions/Music Matters-class) of this title exists, so a clean original mono deep-groove pressing such as this one remains the best-sounding option available to collectors.

albums.albumStory: Recorded at Fine Recording in New York between February and August 1959, this album was built around Dinah Washington's breakthrough crossover single, a dramatically retitled reworking of María Grever's 'Cuando vuelva a tu lado' with English lyrics by Stanley Adams. Producer Clyde Otis and arranger-conductor Belford Hendricks framed Washington's blues-rooted phrasing and gospel-tinged diction within lush, pop-oriented string and rhythm settings, a deliberate step away from her earlier straight blues and jazz sides. The title performance climbed into the pop Top 5 and won Best Rhythm & Blues Performance at the second Grammy Awards, later entering the Grammy Hall of Fame. Surrounding the hit are standards like 'I Remember You,' 'Cry Me a River,' 'Manhattan,' and 'A Sunday Kind of Love,' showcasing Washington's equal command of torch balladry and up-tempo swing. Arriving after fifteen years as a top blues and R&B star billed as 'Queen of the Blues,' the record marked the pivotal pop crossover of her career, paving the way for 'Unforgettable' and her celebrated duets with Brook Benton. Critics and historians regard it as a landmark of late-1950s vocal jazz/pop-R&B fusion and among the definitive statements of Washington's artistry.
albums.lpNotes: Original US mono issue (1959) - black/silver Mercury A2 deep-groove labels; MG 20479A MS1/MG 20479B MS2 Richmond-style matrices.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries Mercury's early black/silver mono 'A2' label design: arched MERCURY logo, LONG PLAYING/MICROGROOVE rim text, catalog number and 'Side' at left, 'A Custom High Fidelity Recording' at right, no oval logo above the spindle hole, and a pronounced deep groove visible on both side photos. Mercury's mono MG-20000 labelography places this plain-arch, no-oval-logo A2 style in the earliest configuration used circa 1958-59, before the label added the three-stroke 'A3' variant and later the oval-logo 'B' design used into the early 1960s, and well before the red 'Mercury head in black banner' reissue label used by the mid-1960s. The typed runouts MG 20479A MS1 (side 1) and MG 20479B MS2 (side 2) sit within Mercury's original Richmond-era mono matrix run; Discogs documents an MS1/MS1 stamped variant with an etched 'F' finisher mark as one known configuration, so this MS1/MS2 pairing is a distinct, slightly later-lacquered stamper for side 2 within the same first-issue label design. This places the copy solidly in the 1959 original mono first-issue window, just not the earliest-possible both-sides-MS1 stamper combination.
albums.fidelity: George Piros engineered the New York sessions at Fine Recording, with separate mono and stereo masters cut; this disc carries the original mono tape via an MS1/MS2 Richmond-style lacquer pairing. No cutting-engineer initial appears in the typed matrix, so it cannot be credited as a Fine Recording 'FF' cut. Deep-groove manufacture ties it to Mercury's late-1950s National Record Pressing-era plants, generally a step above routine 1960s black-label and later red-label reissues. Collectors often prize the companion stereo SR-60158 for its wide, if unusually hard-panned, soundstage, while this mono pressing gives the more centered, focused vocal image typical of era mono cuts. The 2026 Verve Vault all-analog reissue (Ryan K. Smith, Optimal) is the modern benchmark for clean transfer quality, but this original mono pressing remains the reference vintage mono listening choice.

albums.musicians: Dizzy Gillespie (trumpet, vocals on track 1), Sonny Rollins (tenor saxophone), Sonny Stitt (tenor saxophone), Ray Bryant (piano), Tommy Bryant (bass, credited as "Tom Bryant" on this jacket), Charlie Persip (drums)
albums.vinylGrade: NM DEEP GROOVE TRUMPETER LABEL/VG+ DEEP GROOVE TRUMPETER LABEL
sides:
1. On the Sunny Side of the Street
2. The Eternal Triangle

1. After Hours
2. I Know That You Know
albums.albumStory: Sonny Side Up was recorded on December 19, 1957 at Nola Penthouse Sound Studios in New York, uniting trumpet giant Dizzy Gillespie with tenor saxophonists Sonny Rollins and Sonny Stitt for a single, high-stakes session under Norman Granz's Verve banner. The pairing was conceived as a study in contrasting modern jazz sensibilities: Stitt's driving, Parker-descended intensity set against Rollins's more exploratory, thematically-minded improvising. The album's centerpiece, Stitt's original "The Eternal Triangle," became an enduring jam-session vehicle and a signature cutting-contest tune for both saxophonists, trading increasingly heated choruses over a relentless tempo. Gillespie, already a titan of bebop's founding generation, anchors the session and even takes a rare vocal turn on the opener, while pianist Ray Bryant, bassist Tommy Bryant, and drummer Charlie Persip supply a tight, propulsive rhythm section. Released in January 1959, the record arrived as both Rollins and Stitt were consolidating reputations as premier tenor stylists, and the session has since become one of the most celebrated tenor-battle records in jazz history. It remains prized as a hard-bop touchstone for its head-to-head improvisational fireworks and its enduring influence on jazz musicians as a jam-session standard.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1959) - Verve MG V-8262 gray trumpeter label, deep groove; matrix MGV-8262-A/B 50564/50565.
albums.labelNotes: Both side labels show the gray Verve "trumpeter" design: a single trumpet-playing silhouette logo at left, "VERVE RECORDS" script logo at top, "CLEF SERIES" catalog line, "Under the personal supervision of Norman Granz" credit, and "MADE IN U.S.A." rim text, with deep groove construction visible on the pressing. This design was Verve's house label from the company's 1956 founding through roughly 1960-61, before Norman Granz sold Verve to MGM in 1961 and the trumpeter graphic was dropped for a plain black label. The runout matrix numbers stamped on this copy (MGV-8262-A 50564 / MGV-8262-B 50565) match Discogs' catalogued first-issue stampers exactly, placing this copy at the top of the pressing hierarchy as the true January 1959 first issue rather than a later MGM-era black-label repress.
albums.fidelity: No mastering engineer is credited on the jacket, typical of Verve's late-1950s Clef/Norgran-descended releases produced under Norman Granz's direct supervision; the original US pressing plant work is generally solid though period-typical surface noise can occur. Collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv regard these early deep-groove trumpeter-label Verves as full-bodied and dynamic compared to the flatter, more compressed later 1960s MGM-era black-label pressings and 1990s/2000s European CD-era reissues. A 2025 Verve Vault Audiophile Series 180g reissue, mastered by Ryan K. Smith from the analog tapes and pressed at Optimal, is now the best modern audiophile option, but this original trumpeter pressing remains the vintage reference cut for the title.
albums.generalNotes: 1959 Verve MG V-8262 mono - original first pressing. Gray "trumpeter" Verve labels with deep groove and Clef Series text on both sides match the earliest Verve house design used before the 1961 MGM buyout dropped the trumpeter logo. Runout matrix numbers (50564/50565) correspond exactly to Discogs' catalogued first-issue stampers. Side 1 grades NM, Side 2 VG+, jacket VG+; no later black-label or MGM-era markings are present.

albums.title: Presenting The Gerry Mulligan Sextet
albums.musicians: Gerry Mulligan (baritone sax), Zoot Sims (tenor sax), Bob Brookmeyer (valve trombone; piano on "Everything Happens To Me", uncredited on the jacket), Jon Eardley (trumpet), Dave Bailey (drums), Peck Morrison (bass)
sides:
1. Mud Bug
2. Sweet And Lovely
3. Apple Core
4. Nights Of The Turntable

1. Broadway
2. Everything Happens To Me
3. The Lady Is A Tramp
4. Bernie's Tune
albums.albumStory: Recorded in New York during September and October 1955, this was the first album by Mulligan's short-lived sextet and his first session as a leader for EmArcy. Mulligan formed the group after dissolving his celebrated pianoless quartet and taking several months away to reassess his musical direction. The new band expanded the quartet's spare, contrapuntal language into a four-horn ensemble while retaining an unusually open rhythmic foundation. Mulligan originals such as "Apple Core" and "Nights Of The Turntable" sit beside radically reworked standards, while "Broadway" and "Bernie's Tune" give the musicians room for extended collective interplay. Mulligan was already a central figure in modern jazz through his writing for Miles Davis's Birth of the Cool sessions, his big-band arrangements, and his success in bringing the baritone saxophone forward as a nimble lead voice. Contemporary reviewers praised the sextet's organic interplay, swing, and taste, with Whitney Balliett calling it perhaps the best modern small band then working. The group's brief existence and the overshadowing fame of Mulligan's earlier quartet long kept the album underrated, but it remains an important bridge between his pianoless small groups and his later Concert Jazz Band.
albums.lpNotes: 2nd US press (mono, c. 1956-57) - black-back cover; blue small-drummer deep-groove labels; MF2/etched MS Indianapolis metal.
albums.labelNotes: This copy has the blue EmArcy Type B small-drummer deep-groove label, curved "LONG PLAYING HIGH FIDELITY" rim text, and "MERCURY RECORD CORPORATION / MADE IN U.S.A." at the bottom. EmArcy, Mercury's jazz subsidiary launched in 1954, used blue-printed back covers through MG-36056; MG-36056 was the last title known in that form, with black-back jackets indicating a second issue from approximately 1956-57. This copy's black-printed back and typed MF2/MSII and MF2/MS markings therefore place it behind the documented MF1/MI/A1/I blue-back first issue. The matrix combination matches the Discogs RCA Indianapolis variant family, even though the small-drummer blue label itself also appears on the earliest copies.
albums.fidelity: This is a contemporary all-analog mono pressing from stamped MF2 metal with etched MS markings, made at RCA Indianapolis; no cutting engineer is independently documented. It sits behind the documented MF1/MI/A1/I first-cut copies but remains an early EmArcy pressing, with warm, naturally balanced mono well suited to the largely pianoless four-horn arrangements. RCA's Indianapolis work for Mercury is generally well regarded, although title-specific audiophile and Steve Hoffman forum commentary is sparse. The 1958 US repress is a lower vintage alternative, the 1979/1982 Japanese pressings offer quieter surfaces, and the 2016 Mosaic EmArcy Sextet Recordings box, mastered from the original mono tapes by Kevin Reeves and Ryan Smith, is the reference modern source.
albums.generalNotes: US EmArcy MG 36056 mono, best identified as a c. 1956-57 RCA Indianapolis second pressing rather than the blue-back first issue. The decisive evidence is the black-printed back cover, blue small-drummer deep-groove labels, and typed MF2/etched MS runouts; documented earlier copies pair the blue-back jacket with MF1/MI/A1/I metal. The music was recorded in September and October 1955 and was being reviewed as a new LP by February 1956.

albums.title: Famous Blue Raincoat (The Songs of Leonard Cohen)
albums.composer: Leonard Cohen
albums.musicians: Jennifer Warnes (vocals, vocal harmonies), Leonard Cohen (guest vocal on 'Joan of Arc'), Roscoe Beck (bass, fretless bass, string bass), Vinnie Colaiuta (drums), Bill Ginn (piano, synthesizer, conductor), Bill Payne (synthesizers, 'Came So Far for Beauty'), David Lindley (lap steel guitar), Fred Tackett (guitar), Michael Landau (guitar), William 'Smitty' Smith (Hammond organ), Russell Ferrante (synthesizer/organ), Jorge Calderón (bass), Steve Forman (percussion), Van Dyke Parks (arrangement, 'A Singer Must Die'), Jeremy Lubbock (string arrangements), Sid Page, Barbara Porter (violins), Novi Novog (viola), Larry Corbett (cello), Richard Feves (bass), Bobby King, Terry Evans, Willie Greene Jr. (backing vocals). Stevie Ray Vaughan (guitar on 'First We Take Manhattan') and Robben Ford (guitar) are documented session contributors not legible in the photographed liner pages.
sides:
1. First We Take Manhattan
2. Bird on a Wire
3. Famous Blue Raincoat
4. Joan of Arc (with guest vocal by Leonard Cohen)

1. Ain't No Cure for Love
2. Coming Back to You
3. Song of Bernadette
4. A Singer Must Die
5. Came So Far for Beauty
albums.albumStory: Jennifer Warnes spent much of the 1970s as a backing singer in Leonard Cohen's touring band, and Famous Blue Raincoat grew directly out of that long friendship and musical apprenticeship as a full-album tribute to his songwriting, released in November 1986. A key impetus was 'Song of Bernadette,' which began as Warnes' own composition sketch before Cohen helped shape it, and the album also premiered 'First We Take Manhattan' and 'Ain't No Cure for Love' before Cohen recorded his own versions. Co-produced by Warnes and bassist Roscoe Beck, the record surrounds her warm, precise readings with lush, cinematic arrangements from an elite bench of West Coast session players - a deliberate contrast to the spare textures of Cohen's originals - and Cohen himself duets with her on 'Joan of Arc,' taking the role of the fire to her Joan. Initial critical reaction was mixed, with some reviewers finding the production overblown next to Cohen's austerity, but the album became a slow-burning commercial phenomenon, introducing a wide pop audience to Cohen's catalog at a low point in his visibility. It stands as Warnes' best-known and most enduring solo statement, cementing her reputation as an interpretive singer of exceptional taste. Its standing has only grown with time: it is now routinely cited as one of the finest tribute albums in popular music and is credited with helping revive broad interest in Leonard Cohen's work during the late 1980s.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (US stereo, 1986) - Cypress 661 111-1 tree label, PolyGram-distributed; '49' label code = Specialty (Olyphant PA) pressing, Grundman-mastered, matrix 661-111-1-A/B.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the original 1986 Cypress 'tree silhouette' stereo label: pink/black tree artwork, block CYPRESS RECORDS logo, ©1986 copyright line, 'Printed in U.S.A.' and 'Distributed by PolyGram Records, Inc.' rim text. Cypress was a short-lived Los Angeles boutique label (division of Cypress Entertainment, Corinth Street address on the jacket) whose entire 1986-87 catalog run was PolyGram-distributed, so this design is the sole first-issue US configuration. Crucially, the '49' printed below the speed line on the Side 1 label is the documented Specialty Records (Olyphant, PA) plant code - Discogs splits this release into a '49' Specialty pressing and a '57' Columbia Carrollton pressing sharing the identical 661-111-1-A/B stamped matrix family. That printed code settles this copy as the Specialty pressing; the two plant sub-variants are otherwise contemporaneous first issues and trade interchangeably.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Bernie Grundman (Bernie Grundman Mastering credit on the jacket); the album itself was digitally tracked (the original CD carries a DDD SPARS code), so the LP is a Grundman cut of the digital-era production rather than all-analog. The original Cypress LP has long been an audiophile reference disc, prized for pristine, close-miked vocal clarity and dynamic low end, with no meaningful sonic difference reported between the Specialty and Carrollton runs. In the album's fidelity hierarchy it remains the reference vintage cut - above the Private Music reissue and the various CD/gold-CD editions - but it now sits below the modern summit editions: the 2015 Impex 180g 33rpm (Grundman cut from Warnes' personal analog mixdown masters) and especially the 2023 Impex 35th Anniversary 1STEP 45rpm box, which reviewers rank as the ultimate presentation.
albums.generalNotes: Original 1986 US first pressing on Cypress Records 661 111-1, stereo, Specialty (Olyphant PA) plant. Decisive evidence: the printed '49' plant code under the speed line on the Side 1 label is the documented Specialty identifier (the companion '57' code marks the Columbia Carrollton sub-variant), the ©1986 tree label with 'Distributed by PolyGram Records, Inc.' and 'Printed in U.S.A.' matches the sole first-issue US configuration, and the typed runouts 661-111-1-A/B match the shared original-issue matrix exactly. Released November 1986.

albums.title: Like Wow!
albums.producer: Robert Scherman (credited as "Directed by"; no formal producer credit)
albums.musicians: Marty Paich (piano), Art Pepper (alto sax, guest - on Art's Opus, All The Things You Are, Pitfall, Marty's Blues, What's Right For You), Larry Bunker (vibraphone, drums), Joe Mondragon (bass); documented but uncredited on the jacket: Howard Roberts (guitar) and Frank Capp (drums) on the ex-"Hot Piano" tracks, Buddy Clark (bass) and Frank Capp (drums) on the Pepper quartet tracks
sides:
1. Art's Opus
2. I'll Remember April
3. Lullaby Of The Leaves
4. Jump For Me
5. All The Things You Are

1. Marty's Blues
2. Pitfall
3. Dool's Blues
4. Theme From Lighthouse
5. What's Right For You
albums.albumStory: Despite the "Jazz 1960" banner splashed across the cover, every note here was recorded in Hollywood in 1956 at Radio Recorders, during one of the most poignant stretches of Art Pepper's life: he had just been released from his first prison term in mid-1956 and cut these sides with pianist-arranger Marty Paich only weeks later, months before his career-defining "Art Pepper Meets the Rhythm Section" session. Five tracks feature Pepper's alto in a quartet with Paich, first issued on the rare Tampa LP pairing the two, including Pepper's own composition "Art's Opus"; the other five are Paich-led sides with Larry Bunker's vibes and Howard Roberts' guitar, drawn from an earlier Tampa 10-inch. By the time these masters resurfaced on Interlude with a glossy, bachelor-pad cover and a fabricated later release date, Pepper himself was once again behind bars, making the album an odd, bittersweet placeholder for an absent star. Paich, meanwhile, was emerging as one of the most important arrangers on the West Coast scene, later responsible for the charts on "Art Pepper + Eleven" and numerous Mel Torme sessions. Pepper's playing throughout is light, buoyant and melodically generous - the sound of a newly free man breezing through standards and originals - and the set is valued today as an important, if commercially obscure, early document of his mature alto voice.
albums.lpNotes: Original and only documented US pressing (mono, 1960) - Interlude MO-514 gray deep-groove Hollywood label; a recompilation of 1956 Tampa masters.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the gray-silver deep-groove label with the large white lowercase "i" Interlude logo and "INTERLUDE RECORDS INC - HOLLYWOOD" rim text, catalog MO-514 with printed "int 134-A/B" matrix numbers - the sole documented US pressing configuration for this title. Interlude Records Inc. was a short-lived Hollywood independent (c. 1959-62) run by Robert Scherman, and its catalog leaned heavily on earlier Tampa Records masters (TP series, 1956-57) that Scherman also controlled; MO-514 is a recompilation of that Tampa material rather than a new 1960 recording. The deep-groove pressing and single mono MO-500 series number place this firmly within the label's original 1960 issue window, with no second pressing or label-design change documented for the title.
albums.fidelity: The source tapes were engineered at Radio Recorders in 1956 by Val Valentin, later Verve's house engineer, which accounts for the unusually warm, present mono sound on this LP. Collector commentary (londonjazzcollector.wordpress.com) rates this Interlude pressing highly for the material, describing it as sonically superior to the rarer, reportedly rougher-sounding original Tampa 10-inch/LP issues. In the overall fidelity hierarchy for this material, this Interlude mono pressing sits at or near the top: the Tampa originals are scarcer collector objects but not better sounding, later reissues on Charlie Parker Records (as "Chile Pepper") and V.S.O.P. are a tape generation removed and more variable, and no audiophile reissue of this specific compilation exists.
albums.generalNotes: 1960 Interlude MO-514 mono is the original and only documented US pressing configuration for this title. The gray deep-groove labels with "INTERLUDE RECORDS INC - HOLLYWOOD" rim text and printed "int 134-A/B" matrix numbers match the expected original-issue design, and the deep-groove pressing plus the mono MO-500 series numbering place this firmly in the label's 1960 issue window. The typed runouts (134-A/B-21749 and 133-B/B-21750) are broadly consistent, though the Side 2 transcription reads "133-B" against the label's printed "int 134-B" - a discrepancy likely due to a transcription slip rather than a second variant, best confirmed with a dead-wax photo. The surviving original "Monaural Dimensional Realism" corporate inner sleeve further supports period provenance; the actual recordings date from August 1956 Radio Recorders sessions, not 1960 as the cover implies.

albums.title: Kind of Blue
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet, leader), Julian "Cannonball" Adderley (alto saxophone), John Coltrane (tenor saxophone), Bill Evans (piano), Wynton Kelly (piano, on "Freddie Freeloader" only), Paul Chambers (bass), James Cobb (drums)
sides:
1. So What
2. Freddie Freeloader
3. Blue in Green

1. All Blues
2. Flamenco Sketches
albums.albumStory: Kind of Blue was recorded by the Miles Davis Sextet at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York across two sessions in March and April 1959, with the group reading Bill Evans's sketched modal frameworks for the first time at the session rather than rehearsing beforehand, a working method Evans himself described in his own liner-note essay printed on the back cover. Davis had been moving away from dense chord-change improvisation toward modal composition, and this album became the definitive statement of that shift, built on scales rather than chord changes across all five performances. The sextet united Davis with Cannonball Adderley and John Coltrane on saxophones, Paul Chambers on bass, Jimmy Cobb on drums, and both Bill Evans and Wynton Kelly sharing the piano chair, an unusually stacked lineup of musicians who were each already, or would soon become, major bandleaders in their own right. The record arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, following his hard-bop and orchestral collaborations with Gil Evans, and it redirected jazz improvisation toward modal harmony for the following decade. It is widely regarded as the best-selling and most influential jazz album ever made, cited as the entry point to jazz for generations of listeners and a foundational document of modal jazz. Critical reception was immediate and has only grown over the decades, with the album consistently ranked among the greatest recordings in American music.
albums.lpNotes: Original six-eye mono pressing (Columbia CL 1355, c. 1959-60) - late-run stamper pair (1BH/1AL), not first-stamper, but within the authentic original six-eye pressing window.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the classic Columbia six-eye red-and-black label with the arched white COLUMBIA logotype and six perimeter eye-logos surrounded by black wedge panels, the design bsnpubs and LondonJazzCollector date to roughly 1958-1961 for Columbia mono releases, before the switch to the plain 2-eye "Guaranteed High Fidelity" label around 1961-62. The runout suffixes XLP47324-1BH / XLP47325-1AL sit well down the documented mother/stamper alphabet sequence for this title compared to the coveted 1A/1B/1C first-stamper lacquers cited in LondonJazzCollector's matrix census. Side 2 here lists All Blues before Flamenco Sketches, the corrected order associated with post-earliest six-eye runs rather than the very first pressings which sometimes reversed the two tracks. This places the copy solidly within the authentic original six-eye mono pressing window, but toward the later end of that run's stamper sequence, below the handful of true first-stamper copies collectors chase.
albums.fidelity: This is an original 1959-era Columbia mono cutting, mastered from Fred Plaut's session tape by Columbia's in-house mastering staff rather than an outside engineer; the mono mix is generally regarded by collectors, including threads on forums.stevehoffman.tv, as the most faithful rendering of the album's original session balance, since the commonly circulated stereo mix has documented channel and speed anomalies from the master tape. Within the six-eye mono pressing run, sound quality varies by stamper generation, and this copy's later mother/stamper pair (1BH/1AL) places it below the handful of prized first-stamper (1A/1B/1C) copies that collectors and forum posters single out as sonically superior, though it remains a legitimate vintage flat, non-remastered six-eye cut. Later audiophile mono reissues, notably Classic Records' 1997 200-gram mono LP and Mobile Fidelity/Music Matters stereo cuts, are prized for quieter surfaces and modern mastering but are generally regarded by mono purists as less essential than an authentic six-eye original for hearing the record as first issued.
albums.generalNotes: This is a genuine Columbia six-eye mono first-issue-era pressing of CL 1355, identified by the red/black six-eye label design used circa 1958-1961 before Columbia moved to the plain 2-eye label. However, the runout suffixes XLP47324-1BH and XLP47325-1AL are well down the documented mother/stamper alphabet sequence for this title, meaning this is a later six-eye pressing rather than a first-stamper (1A/1B/1C) copy. The side 2 label here lists "All Blues" before "Flamenco Sketches" in the corrected order, consistent with post-earliest-run six-eye copies. No deep-groove or dead-wax photo was available to confirm the deep-groove ridge; that detail would help further narrow the exact stamper generation.

albums.producer: Irving Townsend (original 1959 production); Michael Hobson (Classic Records reissue producer); Bernie Grundman (mastering)
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet, leader), John Coltrane (tenor saxophone), Julian "Cannonball" Adderley (alto saxophone, courtesy of Riverside Records; not on "Blue in Green"), Bill Evans (piano, all tracks except "Freddie Freeloader"), Wynton Kelly (piano, courtesy of Riverside Records, "Freddie Freeloader" only), Paul Chambers (bass), Jimmy Cobb (drums)
sides:
1. So What
2. Freddie Freeloader
3. Blue in Green

1. All Blues
2. Flamenco Sketches
albums.albumStory: Recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York on March 2 and April 22, 1959, Kind of Blue grew out of Miles Davis's turn toward modal composition, developed in dialogue with pianist Bill Evans, with the band given only skeletal scales and melodic sketches rather than fully written charts. The septet paired Davis with John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley on saxophones, Bill Evans on piano (with Wynton Kelly sitting in for "Freddie Freeloader"), Paul Chambers on bass, and Jimmy Cobb on drums, letting contrasting horn voices and two pianists explore the same modal frameworks from different angles. The album arrived at the peak of Davis's late-1950s creative run and marked a decisive break from bebop's harmonic density toward a spacious, scale-based improvisational language. Its relaxed tempos, blues-inflected melodies, and largely first-take performances captured a spontaneity that Evans, in his own liner note, likened to a painter working directly onto parchment without revision. Kind of Blue is widely regarded as the best-selling and most influential jazz album ever recorded, routinely cited as the genre's essential entry point and a fixture on best-album lists across all styles of music. Its introduction of modal improvisation reshaped jazz soloing vocabulary for generations of musicians who followed.
albums.lpNotes: 1997 RTI white-label TEST PRESSING for the Classic Records CS 8163 audiophile reissue - stamped 'APR 2 1997', matrix CS 8163 A1/B1 with BG (Bernie Grundman) lacquer suffix, sitting above the retail 200g run in the pressing hierarchy.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are plain white RTI (Record Technology Incorporated) stock printed only with the RTI logo, the words "TEST PRESSING," and blank DATE/MATRIX NUMBER fields that have been hand-stamped "APR 2 1997" and "CS 8163 A1/B1" - there is no Columbia or Classic Records branding, deep groove, or track information printed on the label itself. This identifies the disc as a pre-release quality-control pressing struck at RTI for Classic Records' licensed audiophile reissue of Columbia's CS 8163, not a retail copy; Classic Records began issuing CS 8163 on 200g Quiex SV-P vinyl in the mid-1990s with Bernie Grundman recutting lacquers from the original three-track masters (the "BG" suffix in the runout confirms this cutting engineer). The jacket paired with this copy is the eventual 2001-copyright Classic Records/Sony licensed sleeve, but the stamped test-pressing date shows this specific BG lacquer/stamper pair was approved in April 1997, well ahead of that later retail print run. As an approval-stage RTI test pressing, this sits at the top of the Classic Records CS 8163 hierarchy, above the routine 200g retail copies that used the same or a subsequent stamper generation.
albums.fidelity: The lacquers were cut by Bernie Grundman directly from the original three-track analog session masters with no additional EQ, using Classic Records' all-tube cutting chain, then pressed at RTI on audiophile-grade vinyl; this test pressing captures that same Grundman cut at its earliest, pre-approval stage. Steve Hoffman forum consensus rates the Classic Records Kind of Blue highly among tape-sourced reissues for openness and low-level detail versus standard CBS/Columbia pressings, though some prefer the later Analogue Productions/QRP 45rpm cut for outright resolution. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy this sits below the original 1959 six-eye Columbia lacquers (prized for tape freshness) and below the 2020s Analogue Productions 'Corrected Speed' 45rpm QRP pressing, but above routine 1970s-80s Columbia reissues and most CD/digital editions; as a test pressing it also offers an unusually clean, low-wear playback surface from that stamper pair.
albums.generalNotes: This is not a retail copy but an RTI test pressing for Classic Records' audiophile reissue of Kind of Blue (CS 8163). The generic RTI 'TEST PRESSING' labels, rubber-stamped 'APR 2 1997' with matrix 'CS 8163 A1/B1,' identify the lacquer/stamper pair used for quality-control approval ahead of the commercial run. The 'BG' suffix ties the cut to Bernie Grundman's mastering from the original three-track analog masters, distinguishing this from both the vintage Columbia originals and the later retail 200g Quiex pressings. The plain white jacket-adjacent insert matches a test configuration rather than a packaged consumer product, confirming pre-release status.

albums.albumStory: Miles Davis and Horns compiles two early Prestige sessions from opposite ends of Davis's formative post-Parker period: a January 17, 1951 sextet date with Sonny Rollins (their first-ever studio pairing) and Bennie Green, and a February 19, 1953 septet session built around Al Cohn's compositions and arrangements, featuring the contrasting tenors of Cohn and Zoot Sims. Both dates capture Davis still finding his voice after leaving Charlie Parker's group, working in a harmonically rich, horn-heavy format that let him experiment with ensemble textures beyond the standard quartet or quintet. The Cohn-associated material, including "Tasty Pudding" and "Willie The Wailer," showcases a warmer, more relaxed strand of early-1950s bop-adjacent jazz, with Zoot Sims's soloing singled out by critics as a highlight of the session. The 1951 date, meanwhile, is historically important as the first recorded meeting of Davis and Rollins, two musicians who would go on to shape the language of modern jazz. Coming before Davis's mid-1950s quintet breakthroughs, this album offers a glimpse of a still-developing artist testing group concepts that would later inform his more celebrated Prestige and Columbia work. It remains a minor but valued entry in the Davis and Prestige catalogs, prized by collectors more for its personnel and historical placement than for landmark musical innovation, though the Davis-Rollins pairing gives it lasting documentary importance.
