albums.labelNotes: The side-label photos show a yellow center label with a black outer rim, "PRESTIGE" arched in yellow-on-black at the top, "LONG PLAYING MICROGROOVE" arched at the bottom, and the characteristic OJC-era decorative motifs (a spiral/comma logo at upper left, a star logo and directional arrows scattered around the rim); the catalog is printed as "OJC-053 (P-7025)" with no deep groove and no 446 W. 50th St. or Bergenfield NJ Prestige address visible. This yellow/black spiral-and-star design (not the earlier Prestige "fireworks" art, and not a blue/cream design as an earlier note mistakenly stated) is the standard Original Jazz Classics label introduced by Fantasy Records in 1982-83 to reissue out-of-print Prestige, Riverside, and Milestone titles, replacing the original PRLP catalog numbers with new OJC-prefixed numbers. Placement of this design, combined with the etched "OJC 053 A/RE1 P" and "OJC 053 B/RE2 P (AP)" runout codes, firmly dates this copy to the 1983 Fantasy-era flat reissue rather than any vintage 1950s-70s Prestige pressing, putting it near the bottom of the PRLP 7025 pressing hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: The 1983 OJC-053 reissue was mastered flat from tape by George Horn's team at Fantasy Studios (Berkeley), not cut from Rudy Van Gelder's original lacquers, though it still derives from the same 1951/1953 Van Gelder-engineered Prestige sessions. Collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv generally rate early-1980s OJC flat transfers as accurate and listenable but noticeably less punchy and dynamic than a genuine 1956 Prestige NYC "fireworks" mono original. Within the album's full fidelity hierarchy, this OJC-053 pressing sits in the middle-to-lower tier: above later Fantasy/ABC-era commercial reissues in transfer fidelity, but well below an original NYC first pressing, and there is no audiophile-grade reissue (Music Matters, Analogue Productions, Tone Poet, etc.) of this particular title to compare against.

The etched runout reading "OJC 053 A RE1 P" / "OJC 053 B RE2 P (AP)" is decisive dead-wax evidence confirming the Fantasy-era flat reissue rather than an original pressing. albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain was the third and final large-scale orchestral collaboration between Miles Davis and arranger Gil Evans, following Miles Ahead (1957) and Porgy and Bess (1959). Davis became fixated on Joaquín Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez after hearing it, and Evans reimagined its adagio movement as the album's centerpiece, recording across sessions in November 1959 and March 1960 at Columbia's 30th Street Studio. Evans built an unconventional ensemble around Davis's trumpet and flugelhorn - French horns, tuba, harp, bassoon, and flamenco-inflected percussion - blending Spanish classical and folk sources with his own compositions, including "Saeta," drawn from Holy Week processional music, and the closing "Solea." The sessions were exacting and demanding, with Evans meticulously shaping every orchestral texture, and the resulting album is often held up as the fullest realization of the Third Stream fusion of jazz improvisation and classical form. Davis himself counted it among his favorite recordings, and it marks a creative peak in both his and Evans's careers. The album won a Grammy Award, became one of the best-selling jazz records of its era, was later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, and remains a touchstone of orchestral jazz.

The barcoded back cover, Legacy/Sony copyright strings, and the reproduced "The Inner Sleeve" newspaper-style Columbia promo insert further confirm this as a manufactured retro package rather than an original artifact. albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain grew out of the extraordinary partnership Miles Davis had already forged with arranger Gil Evans on Miles Ahead and Porgy and Bess, pushing it furthest into orchestral, Spanish-tinged territory. The centerpiece, an adaptation of Joaquin Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, originated when Davis heard the concerto's adagio and asked Evans to rework it as a feature for his trumpet against a large studio orchestra rather than a working jazz combo. Recorded in New York across sessions in November 1959 and March 1960, the album folds flamenco-inflected themes, bullfight and Holy Week processional imagery, and material drawn from Manuel de Falla into Evans's dense, coloristic orchestration, with Davis's trumpet and flugelhorn functioning almost as a classical soloist floating over shifting textures rather than trading bebop lines. It arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, sandwiched between the hard-bop and modal breakthroughs of Milestones and Kind of Blue and his later electric period, confirming Evans and Davis as jazz's foremost orchestral colorists outside the big-band tradition. The record was a critical and commercial success, widely praised for its atmosphere and for Davis's uniquely vocal, vibrato-laden trumpet tone, and it won a Grammy for Best Jazz Composition. It remains one of the most acclaimed "third stream" recordings in jazz history and a touchstone for orchestral jazz, cited by critics as a high point of both Davis's and Evans's catalogs and a work that expanded jazz's vocabulary.

The orchestra credit is spelled out in full ("Orchestra arranged and conducted by Gil Evans") and the side indicators use regular, equal-sized capitalization ("SIDE 1" with the numeral not enlarged), the textual markers Discogs uses to identify the earliest "six-eye" sub-variant of CL 1480, catalogued there as the "Terre Haute Pressing." This places the disc in the earliest issue window for CL 1480, shortly after the album's July 1960 release and ahead of later six-eye pressings with abbreviated credit/enlarged numerals, and well ahead of the mid-1960s two-eye/CBS and later reissue labels.
albums.fidelity: Original Columbia in-house engineering (uncredited on the jacket) captured Evans's dense orchestration with considerable depth for 1960; the six-eye mono cut is generally regarded by collectors on forums.stevehoffman.tv as the most natural-sounding version, since the era's stereo mixdown involved more compromises and the mono fold gives a more cohesive orchestral blend. This deep-groove six-eye pressing sits at the top of the fidelity hierarchy for CL 1480, ahead of later 1960s two-eye/360 Sound reissues and electronically rechanneled stereo pressings; later audiophile reissues (Mobile Fidelity, Speakers Corner/Music on Vinyl) are respected for quiet surfaces but are generally regarded by mono purists as secondary to a clean original six-eye mono copy for tonal accuracy.

albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain (1960) was the third of Miles Davis's landmark orchestral collaborations with arranger Gil Evans, following Miles Ahead and Porgy and Bess, pushing their partnership further into a hybrid of jazz improvisation and Spanish/flamenco idiom. Its centerpiece, an adaptation of the adagio from Joaquín Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, became the emotional core of the record, with Evans's lush, cinematic orchestration framing Davis's spare, vocal-like trumpet lines. Recorded with a large ensemble of woodwinds, brass, and percussion rather than a conventional combo across sessions in late 1959 and spring 1960, the album found Davis functioning as a soloist within an orchestral tone poem rather than a small-group bandleader, a departure that divided critics between those who found it beautiful and those who missed jazz spontaneity. Arriving between the modal breakthrough of Kind of Blue and his later 1960s quintet work, it cemented Davis and Evans as one of the most important composer-soloist pairings in jazz history. Its fusion of European classical form, Spanish folk color, and jazz phrasing proved deeply influential on third-stream and later orchestral/exoticist jazz projects. The album remains one of the most acclaimed entries in both artists' discographies, prized for its haunting atmosphere and orchestral ambition.

albums.albumStory: Stage Fright is The Band's third album, recorded in spring 1970 at the Woodstock Playhouse near their adopted hometown of Woodstock, New York, following the acclaimed Music from Big Pink and The Band and an exhausting run of touring that had left the group famous but strained. With longtime mentor John Simon stepping back, the five members self-produced for the first time, bringing in the young Todd Rundgren to engineer via a remote truck and Glyn Johns to handle the mix. Robbie Robertson's songwriting turns inward here, confronting the anxieties of sudden fame: the title track dramatizes stage fright itself, "The Shape I'm In" channels Richard Manuel's personal unraveling, "Daniel and the Sacred Harp" ponders art versus commerce, and closer "The Rumor" ends the record on a note of paranoia. The album became The Band's highest-charting release, reaching the Billboard top five, and earned a gold certification within months. Critics recognized a darker, more troubled tone than the group's earlier sepia-toned work, and Stage Fright is now regarded as the closing chapter of the classic trilogy that established The Band as foundational figures of Americana and roots rock. Songs from the record, especially the title track and "The Shape I'm In," remained fixtures of the group's live sets through The Last Waltz, and its unflinching look at fame's cost has only deepened its critical standing over time.

albums.albumStory: Recorded live at London's Talk of the Town cabaret venue, this 1967 album captured Tom Jones at the moment he was moving from teen-idol pop hitmaker into a full-blown Vegas-style showman, backed by a tuxedoed orchestra under Johnny Harris. The set mixes Jones's own hits - "It's Not Unusual", "What's New Pussycat?", "Green, Green Grass of Home" and the Bond theme "Thunderball" - with soul and R&B staples by Sam Cooke ("Ain't That Good News", "Shake") and the Chris Kenner/Fats Domino classic "Land of a Thousand Dances", alongside show-tune and pop standards like "Hello Young Lovers" and "That Old Black Magic". Produced by Peter Sullivan, Jones's regular Decca producer through the decade, the record documents the powerful, theatrical baritone and stagecraft already making Jones one of Britain's biggest live draws, a persona that would soon carry him into a long, hugely successful Las Vegas residency career. It stands as a notable document of the mid-1960s British vocal-pop and blue-eyed-soul crossover, showing a UK pop star confidently working American R&B repertoire for a supper-club audience, and remains a well-regarded snapshot of peak-1960s Tom Jones as a live performer rather than a studio hitmaker.

albums.albumStory: Lady in Satin was recorded February 18-21, 1958 at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York, produced by Irving Townsend - Billie Holiday's last completed album for Columbia and the penultimate studio statement of her life, released little more than a year before her death in July 1959. Holiday herself pushed for the project, insisting she wanted to record with Ray Ellis's lush strings-and-voices arrangements, a deliberately un-jazzy setting she chose over the objections of purists; she called it the favorite record she ever made. Her voice, weathered by decades of hard living, had lost its youthful suppleness, and critics at the time were divided over pairing that frayed instrument with Ellis's satin-smooth orchestra. But the emotional directness of performances like 'I'm a Fool to Want You' (co-written by Sinatra, who reportedly left the studio in tears at the power of her rendition) and 'You've Changed' transformed frailty into devastating expressive force. The album reframed Holiday not as a swinger but as one of the great dramatic interpreters of American song. It has since been inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame and is widely regarded as one of the essential vocal albums in jazz - the late-career companion piece to her 1930s-40s prime.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1958) - Columbia six-eye deep-groove label, T.M. in rim print, no CBS overprint; plant unconfirmed without dead-wax photos.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the red Columbia six-eye label (six walking-eye logos ringing the perimeter) with deep groove on both sides, 'NONBREAKABLE' beneath the catalog number, and rim text reading 'COLUMBIA ... MARCAS REG. ... T.M. MADE IN U.S.A.' with no CBS overprint. The six-eye design ran from mid-1955 to about 1962; around 1961-62 a small CBS overprint was added beneath the Columbia name marking repressings, and the two-eye '360 Sound' label replaced the six-eye entirely after 1962. The label-printed matrices x'Lp'43015/43016 match the first-issue mono. This copy therefore sits at the top of the mono pressing hierarchy - the earliest retail configuration of the June 1958 release.
albums.fidelity: Recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studio with its famed natural reverb, the original six-eye mono is prized by collectors for a warm, close, emotionally immediate vocal presence that puts Holiday front and center; many on the Steve Hoffman forums consider it the definitive way to hear the album despite the limited bandwidth of 1958 mono. Six-eye-era Columbia pressings are generally quiet and well cut. The original stereo CS 8048 six-eye is the audiophile grail but spreads the voice in a more diffuse orchestral field. Among modern reissues, the Analogue Productions editions (stereo 33 and the 2023 Ryan Smith/Sterling-cut 45rpm 2xLP pressed at QRP) outresolve the original, while Speakers Corner's mono reissue is the closest modern stand-in for this pressing. This copy's G-grade vinyl, however, will heavily compromise any of these inherent sonic virtues.
albums.generalNotes: 1958 Columbia CL 1157 mono - original first pressing configuration. Red six-eye deep-groove labels with T.M. in the rim print and no CBS overprint place it in the pre-1961/62 six-eye window, and this exact label variant is documented as the original mono issue; the boxed 'Guaranteed High-Fidelity' cover logo is consistent with the June 1958 release. Label-printed matrices x'Lp'43015/43016 match the first-issue mono. No dead-wax photos were supplied, so the pressing plant (Pitman, Terre Haute, etc.) cannot be pinned - a plant stamp in the runout would settle that, though it does not change the first-pressing verdict.

albums.albumStory: Carole King spent the 1960s as half of the legendary Brill Building-era Goffin-King songwriting team, penning hits like 'Will You Love Me Tomorrow' and 'A Natural Woman' for others before stepping out as a performer. Recorded in January 1971 at A&M's Studio B in Hollywood - concurrently with James Taylor's 'Mud Slide Slim,' using essentially the same band and even the same piano - 'Tapestry' was produced by her manager Lou Adler and captured with a deliberate live-in-the-room intimacy. Released February 10, 1971, it topped the Billboard chart for 15 consecutive weeks, remained on the charts for over six years, and became one of the best-selling albums in history (14x platinum in the US). It swept the 1972 Grammys, winning Album of the Year, Record of the Year ('It's Too Late'), Song of the Year ('You've Got a Friend'), and Best Female Pop Vocal Performance - King was the first woman to take all the top categories. Blending new material with reclaimed versions of her 60s classics ('Will You Love Me Tomorrow,' 'A Natural Woman'), the album defined the 1970s singer-songwriter movement and established the template for the confessional female singer-pianist. Its influence runs through generations of artists from Carly Simon to Adele, and it remains a permanent fixture on all-time greatest-album lists, preserved in the Library of Congress National Recording Registry.
albums.lpNotes: 1st issue (stereo, 1971) - Ode 70 tan/white label with '1416 N. La Brea' rim text; etched ODE-77017 side-1 matrix with 'PM' plant suffix per collector transcription.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the original Ode 70 label: off-white/tan stock with the silver-grey stylized '70' logo, 'SP-77009' catalog with matrix numbers (SP-77017)/(SP-77018) printed beneath, and the rim text 'DISTRIBUTED BY A&M RECORDS - 1416 N. LA BREA, HOLLYWOOD, CALIFORNIA 90028.' Lou Adler founded Ode in 1967 after selling Dunhill; A&M took over distribution in 1970, the label was briefly renamed 'Ode 70' in late 1970, and reverted to plain 'Ode' around November 1972. A&M's 1416 N. La Brea headquarters address appears in the rim text only until roughly 1972-73, when it was replaced by the P.O. Box 782, Beverly Hills address. The combination of the Ode 70 logo plus the La Brea rim text therefore brackets this copy in the 1971-72 first-issue window, at the top of the pressing hierarchy for this title.
albums.fidelity: The original lacquers for Tapestry are generally credited to Bernie Grundman, then chief mastering engineer at A&M, cut from Hank Cicalo's warm, dry, live-in-the-room analog tapes. Original US Ode pressings are the collector benchmark but are notorious for copy-to-copy variance - Better Records/Hot Stamper and forum consensus hold that most copies are dull, murky, or edgy, and a genuinely open, full-bodied early pressing is prized; the Positive Feedback comparison found the original somewhat mid-forward and rolled-off at the extremes. In the wider hierarchy, the 2013 Mobile Fidelity remaster (Krieg Wunderlich/Rob LoVerde) is widely considered a clear sonic improvement over the average original, with Grundman's 1999 Classic Records recut and the 2012 ORG 45rpm (Grundman/Bellman) as the other key audiophile alternatives; a clean, hot-stamper original Ode still competes with all of them and beats the mediocre majority.
albums.generalNotes: 1971 US first-issue Ode SP-77009 stereo gatefold, released February 10, 1971. Decisive evidence: the Ode 70 logo plus 'A&M Records - 1416 N. La Brea, Hollywood, California 90028' rim text - A&M switched to the Beverly Hills P.O. Box address c. 1972-73, so La Brea rim text marks the original issue; the gatefold with lyrics printed on the back cover and inner tapestry photo matches the original packaging. The transcribed runout 'ODE 177017 PM' corresponds to the SP-77017 side-1 matrix; the 'PM' suffix is associated in Discogs data with Columbia's Pitman, NJ plant, which pressed Ode/A&M product, though no dead-wax photo exists to confirm. This is not a rare record - it sold tens of millions - but it is the correct first-issue configuration.

albums.albumStory: Recorded on December 21, 1958 at Rudy Van Gelder's Hackensack studio and released the following year, Off to the Races arrived as trumpeter Donald Byrd was establishing himself as one of the era's most in-demand hard bop leaders and sidemen after his Detroit upbringing and stints with Art Blakey and Max Roach. The session pairs Byrd with a young, fiery Jackie McLean on alto and the underrated baritone specialist Pepper Adams, backed by a crack rhythm section of Wynton Kelly, Sam Jones, and Art Taylor, giving the record a harder, more aggressive edge than some of Byrd's later, more soul-jazz-leaning work. The program mixes a standard ("Lover") and a Sonny Rollins tune ("Paul's Pal") with four Byrd originals, including the boppish title track and the German-tinged blues "Sudwest Funk," named for a Southwest German radio station. Critically, the album is remembered as a solid, unpretentious showcase of late-1950s hard bop craftsmanship rather than a genre-defining statement, valued for its consistently strong blowing and the chemistry between Byrd, McLean, and Adams. It occupies a respected but modest place in Byrd's extensive Blue Note discography, appreciated by hard bop collectors for its personnel and unfussy, swinging character rather than for any singular historical breakthrough.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1959) - deep-groove 47 West 63rd Blue Note label without ® trademark, RVG + Plastylite ear stamps in the dead wax.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the earliest Blue Note 47 West 63rd label design: light-blue rim, white body, deep-groove pressing ring, and no ® trademark symbol next to the address, matching the label style Blue Note used from roughly 1956 into 1959 at its West 63rd Street office (the address the back cover also cites: "47 West 63rd St., New York 23"). Discogs variant tracking shows a nearly identical label used slightly later with a ® added to the 47 West 63rd text, which collectors treat as a second-state pressing; this copy lacks that mark, placing it ahead of that variant in the pressing sequence. The deep groove plus the RVG/Plastylite ear stamps documented in the runout confirm this is a true Van Gelder-cut, Plastylite-pressed New York original rather than the later Liberty-era reissues (Bert-Co labels, no ear) that followed from 1966 onward.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Rudy Van Gelder directly from his December 1958 mono session tapes and pressed by Plastylite (ear stamp), this is the top of the fidelity hierarchy for this title - warm, present horns and a tight, punchy rhythm section typical of Van Gelder's late-50s Hackensack mono cuts. Collectors on forums like Steve Hoffman generally rate original ear/RVG Blue Note mono pressings well above the later Liberty-era reissues, which used different mastering and lack the ear stamp, and well above generic 1970s-80s reissues; no major audiophile remaster (Music Matters, Tone Poet, Classic Records) of this specific title is documented, so the original RVG/ear pressing remains the reference standard. The G/G deep-groove vinyl grading on this particular copy, however, means actual playback surface noise will be well below what a clean example of this pressing can deliver.
albums.generalNotes: 1959 Blue Note BLP-4007 mono - earliest issue of this title. Deep-groove 47 West 63rd St. labels lacking the later-added ® trademark, combined with RVG and Plastylite ear stamps in the runout, place this among the first pressings before Liberty took over the catalog and issued Bert-Co labeled reissues from 1966 onward. No stereo mix of the original session exists, so mono is the only correct configuration for a period-authentic copy.

albums.albumStory: By 1973 Herbie Hancock - already a Blue Note star, Miles Davis alumnus, and composer of 'Watermelon Man' and 'Maiden Voyage' - had taken his sextet through the dense electric explorations of the Mwandishi trilogy on Warner Bros. Watching audiences walk out on that music while crowds erupted for funk acts like Sly Stone and the Pointer Sisters, Hancock made a deliberate turn toward groove, dissolving the septet and building a new band around retained reedman Bennie Maupin, Oakland bassist Paul Jackson, LA session drummer Harvey Mason, and New Orleans percussionist Bill Summers. Recorded in 1973 at Wally Heider Studios in San Francisco with producer David Rubinson and released October 26, 1973, Head Hunters delivered four long tracks: the anthemic 'Chameleon' built on Jackson's two-note bass line and Hancock's clavinet-as-bass-guitar; a reinvention of 'Watermelon Man' opened by Summers' hindewhu-and-beer-bottle imitation of Ba-Benzélé pygmy music; 'Sly,' a layered tribute to Sly Stone; and the brooding closer 'Vein Melter.' The album became a phenomenon - the first jazz LP certified platinum, reaching #13 pop, #2 R&B and #1 on the jazz chart, with an edited 'Chameleon' crossing over to radio and dance clubs. It effectively codified jazz-funk as a commercial language, and its grooves and textures have been sampled by generations of hip-hop producers, making it one of the most influential electric jazz records ever made.
albums.lpNotes: Sony-era reissue (c. 1998-2004) - red Columbia label with '© 1973 Sony Music Entertainment Inc.', KC 32731 + AL/BL label matrix, 3A recut lacquers; not a 1973 original.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the salmon/red Columbia reissue label: white 'COLUMBIA' arch at top, maroon print, label matrix 'KC 32731 / AL 32731' (side 1) and 'KC 32731 / BL 32731' (side 2), and the rim credit '© 1973 Sony Music Entertainment Inc.' CBS Records was renamed Sony Music Entertainment in January 1991, so any label with this credit postdates the CBS era (1973 originals and all 1970s-80s pressings read '© 1973 CBS, Inc.'); combined with the pre-Sony BMG branding, that fixes this copy to roughly 1998-2004. The typed runouts ('AL-32731-3A RJ 3' / 'BL32731-3A BT') are 3A recut lacquers rather than the 1A/1B first cuts found on 1973 pressings, confirming a reissue generation. A further fingerprint matches Discogs' documented Sony-era variant (r37313829): the anomalous A1 composer credit on the label ('Herbie Hancock-A. Willis-D. Rubinson-J. Cohen') that never appears on original labels, which credit Chameleon to Hancock/Jackson/Mason/Maupin. Note: the documented Discogs variant's runouts end in 'RML' while this copy's end 'RJ 3'/'BT', so a parallel pressing run of the same reissue is possible - a dead-wax photo would settle it.
albums.fidelity: The source recording - cut at Wally Heider Studios by Fred Catero and Jeremy Zatkin - is famously robust, with a huge, dry funk low end that flatters almost any pressing. This reissue uses uncredited 3A lacquers, almost certainly derived from Sony's 1990s remaster chain rather than a fresh all-analog cut, and collectors treat it as a serviceable but unexceptional modern pressing. The widely available 1973 US originals (Pitman/Terre Haute/Santa Maria, 1A/1B stampers) remain the value-for-sound benchmark: warm, punchy, and cheap. At the top of the fidelity hierarchy sit the all-analog Analogue Productions reissues mastered by Ryan K. Smith at Sterling from the original tapes (APJ 084 33rpm, 2015; APJ 084-45 2x45rpm, 2017, pressed at QRP), with the Speakers Corner 180g also well regarded; this Sony cut sits clearly below all of those.
albums.generalNotes: Early-2000s US Columbia reissue of KC 32731, not the 1973 first pressing. Decisive evidence: label rim credit reads '© 1973 Sony Music Entertainment Inc.' - a company name that did not exist before January 1991, whereas originals and all 1970s-80s pressings read '© 1973 CBS, Inc.' - and the typed runouts are 3A recut lacquers rather than the 1A/1B first-generation cuts. The anomalous A1 writer credit on the side 1 label (A. Willis/D. Rubinson/J. Cohen) exactly matches the documented Discogs Sony-era variant. One open point: that documented variant's runouts end in 'RML' while this copy's transcriptions end 'RJ 3'/'BT', so a sister pressing run of the same reissue is possible; a dead-wax photo would confirm.

albums.musicians: Kenny Burrell (guitar), Richard Wyands (piano), Martin Rivera (bass), Oliver Jackson (drums)

albums.albumStory: The jacket dates these sessions to April 1966 at RCA Recording Studios in New York, with producer Esmond Edwards presenting Kenny Burrell in a compact quartet setting. The program divides evenly between five Burrell originals and five outside songs, moving from the blues workout Mother-In-Law and Hot Bossa to People, Girl Talk, Erroll Garner's La Petite Mambo, and I'm Confessin'. Despite the romantic title and cover concept, this is not simply mood music: it folds blues, hard bop, bossa nova, and ballad playing into concise three-to-five-minute performances. Burrell, a Detroit musician who arrived in New York in 1956, was already one of the defining post-Charlie Christian jazz guitarists through his Blue Note, Prestige, and Verve recordings and his important work with Jimmy Smith. Midnight Blue and Guitar Forms had recently demonstrated both his popular reach and his orchestral sophistication; The Tender Gender applies those strengths to a leaner small-group format. The album reached Billboard's Top LPs chart in December 1966, peaking at No. 146 during a two-week run, and AllMusic later awarded it three stars. Its lasting reputation is that of an underrated Burrell favorite: less canonical than Midnight Blue or Guitar Forms, but a concentrated display of his melodic economy, blues attack, groove, and stylistic range.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1966) - US second-design blue-fade Cadet deep-groove labels; TR4M matrix, RCA Indianapolis branch.
albums.labelNotes: This copy has BSNPubs' second Cadet design: a light-blue field fading to white, black print, and CADET block letters shaded red, white, and blue; it followed the simpler solid light-blue/dark-blue inaugural Cadet label. Both labels are deep-groove and carry LP-772, MONOPHONIC, and the rim line MFG. BY CHESS PRODUCING CORP., CHICAGO, IL 60616. Chess renamed Argo as Cadet in 1965; the back cover's 2120 South Michigan Avenue address places production before Chess's 1968 move and well before the 1969 GRT sale and 1971 label consolidation. The typed TR4M-0394-1/S-1 and TR4M-0395-1D/S-2 core inscriptions match the Discogs US mono RCA Indianapolis entry, although that entry also records a stamped I in the dead wax that is absent from the supplied transcription; direct inspection of that stamp would provide final plant confirmation.
albums.fidelity: Ray Hall and Bob Simpson engineered the RCA Studios sessions; no separate LP mastering engineer is credited, but the TR4M codes are RCA's custom mono matrix series and this record was pressed at RCA Indianapolis. The 1966 US mono and stereo cuts occupy the top historical tier as the earliest analog LP presentations, although period Cadet/RCA sound is not usually ranked with Blue Note's Van Gelder pressings. Collector reports are mixed: one describes the US record as crystal clear, while another found both domestic vinyl and the 1983 Japanese reissue somewhat dull and compressed, with the Japanese copy possibly marginally better. The later US and Japanese reissues can provide quieter playing surfaces but have no established audiophile advantage. No dedicated Tone Poet, Analogue Productions, Music Matters, or Mobile Fidelity-style modern LP reissue is documented, leaving a clean original US pressing as the default benchmark; this G+ copy will be limited by groove wear regardless of the cut.

albums.albumStory: Pink Floyd developed The Dark Side Of The Moon as a complete live work during 1972 before recording it at Abbey Road between June 1972 and January 1973 with engineer Alan Parsons. Roger Waters deliberately moved the band away from a loose instrumental suite toward a unified song cycle about the pressures that distort human life: time, money, work, conflict, death and mental collapse. The breakdown of former member Syd Barrett shadowed the project, giving its examination of madness a personal rather than merely abstract dimension. Clocks, cash registers, tape loops, synthesizer sequences and interview fragments were integrated into the music as structural elements rather than decorative effects. Clare Torry improvised the celebrated vocal for The Great Gig In The Sky in only a few takes, initially believing that little of her performance would be usable. The album transformed Pink Floyd from a respected underground band into a global act and demonstrated that progressive rock could be conceptually ambitious while remaining concise and immediate. Its critical stature has continued to grow, and it remains a defining example of the album as an immersive, continuous artistic statement.
albums.lpNotes: Late US Harvest-label repress in third-issue packaging (stereo, c. 1983) - long Capitol Industries-EMI rim text, no barcode, Winchester ─◁ mark, Capitol ER G-99/G-79 cuts; probable undocumented double-Side-One mispress.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the US black Harvest prism label with white lettering, boxed Harvest logo, and the long 'Mfd. by Capitol Records, Inc., a subsidiary of Capitol Industries-EMI, Inc.' rim text with the 'All Rights Reserved / Unauthorized duplication' warning and no U.S. Pat. No. 2,631,859 - the third-issue design introduced in September 1975 when Capitol updated its corporate credit. The matching back cover prints SMAS 11163 at top center with no barcode, confirming third-issue packaging rather than the barcode-bearing fourth (c. 1980-81) or rainbow-label fifth (July 1983) issues. However, the typed runouts pair G-99 with G-79 ER cuts, and pinkfloydarchives.com documents G-79 Winchester metal in July 1983 groupings, so this is a late pressing assembled from old-stock third-issue labels and jacket - consistent with the transitional 1983 Winchester Harvest-label variant documented on Discogs. Both side labels print SIDE ONE with the identical track listing, an apparent factory labeling error that the two SMAS-1- matrix transcriptions reinforce.
albums.fidelity: The G-99/G-79 ER cuts are late Capitol Mastering lacquers, not the sought-after 1973 F-series Wally Traugott, Ken Perry or Gene Thompson cuts; the ER attribution remains unresolved and should not be equated with Eddy Schreyer's documented E/ES mark. Winchester pressings of this era are generally quiet and serviceable, but collector consensus ranks later US Capitol cuts below the UK Harvest SHVL 804 original and the best early US pressings. In the broader fidelity hierarchy, the 1979 Mobile Fidelity Stan Ricker half-speed, the 2003 Doug Sax/Kevin Gray edition, the 2016 Bernie Grundman remaster and the 2023 Analogue Productions UHQR all sit well above this routine Capitol repress. This copy's G-grade surface wear will overwhelm subtler mastering differences, and if both faces contain Side One it cannot serve as a complete listening copy.

albums.albumStory: The Wall grew out of Roger Waters' alienation on Pink Floyd's 1977 In The Flesh tour, when he spat at a fan pressing against the stage barrier and afterwards imagined literally walling himself off from the audience. Written almost entirely by Waters as a semi-autobiographical rock opera about Pink, a rock star whose dead wartime father, smothering mother, brutal schoolmasters and failed marriage become the bricks of a psychological wall, it drew directly on Waters' own loss of his father at Anzio and his English postwar boyhood. Recorded through 1979 in France and Los Angeles amid the band's tax exile and near-terminal internal warfare, the sessions saw Richard Wright dismissed and co-producer Bob Ezrin brought in to shape the sprawl into a narrative, pushing the disco-inflected arrangement and children's choir that turned "Another Brick In The Wall Part 2" into an unlikely worldwide number one. David Gilmour's contributions - above all the two solos on "Comfortably Numb," written to a Waters lyric about being medicated before a show - supplied the album's emotional release against Waters' bleakness. It stands as the last Pink Floyd album made by the classic four-piece and the peak of Waters' authorial control, the point where the band's post-Dark Side ambitions became fully theatrical, later realized in the wall-building stadium shows and Alan Parker's film. Contemporary critics were split between admiration for its scale and unease at its self-pity, but the album's stature only grew: it remains one of the best-selling records ever made and the touchstone concept album of its era. Its themes of isolation, authoritarianism and the corrosion of celebrity gave rock a template for the album-length personal epic that artists still work from.
albums.lpNotes: 1st US press (stereo, Dec 1979) - Columbia PC2 36183, Terre Haute plant ('T1' runouts); TML (The Mastering Lab / Doug Sax) stamps on all four sides; no-barcode first-issue gatefold with abbreviated inner credits.
albums.labelNotes: The labels are the custom 1979 US Columbia picture design created for this album: a white brick-wall field with Gerald Scarfe's hand-lettered 'PINK FLOYD THE WALL' and handwritten-style track listings, a different Scarfe character vignette per side (marching hammer/teacher, flower, doll, judge), the Columbia 'walking eye' box logo and 'Marca Reg.' rim text with © 1979 Pink Floyd Music Ltd. / Pink Floyd Music Publishers Ltd. credits. In 1979 Columbia was the CBS flagship US label, and Pink Floyd had moved from Harvest/Capitol to Columbia in the US with Animals (1977), so The Wall appeared on Columbia from day one - there is no earlier US label incarnation of this title. The picture-label design with the abbreviated one-line CBS manufacturing credit and the no-barcode sleeve marks the November/December 1979 first-issue window; the 1982+ repress added a rear barcode and expanded gatefold credits. This places the copy squarely in the original first-issue hierarchy, which the Terre Haute 'T1' plant marks and TML metalwork in the runouts corroborate.
albums.fidelity: Cut by Doug Sax at The Mastering Lab from the Guthrie/Gilmour tapes; having TML stamps on all four sides is the best case for a US copy, as many Columbia sets mix TML lacquers with later in-house recuts. Steve Hoffman forum and collector consensus rates the all-TML US pressing among the best-sounding editions of the album - open, punchy, wide dynamics, less compressed than mid-1980s repressings - and some listeners prefer it even to the UK Harvest SHDW 411 first press. Terre Haute 1979 pressing quality was generally good, though surface noise is the usual lottery, so quiet all-TML copies command the premium. Hierarchy: the UK Harvest first press and this US all-TML cut head the vintage tier, ahead of Pitman/Santa Maria recut sides and well ahead of the 1982 barcode repress; among moderns the 2016 Bernie Grundman/Pink Floyd Records remaster is well regarded and can beat a noisy original, and no Analogue Productions/Classic Records-class all-analogue audiophile LP exists to displace this cut.
albums.generalNotes: 1979 Columbia PC2 36183 US stereo - original first pressing from Columbia's Terre Haute, Indiana plant ('T1' in all four runouts), matching the Discogs 'Terre Haute Press, First Sleeve' variant. All four sides carry P-prefixed PAL/PBL lacquer numbers with TML stamps (S / X / S / M) - a complete set of Doug Sax Mastering Lab metalwork, the configuration collectors look for since many copies mix TML and later recut sides; the typed 'PAL-3184/3185' numbers read as PAL-36184/36185, matching the disc catalog numbers. The jacket is the first sleeve: no rear barcode, only the small Columbia logo box with the one-line manufacturing credit on the back cover. Labels are the correct 1979 brick/Scarfe-character picture design with no promo wording, so this is a retail copy. The handwritten name inside the gatefold reads as an owner inscription, not a band autograph - no signature exemplar match.

albums.albumStory: Wish You Were Here was recorded at Abbey Road between January and July 1975, with the band exhausted and creatively becalmed in the wake of the runaway global success of The Dark Side Of The Moon. Roger Waters shaped the record around the twin themes of absence and the corrosion of the music business, anchoring it with 'Shine On You Crazy Diamond', an elegy for Syd Barrett built on David Gilmour's four-note guitar phrase; the most famous story of the sessions is Barrett's unannounced arrival at the studio in June 1975, overweight and unrecognisable, while the band mixed the very song written about him. 'Welcome To The Machine' and 'Have A Cigar' are direct satires of the record industry, the latter sung by folk singer Roy Harper - who was recording in an adjacent studio - after Waters and Gilmour both struggled with the vocal. The title track's acoustic lament, framed by a car radio and a fake AM-radio guitar intro, became one of rock's most quoted songs of loss. The album marks the point where Pink Floyd shifted from studio-conceptual spectacle toward Waters' increasingly personal, embittered writing, the path that would lead to Animals and The Wall. It topped the charts in both the US and UK on release and, after mixed initial reviews from critics who found it thin next to Dark Side, was steadily re-evaluated as the band's most emotionally direct statement. Gilmour and Wright both named it their favourite Pink Floyd album, and it remains a cornerstone of progressive rock and one of the great records about friendship, disappearance and disillusion.
albums.lpNotes: Early US first-issue pressing (stereo, 1975-77) - Columbia PC 33453 custom handshake labels, no-barcode jacket; A-side lacquer AL 33453-1C with HTM (Harry T. Moss) etched, B-side BL 33453-3C; metalwork matches the documented Santa Maria pressing family, no plant mark in the transcription.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the custom die-cut 'mechanical handshake' labels (robotic arms, Hipgnosis/George Hardie artwork) unique to this title, with the PC 33453 stereo catalog number, AL 33453 / BL 33453 matrix numbers, (P)/(C) 1975 Pink Floyd Music Limited credits and a 'Marcas Reg. Printed in U.S.A.' rim. Wish You Were Here was Pink Floyd's first US release on Columbia after leaving Harvest, and the 1975 first issue paired these custom labels with a no-barcode jacket sealed in black opaque shrink with a round sticker, plus a printed lyric inner and Hipgnosis postcard. Columbia moved to barcoded jackets on late-1970s represses and dropped the custom label entirely when the title shifted to the JC 33453 prefix on standard Columbia labels in the 1980s. This label/jacket combination therefore anchors the copy firmly in the original 1975-77 first-issue window, ahead of every subsequent US variant.
albums.fidelity: The 'HTM' etch is Harry T. Moss, EMI's mastering engineer at Abbey Road, who cut the original UK SHVL 814 lacquers - its presence on this US Columbia means the American metalwork derives from Moss's cut, which is why early PC 33453 copies are praised on forums.stevehoffman.tv for warmth, weight and an easy top end versus the thinner late-'70s represses and 1980s JC/plain-label copies. Pressing quality on early Columbia stock is decent but variable, and the plant here is unconfirmed. In the album's fidelity hierarchy this sits just below the UK Harvest SHVL 814 first pressing (the vintage reference cut, from the same Moss lineage) and roughly level with the best US originals, ahead of all later standard US repressings. The 1981 CBS Mastersound half-speed and the 2016 Bernie Grundman-cut reissue offer quieter surfaces and more modern detail, but the Moss-derived cut remains the satisfying vintage analogue choice.
albums.generalNotes: 1975 Columbia PC 33453 stereo - early US first-issue pressing, not a later repress. The decisive evidence: custom die-cut handshake labels with the PC prefix, a back cover with no barcode, and first-generation A-side metalwork AL 33453-1C etched 'HTM' (Harry T. Moss's EMI cut) with B-side BL 33453-3C from the same first-issue family. The Discogs Santa Maria variant lists this exact AL-33453-1C/HTM and BL-33453-3C combination, making Santa Maria the likely plant, but no stamped plant mark appears in the typed runout transcription, so the plant attribution stays probable rather than confirmed. The printed lyric inner sleeve is present; the original black shrink/sticker are gone and the Hipgnosis postcard's status is unconfirmed from the photos.

albums.albumStory: Recorded over three sessions in January 1955 at Fine Sound in New York, this project paired trumpeter Clifford Brown with a nine-piece string section arranged and conducted by Neal Hefti, produced for EmArcy by Bob Shad. Rather than showcasing the fiery bebop lines that had made his reputation, Brown here plays as a melodic balladeer, drawing on twelve songbook standards by Kern, Rodgers and Hart, Gershwin, and Carmichael among others, with his working rhythm section of Max Roach, Richie Powell, George Morrow, and guitarist Barry Galbraith supporting rather than soloing. albums.lpNotes: 1st press (US mono, 1955) - blue/silver EmArcy big-drummer deep-groove labels and blue-back jacket; typed YMG36005A runout.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the blue EmArcy 'big-drummer' label in silver ink, showing the drummer pouring paint onto a cymbal logo once (not the later small-drummer redesign), a deep groove pressed near the label edge, and curved rim text reading LONG PLAYING HIGH FIDELITY / MERCURY RECORD CORPORATION / MADE IN U.S.A. This large-drummer, deep-groove EmArcy design is the label company's earliest 12-inch jazz-series look, used circa 1954-56 before Mercury shrank the drummer graphic and eventually moved to the EmArcy Jazz oval-logo label in 1958. Discogs collectors confirm the blue-printed (not black) back cover as the decisive first-issue marker for MG-36000-series titles through early 1956, and this copy's back cover print matches that blue-ink first state, placing it at the top of the pressing hierarchy for this title.
albums.fidelity: This is an original-era mono cut from the January 1955 Fine Sound session tape; neither the jacket nor the supplied matrix identifies the cutting engineer, and the incomplete runout transcription prevents a firm mother/stamper/plant attribution. A clean first US pressing remains the fidelity benchmark, delivering strong center-image presence for Brown's trumpet and a warm, if narrow-bandwidth, mono blend with the small string group. Later 1950s drummer-label and Mercury EmArcy Jazz oval-label copies are acceptable period alternatives but rank below this blue-back first pressing among collectors. The best-documented modern alternative is Universal Japan's 2004 UCJU-9012, remastered from the original cutting-master tape by Joseph M. Palmaccio on 180g vinyl; no Tone Poet, Music Matters, Analogue Productions, or Speakers Corner edition of this title exists.
